properties.heading: Agent-native by design
properties.text: What does it mean for a database to be agent-native? An agent reads every byte a command prints, pays for each one in its context window, and decides its next step from the result alone. relate's CLI is built for that reader: it prints results in shapes a model can parse, reports failures as typed objects with stable exit codes, keeps large results from flooding the context, and notices when an [agent harness](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#agent-harness) is running it. The skill and the [MCP](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#mcp) surface carry the same contract to agents that never open a shell.

properties.heading: The loop
properties.text:
An agent runs a statement, reads what comes back, and decides: use the rows, fix the statement, or retry. Each piece of the design shortens one turn of that loop. ```mermaid flowchart TB accTitle: The agent loop around relate accDescr { An agent sends a statement to relate, through the CLI or an MCP tool. relate answers with a result envelope, or with an error object and an exit code. On rows, the agent uses them; on an error it fixes the statement, and it retries only when the error says retryable. The skill and agent-context give the agent the commands and flags before the first turn. } K["Skill and agent-context"] -.-> A["Agent"] A -->|"statement"| R["relate: CLI or MCP tool"] R -->|"rows"| V["Envelope: columns, types,
rows, truncated"] R -->|"failure"| X["Error object: code, kind,
retryable, exit code"] V -->|"use the rows"| A X -->|"fix, or retry if retryable"| A ``` An agent sends a statement to relate, through the CLI or an MCP tool. relate answers with a result envelope, or with an error object and an exit code. On rows, the agent uses them; on an error it fixes the statement, and it retries only when the error says retryable. The skill and agent-context give the agent the commands and flags before the first turn. **Shapes a model can parse.** `--mode envelope` prints one JSON object per result set. The [envelope](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#envelope) keeps the column list even when there are no rows, so "no rows" never reads as "no output". `columnTypes` gives one type per column, taken from the first row, so an empty result reports `ANY`. The envelope also carries the query notifications. When stdout is piped, the default is one JSON object per row (`jsonl`). **Typed failures.** A failed statement prints its message on stderr and exits with the [exit code](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#exit-code) of its class: 6 for a statement the engine rejected, 5 for a conflict or a locked store, 7 for a timeout. In the JSON modes it also prints an error object on stdout whose `code`, `kind` and `retryable` fields an agent branches on without parsing prose. `retryable` is `true` for a write-write conflict and for a `--concurrent-logical-workspace-limit` refusal while other statements hold the workspace pool, so an agent never loops on an error that cannot succeed. **A row cap.** One statement that returns every node of a large graph can fill a context window. Under a detected agent harness with stdout not a terminal, the CLI prints at most 100 rows per statement and says so in-band. Here the same cut is forced with `--max-rows 2`: ```bash verify relate --mode envelope --max-rows 2 "UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name" ``` The first line is the warning on stderr; the envelope on stdout names both counts: ```text warning: result truncated to 2 rows (the statement returned 3); pass --max-rows 0 for all rows {"columnTypes":["STRING"],"columns":["name"],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rowCap":{"kept":2,"total":3},"rows":[{"name":"Ada"},{"name":"Grace"}],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":0.678416,"execute_ms":0.5296660000000001,"lex_parse_ms":0.023083,"lower_ms":0.032458,"parse_ms":0.098,"plan_ms":0.041625,"result_generation_ms":0.00041600000000000003,"rewrite_ms":0.007083},"truncated":true} ``` **Harness detection.** relate turns on [agent mode](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#agent-mode) when it sees an agent harness's environment variable, such as `CLAUDECODE` or `CURSOR_AGENT`, and stdout is not a terminal. Agent mode sets two defaults: the 100-row cap, and TOON as the piped output: one header line, then one line per row, then the statement's timings and plan-cache outcome. The same statement, run plainly and then as Claude Code would run it; both modes close with the [timing record](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/output-modes/#timings-and-the-plan-cache): ```bash verify relate "UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name" CLAUDECODE=1 relate "UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name" ``` ```text {"name":"Ada"} {"name":"Grace"} {"name":"Noor"} rows[3]{name}: Ada Grace Noor timings: {"elapsed_ms":0.38104099999999996,"execute_ms":0.222542,"lex_parse_ms":0.024708,"lower_ms":0.034208999999999996,"parse_ms":0.10475,"plan_ms":0.043292,"result_generation_ms":0.0005,"rewrite_ms":0.007500000000000001} planCache: miss ``` Detection changes output only. It never gates writes and never turns on `--safe`; those stay explicit choices, because a heuristic that changed what a statement may do would make the same command mean different things in different terminals. **Facts from the binary.** `relate agent-context` prints the commands, flags and exit codes of the binary that is installed, so the briefing cannot describe another version. The skill, relate's cheat sheet for agents, ships inside the binary, and `relate skill install` copies it into each detected agent's skills folder. **MCP.** `relate serve --database --read-only --mcp stdio` serves one store to an agent host as two tools, `read_cypher` and `get_schema`; without `--read-only` it also lists `write_cypher`. A result is one JSON object with the `rows`, `columns`, `columnTypes` and `notifications` the envelope has, plus `stats`, the `plan` and timings; it has no `truncated` or `rowCap` field. The server classifies each statement from its plan before running it, so `read_cypher` refuses a write with `Only MATCH queries are allowed for read-query`. Internal failures reach the host as `Error: internal error`, so engine detail stays out of tool-call logs. The terminal and the tryout below run on an empty database in this page, opened by the engine the page loads. The terminal takes this statement, the one in the row-cap and harness examples: ```cypher run name=names UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name ``` ```table | name | |---------| | "Ada" | | "Grace" | | "Noor" | 3 rows ``` It prints the statement as relate does in four output modes, `table`, `envelope`, `jsonl` and `toon`, with the exit code, and opens on TOON with "Run as an agent harness" on, as Claude Code runs it; its 250-row preset shows the cap. The tryout sends the MCP tools: `read_cypher` with the same statement, the same tool with a `CREATE`, which the plan check refuses before it runs, then `write_cypher` and `get_schema`. Each reply carries the plan, the notifications and the timings of its own run, and no `truncated` or `rowCap`. ```json data=mcp-calls {"calls": [ {"tool": "read_cypher", "arguments": {"statement": "UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name"}}, {"tool": "read_cypher", "arguments": {"statement": "CREATE (:Person {name: $name})", "parameters": {"name": "Ada"}}}, {"tool": "write_cypher", "arguments": {"statement": "CREATE (:Person {name: $name})", "parameters": {"name": "Ada"}}}, {"tool": "get_schema", "arguments": {}} ]} ``` The statement as relate 1.0.1 prints it in four of its output modes under an agent harness (`CLAUDECODE=1`), rendered from this page's recorded result by the terminal's renderers, which match the relate 1.0.1 binary byte for byte on the recorded runs, timing values aside. The recording keeps no timings, so each one shows as ``; relate prints the milliseconds of its own run, and the live terminal prints the engine's. Exit code 0, as relate 1.0.1 returns it. `--mode table` prints seven lines on stdout: ```bash CLAUDECODE=1 relate --read-only --mode table "UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name" ``` ```text +---------+ | name | +---------+ | "Ada" | | "Grace" | | "Noor" | +---------+ ``` `--mode envelope` prints one line on stdout: ```bash CLAUDECODE=1 relate --read-only --mode envelope "UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name" ``` ```text {"columnTypes":["STRING"],"columns":["name"],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[{"name":"Ada"},{"name":"Grace"},{"name":"Noor"}],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":,"execute_ms":,"lex_parse_ms":,"lower_ms":,"parse_ms":,"plan_ms":,"result_generation_ms":,"rewrite_ms":},"truncated":false} ``` `--mode jsonl` prints three lines on stdout: ```bash CLAUDECODE=1 relate --read-only --mode jsonl "UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name" ``` ```text {"name":"Ada"} {"name":"Grace"} {"name":"Noor"} ``` `--mode toon` prints eight lines on stdout: ```bash CLAUDECODE=1 relate --read-only --mode toon "UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name" ``` ```text rows[3]{name}: Ada Grace Noor timings: {"elapsed_ms":,"execute_ms":,"lex_parse_ms":,"lower_ms":,"parse_ms":,"plan_ms":,"result_generation_ms":,"rewrite_ms":} planCache: miss ``` Under a detected agent harness, relate prints at most 100 rows per statement; this statement returns three rows, so the cap leaves it whole. Live: the statement runs in your browser on an empty read-only database, as `relate --read-only` opens one, and the pane shows what relate prints in the mode you pick, with the exit code and, under "Run as an agent harness", the row cap; the statement can be edited or swapped for a preset. These calls ran when the page was recorded, on a database that holds what this page's cells write, through the same mapping the live tryout uses. Timings show as ``; live, each reply carries the timings of its own run. The server lists `write_cypher`, `read_cypher`, `get_schema`. **`read_cypher`**: the request a host sends, then the reply. ```json {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"read_cypher","arguments":{"statement":"UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name"}}} ``` ```json {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"content":[{"text":"{\"columnTypes\":[\"STRING\"],\"columns\":[\"name\"],\"elapsed_ms\":,\"error\":null,\"execute_ms\":,\"lex_parse_ms\":,\"lower_ms\":,\"notifications\":[],\"parse_ms\":,\"plan\":{\"profiled\":false,\"root\":{\"actual\":null,\"children\":[{\"actual\":null,\"children\":[],\"details\":\"AS name\",\"estimated_rows\":null,\"identifiers\":[\"name\"],\"operator\":\"Unwind\",\"warnings\":[]}],\"details\":\"1 item(s)\",\"estimated_rows\":null,\"identifiers\":[],\"operator\":\"ProduceResults\",\"warnings\":[]},\"schema\":\"relate.plan/v1\",\"statement\":\"UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name\"},\"plan_cache\":\"hit-raw-fastpath\",\"plan_ms\":,\"result_generation_ms\":,\"rewrite_ms\":,\"rows\":[{\"name\":\"Ada\"},{\"name\":\"Grace\"},{\"name\":\"Noor\"}],\"stats\":{\"constraints_added\":0,\"constraints_removed\":0,\"indexes_added\":0,\"indexes_removed\":0,\"labels_added\":0,\"labels_removed\":0,\"nodes_created\":0,\"nodes_deleted\":0,\"properties_set\":0,\"relationships_created\":0,\"relationships_deleted\":0}}","type":"text"}],"isError":false}} ``` | name | | ----- | | Ada | | Grace | | Noor | **`read_cypher`** with a write: the plan's operators read as query type `w`, so the server refuses the call before it runs. The request a host sends, then the reply: ```json {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"read_cypher","arguments":{"statement":"CREATE (:Person {name: $name})","parameters":{"name":"Ada"}}}} ``` ```json {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"content":[{"text":"Only MATCH queries are allowed for read-query","type":"text"}],"isError":true}} ``` Tool error: `Only MATCH queries are allowed for read-query`. **`write_cypher`**: the request a host sends, then the reply. ```json {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"write_cypher","arguments":{"statement":"CREATE (:Person {name: $name})","parameters":{"name":"Ada"}}}} ``` ```json {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"result":{"content":[{"text":"{\"columnTypes\":[],\"columns\":[],\"elapsed_ms\":,\"error\":null,\"execute_ms\":,\"lex_parse_ms\":,\"lower_ms\":,\"notifications\":[],\"parse_ms\":,\"plan\":{\"profiled\":false,\"root\":{\"actual\":null,\"children\":[],\"details\":\"(:Person)\",\"estimated_rows\":null,\"identifiers\":[],\"operator\":\"Create\",\"warnings\":[]},\"schema\":\"relate.plan/v1\",\"statement\":\"CREATE (:Person {name: $name})\"},\"plan_cache\":\"miss\",\"plan_ms\":,\"result_generation_ms\":,\"rewrite_ms\":,\"rows\":[],\"stats\":{\"constraints_added\":0,\"constraints_removed\":0,\"indexes_added\":0,\"indexes_removed\":0,\"labels_added\":1,\"labels_removed\":0,\"nodes_created\":1,\"nodes_deleted\":0,\"properties_set\":1,\"relationships_created\":0,\"relationships_deleted\":0}}","type":"text"}],"isError":false}} ``` Counters: `nodes_created` 1, `properties_set` 1, `labels_added` 1; `rows` is empty, as `write_cypher` returns counters. **`get_schema`**: the request a host sends, then the reply. ```json {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_schema","arguments":{}}} ``` ```json {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"result":{"content":[{"text":"{\"Person\":{\"count\":1,\"properties\":{\"name\":{\"type\":\"String\"}},\"type\":\"node\"}}","type":"text"}],"isError":false}} ``` | Label | Nodes | Properties | Relationships out | | ------ | ----- | ------------- | ----------------- | | Person | 1 | name (String) | - | **`write_cypher` on a server started `--read-only`**: it lists only `read_cypher` and `get_schema`, and answers a `write_cypher` call with a tool error before the engine sees the statement. This run is recorded from relate 1.0.1 (errors.json `mcp-unknown-tool`, replayed against the binary by `docs:cli-check`); the page quotes it as the binary printed it: ```bash printf '%s\n' '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"check","version":"0"}}}' '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}' '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"write_cypher","arguments":{"query":"CREATE (:B)"}}}' | relate serve --mcp stdio --database ./graph.rl --read-only ``` ```text {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"capabilities":{"tools":{}},"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","serverInfo":{"name":"relate-mcp","version":"1.0.1"}}} {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"content":[{"text":"unknown tool 'write_cypher'","type":"text"}],"isError":true}} ``` Transport answers (HTTP 401, 403 and 415, the body cap, the header deadline) are not part of the tryout; the [MCP server reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/server/mcp/#errors-and-refusals) lists them. Live: each call is a button that sends its `tools/call` request to the page's database in your browser and shows the request and the reply, built from the engine's result the way `relate serve --mcp` builds it, with the statement and parameters editable; "Serve read-only" drops `write_cypher` from the tool list, as `--read-only` does, and shows the engine's own refusal of the write on a read-only database beside the server's recorded answer.

properties.heading: What it costs
properties.text:
| Choice                                     | What it buys                                                                       | What it costs                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Row cap under a harness                    | A runaway result cannot flood the context                                          | The engine still computes the whole result; the cap bounds printing, not work. A Cypher `LIMIT` bounds the work                                                                                                                          |
| TOON as the piped default under agent mode | Fewer bytes per row than JSON                                                      | TOON is not JSON. A tool that expects one JSON object per row gets it with `--mode jsonl` (or `--no-agent-mode`), with one timing line per statement when `--timings` is set; `--mode envelope` gives one JSON object per result set     |
| Detection from environment variables       | No flag to remember inside a harness                                               | A variable set for another reason turns agent mode on; `--no-agent-mode` or `RELATE_AGENT_MODE=0` turns it off. Detection is silent, so the same command prints differently inside and outside a harness unless `--mode` pins the output |
| The skill as a copy in each agent's folder | The agent reads relate's rules before its first command                            | A copy can fall behind the binary after an upgrade; `relate skill check` exits 1 when an installed copy differs                                                                                                                          |
| MCP classification before execution        | A read tool, annotated `readOnlyHint`, that cannot change the graph or its indexes | One extra planning pass per call                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

The other path was to leave agents with the human table and free-text errors, and let each harness parse them. That puts the parsing in every agent's prompt and the failures in every agent's context. relate puts it in the binary once, where it can be tested.

properties.heading: Architecture
properties.text: How is relate put together? It is one engine written in Rust, with every front door wrapped around it. A statement is parsed, bound against the catalog, planned, and executed against a graph held in memory; each commit goes to a write-ahead log on its way in. The CLI, the language clients, the browser build and the network servers all call the same `relate::Database`, so a statement means the same thing through each of them.

properties.heading: A large graph in a browser tab
properties.text:
The graph lives in the memory of the process that opens the store, and in a browser that process is the tab running the WebAssembly build. The three cells in this section build a tree and read it back: node `i`, from 1 up, is the child of node `(i - 1) / 2`, which makes it a binary tree as shallow as its size allows. They take `n`, the number of nodes, and `start`, the node the walk begins at, from this block:

```json data=tree
{"n": 1000, "start": 1}
```

The first cell writes `n` nodes labelled `Item` and joins each one, except node 0, to its parent with a `CHILD_OF` relationship:

```cypher run name=tree-build params=tree
UNWIND range(0, $n - 1) AS i
CREATE (item:Item {i: i})
WITH collect(item) AS items
UNWIND range(1, size(items) - 1) AS i
WITH items[i] AS child, items[(i - 1) / 2] AS parent
CREATE (child)-[:CHILD_OF]->(parent)
RETURN count(*) AS relationships
```

```table
| relationships |
|---------------|
| 999           |
1 row · nodes created: 1000, relationships created: 999, properties set: 1000, labels added: 1000
```

The second counts the nodes and the relationships between them:

```cypher run name=tree-count
MATCH (item:Item)
OPTIONAL MATCH (item)-[r:CHILD_OF]->()
RETURN count(item) AS nodes, count(r) AS relationships
```

```table
| nodes | relationships |
|-------|---------------|
| 1000  | 999           |
1 row
```

The third follows every chain of `CHILD_OF` relationships that ends at node `start`, and counts the nodes it reaches:

```cypher run name=tree-walk params=tree
MATCH (:Item {i: $start})<-[:CHILD_OF*]-(descendant:Item)
RETURN count(descendant) AS descendants
```

```table
| descendants |
|-------------|
| 510         |
1 row
```

The scale demo runs the same three cells with `n` up to 100,000, on a database of its own, and shows what each returns and how long the engine took. Nothing runs until **Build the tree** is pressed; the tree then holds memory in the tab until **Free** closes the demo's engine.

The scale demo runs cells `tree-build`, `tree-count` and `tree-walk` again with `n` set to 1,000, 10,000 or 100,000, on an in-memory database of its own in the browser tab: a second copy of the engine, so the page's database never holds the large graph. `tree-build` creates the tree, `tree-count` counts its nodes and relationships, and `tree-walk` follows every chain of relationships down from one node. It shows each cell's first row and the time the engine took, beside the cell's recording. It offers 100,000 nodes first on a wide screen and 10,000 on a narrow one, says how much memory the second engine holds, and closes that engine on Free, on the engine bar's Reset, and when the page is left.

| Cell         | Recorded on this page, with `n` = 1,000 |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| `tree-build` | relationships: 999                      |
| `tree-count` | nodes: 1,000, relationships: 999        |
| `tree-walk`  | descendants: 510                        |

Live: a button runs the three cells again at the size picked (the largest by default, the middle size on a narrow screen) on a separate in-memory database in your browser, apart from the page's database, and shows each cell's result and engine time; a second button runs the count and the walk again from a node you name; it shows how much memory that database's engine holds; Free closes it and returns the memory.

properties.heading: A statement's path
properties.text:
The parser turns Cypher text into a syntax tree, and a front end lowers it into the planner's own representation. Binding resolves labels, relationship types, properties and variables against the catalog without running anything, which is where an undefined variable fails; a missing parameter fails when the statement runs, not under `EXPLAIN`. The planner then produces a logical plan, and the executor runs that plan against the graph as of the statement's pinned commit.

The cells below follow one statement through the pipeline on the shared example graph, in this page's database. The first writes the graph:

```cypher run name=seed
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace)
```

```table
(no rows) · nodes created: 5, relationships created: 5, properties set: 13, labels added: 5
```

`EXPLAIN` stops after the planner: the statement is parsed, bound and planned, and the logical plan comes back without being executed.

```cypher run name=plan
EXPLAIN MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Ada'})-[:WORKS_ON]->(r:Project) RETURN r.name AS project
```

```table
(no rows)
```

The plan viewer shows that plan. In a browser it draws the operator tree; **PROFILE** executes the plan and adds what each operator did, and **Compare with the index** shows the planner choosing another start once a range index exists.

The plan recorded for cell `plan`, as `relate --mode table` prints it:

```text
Query: MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Ada'})-[:WORKS_ON]->(r:Project) RETURN r.name AS project
Plan:
+------------------+----+-------------------------------------+
| Operator         | Id | Details                             |
+------------------+----+-------------------------------------+
| + ProduceResults | 0  | 1 item(s)                           |
+------------------+----+-------------------------------------+
| | + Expand       | 1  | (r:Project)<-[:WORKS_ON]-(p:Person) |
+------------------+----+-------------------------------------+
Notifications:
Id 1: INFORMATION 03C91 Relate.Notification.Statement.MissingIndex: the equality predicate on name filters :Person without a range index on (:Person {name}) Remedy: CREATE INDEX relate_Person__name FOR (n:Person) ON (n.name)
```

Notifications, each with its remedy:

- [`03C91` Missing index](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/#notif-03c91) on operator 1: the equality predicate on name filters :Person without a range index on (:Person {name}). Remedy: `CREATE INDEX relate_Person__name FOR (n:Person) ON (n.name)`

In a browser, the viewer's comparison runs `CREATE INDEX relate_Person__name FOR (n:Person) ON (n.name)` on the page's in-memory database only.

Live: the plan is drawn as a tree, and PROFILE runs the statement on the page's database in your browser and adds each operator's rows, time and database hits as bars; the index button creates the index on the page's database, plans the statement with and without it side by side with the changes, and drops it again; a PROFILE downloads as a speedscope file.

Without a prefix, the same statement goes through all three phases. After a run in your browser, the bar under the result splits the engine's elapsed time into parse, plan and execute:

```cypher run name=run timing
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Ada'})-[:WORKS_ON]->(r:Project) RETURN r.name AS project
```

```table
| project  |
|----------|
| "relate" |
1 row
```

**The in-memory graph.** Labels, relationship types and property keys are interned, so each is stored once and compared as a number. Each node keeps its relationships in lists split by type, so expanding over `[:WORKS_ON]` walks only that type's list. A change installs a new version of the node or relationship stamped with its commit, which is how readers keep a consistent view while writers work; [transactions and concurrency](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/transactions-and-concurrency/) covers that model. Disk holds the durable copy, and queries never scan it.

**The planner.** It validates the statement, then rewrites each `MATCH`: equality predicates fold into the pattern so they can seek, and the start of each pattern and the order of comma-separated patterns come from estimates the graph keeps: label counts and index entries. Other clauses run in the order written. `EXPLAIN` shows the result without running the statement.

**Indexes.** Label lookups and the typed relationship lists come with the graph. `CREATE INDEX` adds a range index on a label and property, which equality and range predicates seek through; vector and full-text indexes serve the `SEARCH` clause, and point indexes serve spatial predicates. The planner notices a missing range index and says so. One command on `:memory:`, the default store, shows the difference and writes nothing to disk: it creates the example graph, explains a statement, adds a range index on `:Person(name)`, and explains the same statement again:

```bash verify
relate --mode table "CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace);
EXPLAIN MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Ada'})-[:WORKS_ON]->(r:Project) RETURN r.name AS project;
CREATE INDEX person_name FOR (p:Person) ON (p.name);
EXPLAIN MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Ada'})-[:WORKS_ON]->(r:Project) RETURN r.name AS project"
```

The first plan has no index to use: it starts from `:Project`, which has fewer nodes, walks back to `:Person`, and the [notification](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#notification) names the index that would help. The second plan seeks Ada through the new index and estimates one row:

```text
Query: MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Ada'})-[:WORKS_ON]->(r:Project) RETURN r.name AS project
Plan:
+------------------+----+-------------------------------------+
| Operator         | Id | Details                             |
+------------------+----+-------------------------------------+
| + ProduceResults | 0  | 1 item(s)                           |
+------------------+----+-------------------------------------+
| | + Expand       | 1  | (r:Project)<-[:WORKS_ON]-(p:Person) |
+------------------+----+-------------------------------------+
Notifications:
Id 1: INFORMATION 03C91 Relate.Notification.Statement.MissingIndex: the equality predicate on name filters :Person without a range index on (:Person {name}) Remedy: CREATE INDEX relate_Person__name FOR (n:Person) ON (n.name)
Query: MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Ada'})-[:WORKS_ON]->(r:Project) RETURN r.name AS project
Plan:
+-------------------+----+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------+
| Operator          | Id | Details                                                                            | Estimated Rows |
+-------------------+----+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------+
| + ProduceResults  | 0  | 1 item(s)                                                                          | -              |
+-------------------+----+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------+
| | + NodeIndexSeek | 1  | RANGE INDEX p:Person(name) WHERE name = 'Ada', (p:Person)-[:WORKS_ON]->(r:Project) | 1              |
+-------------------+----+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+----------------+
```

**Storage.** A commit appends physical changes to the write-ahead log ([WAL](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#wal)), then applies them to the graph. A [checkpoint](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#checkpoint) writes the committed graph to a snapshot in one [codec](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#codec), such as Parquet (the default) or JSON, and recycles old log segments. A virtual file system puts the same files in a directory, packs them into one `.rl` file, or keeps them in memory. [Storage and durability](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/storage-and-durability/) explains when a commit is safe on disk.

properties.heading: The crate map
properties.text:
The source is one Cargo workspace, split into groups by role. Engine crates depend only on other engine crates; [surfaces](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#surface) depend on the engine and on each other; a boundary check in the build keeps it that way.

| Group      | Crates                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Role                                                                                                             |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Engine     | `relate`, `relate-parser`, `relate-front`, `relate-ir`, `relate-planner`, `relate-executor`, `relate-storage`, `relate-catalog`, `relate-core`, `relate-model`, `relate-error` and a few small helpers | The public API, the query pipeline, the live graph, and the write path                                           |
| Surfaces   | `relate-cli`, `relate-python`, `relate-ffi`, `relate-wasm`, `relate-serve`, `relate-bolt`, `relate-http`, `relate-mcp`, `relate-auth`, `relate-formatter`, `relate-arrow`, `relate-load`               | Each front door, plus the output formats, Arrow conversion, served-surface auth, and the Neo4j loader they share |
| Clients    | Node.js, Java, Go, and Swift packages                                                                                                                                                                  | Thin wrappers over the C ABI that `relate-ffi` builds                                                            |
| Extensions | `relate-wire` and the first-party extensions                                                                                                                                                           | The protocol `relate run` speaks to extension packages                                                           |

properties.heading: The layers
properties.text:
```mermaid flowchart TB accTitle: The layers of relate accDescr { Surfaces sit on top: the CLI and relate serve with Bolt, HTTP and MCP; the Python client and the WebAssembly build; and the C ABI that the Node.js, Java, Go and Swift clients load. Every surface calls one public Rust API, relate::Database. Under it, a statement goes through the parser, the planner and the executor, which runs against the in-memory graph and its indexes. Storage keeps the graph durable with a write-ahead log and snapshots in a directory, a .rl file or memory. } S1["CLI, and relate serve
for Bolt, HTTP, MCP"] --> DB S2["Python client,
WebAssembly build"] --> DB S3["C ABI: Node.js,
Java, Go, Swift"] --> DB DB["relate::Database"] --> Q["Parser, planner, executor"] Q --> GRAPH[("In-memory graph
and indexes")] Q -->|"commit"| STORE[("WAL and snapshots")] STORE -->|"open: load, replay"| GRAPH ``` Surfaces sit on top: the CLI and relate serve with Bolt, HTTP and MCP; the Python client and the WebAssembly build; and the C ABI that the Node.js, Java, Go and Swift clients load. Every surface calls one public Rust API, relate::Database. Under it, a statement goes through the parser, the planner and the executor, which runs against the in-memory graph and its indexes. Storage keeps the graph durable with a write-ahead log and snapshots in a directory, a .rl file or memory.

properties.heading: The surfaces around the core
properties.text: The CLI links the engine into one binary. The Python client calls it in-process through a native extension module. The C ABI exposes it as a typed C interface, and the Node.js, Java, Go and Swift clients load that one library instead of each building its own binding. The WebAssembly build runs it in a browser page. `relate serve` opens one store and hosts the Bolt, HTTP Query API, and MCP servers over it, with one accept loop and one connection cap for all three.

properties.heading: What the layering buys, and what it costs
properties.text:
One engine under every surface means one behavior to test and document: an error, a result type or a notification is the same in the CLI, in Python, and over Bolt. A fix lands everywhere at once, and the clients stay thin. The same engine crates also compile to WebAssembly, which is how the browser build exists.

The cost is in what one engine cannot be. Every surface inherits the engine's shape: one process per store, the graph in that process's memory, and the client running in the same address space as the engine, so a client process that holds a large graph holds it in its own memory. The four clients that share the C ABI also share its contract of one call at a time per connection. And the planner's rewrites cover `MATCH` patterns while other clauses run in the order written, so how a statement is written still matters; `EXPLAIN` and `PROFILE` show what it chose.

properties.heading: Where this shows up
properties.text:
- [Tune a query](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/tune-a-query/): reading `EXPLAIN` and `PROFILE`, and acting on index notifications.
- [Transactions and concurrency](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/transactions-and-concurrency/): versions, pinned views and conflicts in the in-memory graph.
- [Storage and durability](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/storage-and-durability/): the write path, checkpoints, and codecs.
- [Storage formats](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/storage/formats/): what a directory store and a `.rl` file hold.
- [Where relate fits](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/where-relate-fits/): the conditions that follow from this design.

properties.heading: The Cypher dialect
properties.text: Which Cypher does relate speak? [openCypher](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#opencypher) is the floor: the openCypher Technology Compatibility Kit (TCK) is the language contract. On top of it sits Neo4j's [Cypher 25](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#cypher-25), the version aligned with the ISO GQL standard, and it is the default. Newer syntax that Neo4j has accepted but not settled waits behind an opt-in, `RELATE_PREVIEW`. Where a feature only makes sense on a multi-user server, relate leaves it out and says so with a typed error.

properties.heading: Cypher 25 and GQL
properties.text:
Neo4j's Cypher 25 adds the syntax that brings Cypher toward GQL, and relate follows it. Label expressions combine labels with `&`, `|` and `!`, and `IS` can replace the colon:

```cypher run name=label-expression
MATCH (n IS Person|Project)
RETURN labels(n) AS labels, n.name AS name
ORDER BY name
```

```table
| labels      | name             |
|-------------|------------------|
| ["Person"]  | "Ada"            |
| ["Person"]  | "Grace"          |
| ["Person"]  | "Noor"           |
| ["Project"] | "opencypher-tck" |
| ["Project"] | "relate"         |
5 rows
```

Path selectors and quantified relationships find routes without a hop bound written by hand. The shortest route from Ada to the TCK project, over either relationship type, in either direction:

```cypher run name=shortest
MATCH p = SHORTEST 1 (:Person {name: 'Ada'})-[:KNOWS|WORKS_ON]-+(:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck'})
RETURN [n IN nodes(p) | n.name] AS route
```

```table
| route                              |
|------------------------------------|
| ["Ada", "Grace", "opencypher-tck"] |
1 row
```

`LET` binds a value without a `WITH`, and `FILTER` drops rows as a clause of its own:

```cypher run name=let-filter
MATCH (p:Person)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(r:Project)
LET years = 2026 - w.since
FILTER years >= 3
RETURN p.name AS person, r.name AS project, years
ORDER BY years DESC
```

```table
| person  | project          | years |
|---------|------------------|-------|
| "Grace" | "opencypher-tck" | 4     |
| "Grace" | "relate"         | 3     |
2 rows
```

The rest of the set includes `NEXT` to chain statements, `COUNT { }` and `COLLECT { }` subqueries, `CALL (x) { }` scope clauses, `CALL { } IN TRANSACTIONS`, dynamic labels with `$(…)`, the vector and UUID types, graph types, and the `SEARCH` clause over vector and full-text indexes. The [Cypher overview](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/overview/) lists them all.

Where the proposals, Cypher 5 and Cypher 25 disagree, relate's target is Cypher 25 as Neo4j runs it. That is also why the retired TCK pin carried deviations: a few 2024.3 scenarios expect behavior that Cypher 25 changed on purpose. A statement can still ask for a version with a `CYPHER 5` or `CYPHER 25` prefix ([Cypher versions](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/cypher-versions/) has what each prefix changes). The default is recorded per [namespace](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#namespace) in the [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store), and `SHOW DATABASES` reports it:

```cypher run name=version
SHOW DATABASES YIELD name, defaultLanguage
RETURN name, defaultLanguage
```

```table
| name                | defaultLanguage |
|---------------------|-----------------|
| "neo4j"             | "CYPHER 25"     |
| "system"            | "CYPHER 25"     |
| "system_ontologies" | "CYPHER 25"     |
3 rows
```

properties.heading: openCypher as the floor
properties.text:
The TCK is a suite of scenarios that pins down what each openCypher clause, expression, and error means. relate treats it as the contract: parser, planner, executor, and error classes follow its scenarios. Coverage is measured by a separate spec harness, which runs Neo4j's Cypher suites, the openCypher TCK among them, against the build of each pull request that is ready for review, and reports the result. It reports; it does not block a merge, and no current pass count is published.

Until 2026-11-05 the engine ran a pinned copy of TCK 2024.3 in its own test suite, with a short list of documented deviations. That measurement is retired, so a figure from it is history, not a current claim.

properties.heading: Preview features
properties.text:
A [preview feature](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#preview-feature) is a Cypher feature from a Cypher Improvement Proposal (CIP) that is not yet part of the settled dialect. relate implements several, and each runs only when the `RELATE_PREVIEW` environment variable names it. Without the opt-in, the statement fails before it runs:

```cypher run name=preview expect=error
RETURN datetime('2026-01-01T12:00+01:00') IS SAME INSTANT datetime('2026-01-01T11:00Z') AS same
```

```table
error: semantic error: SemanticError: preview feature 'chronological-comparisons' is not enabled: set RELATE_PREVIEW=chronological-comparisons
```

With the feature named in the environment of the process that opens the store, the same statement runs:

```bash verify
RELATE_PREVIEW=chronological-comparisons relate --mode envelope "RETURN datetime('2026-01-01T12:00+01:00') IS SAME INSTANT datetime('2026-01-01T11:00Z') AS same"
```

```text
{"columnTypes":["BOOLEAN"],"columns":["same"],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[{"same":true}],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":0.934375,"execute_ms":0.371625,"lex_parse_ms":0.028167,"lower_ms":0.428167,"parse_ms":0.49474999999999997,"plan_ms":0.057540999999999995,"result_generation_ms":0.00033299999999999996,"rewrite_ms":0.008042},"truncated":false}
```

`RELATE_PREVIEW` takes a comma-separated list and is read once, when the store opens. An unknown name stops the open with an error that lists every known name, so a typo never passes silently. The names in this build are `hybrid-search`, `local-callables`, `graph-type-opt-props`, `graph-type-default-values`, `graph-type-implied-labels`, `ontology`, `obfuscated-literals`, `mixed-label-syntax`, `float16-coordinate-types`, `chronological-comparisons`, `complex-search-patterns`, `coll-zip`, `coll-has` and `gql-stddev-aliases`. Three of them, `coll-zip`, `coll-has` and `gql-stddev-aliases`, gate function names, and `ontology` gates the `db.ontology.*` procedures; the rest gate syntax. While one of the three function gates is off, a call fails as an unknown function.

The opt-in exists because a preview's shape can still change. Keeping it off by default means a statement that runs today keeps meaning the same thing when the proposal settles.

properties.heading: Three layers
properties.text:
```mermaid
flowchart BT
  accTitle: The layers of relate's Cypher dialect
  accDescr {
    openCypher, measured by the TCK, is the floor.
    Cypher 25 and its GQL-aligned syntax sit on top and are on by default.
    Preview features sit above that and run only when RELATE_PREVIEW names them.
    Server-only features, such as multiple databases and access control, are outside the dialect and fail with a typed error.
  }
  F["openCypher: the TCK floor"] --> C["Cypher 25 and GQL-aligned syntax, on by default"]
  C --> P["Preview features, opt in with RELATE_PREVIEW"]
  S["Server-only features: multiple databases, access control, clustering"] -.-x|"left out: typed error"| C
```

openCypher, measured by the TCK, is the floor. Cypher 25 and its GQL-aligned syntax sit on top and are on by default. Preview features sit above that and run only when RELATE_PREVIEW names them. Server-only features, such as multiple databases and access control, are outside the dialect and fail with a typed error.

The examples on this page run on the docs' example graph: three people, two projects, who works on what and who knows whom.

```cypher run name=seed
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace)
```

```table
(no rows) · nodes created: 5, relationships created: 5, properties set: 13, labels added: 5
```

properties.heading: Trade-offs
properties.text: Following Cypher 25 gives relate one target, the Cypher that current Neo4j runs, so statements and documentation written for it carry over, apart from the departures in the differences table. The cost is that relate inherits Cypher 25's deliberate breaks from older openCypher, which is why the floor is described as measured coverage rather than a single pass figure. Gating previews behind a named opt-in costs one environment variable, and buys statements whose meaning does not shift under them.

properties.heading: Where relate departs from Neo4j, and why
properties.text:
Most departures come from relate being an embedded, single-process engine. Server features have nothing to act on: there is one user graph per store, no users or roles, and no cluster. So a store holds three fixed namespaces: `neo4j` for data, `system`, and `system_ontologies`, which is listed but not queryable. `USE` routes a statement to `neo4j` or `system`. Any other graph name fails before the statement runs:

```cypher run name=use-other expect=error
USE friends
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN p.name AS name
```

```table
error: semantic error: DatabaseNotFound: Graph not found: friends
```

Database administration follows Neo4j Community Edition: `SHOW DATABASES` and setting the default language work, and the other administration commands fail with `Unsupported administration command`. A few departures are safety limits: an explicit variable-length bound of more than 500 hops is refused at admission unless `--max-traversal-depth` raises it, because a deeper walk can overflow the native stack.

The [differences from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/differences-from-neo4j/) table lists each one with the error it produces and what to write instead.

properties.heading: Where this shows up
properties.text:
- [Cypher overview](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/overview/): the clauses, expressions, and features relate supports.
- [Differences from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/differences-from-neo4j/): each departure, its error, and the replacement.
- [Search](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/search/): the `SEARCH` clause and its preview forms.
- [Limitations](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/limitations/): namespaces, nesting, and traversal limits.
- [Search by vector similarity](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/vector-search/): Cypher 25's vector type and indexes in use.

properties.heading: Namespaces
properties.text: Can a relate store hold several databases, the way a Neo4j server does? No: every [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store) has the same three fixed [namespaces](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#namespace), `neo4j`, `system` and `system_ontologies`, and only `neo4j` holds your graph. There is no `CREATE DATABASE`. A `USE` clause or a session setting routes a statement to one of the three names, and any other name fails before the statement runs. An application that needs several graphs opens several stores, one per graph.

properties.heading: How a statement picks its namespace
properties.text:
A statement runs in one namespace. Two settings choose it, and the narrower one wins:

- **The session namespace.** It is `neo4j` unless the session chose another: `--namespace` on the CLI, `namespace=` when a Python [client](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#client) connects (and `set_namespace()` between transactions), or the database a Neo4j driver names in its session over Bolt. An unknown name on the CLI exits 2 before the store opens.
- **A `USE` clause.** It routes one [statement](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#statement), whatever the session namespace is.

Names match without regard to case, so `USE NEO4J` reaches `neo4j`. In `system`, a procedure call runs, and the result names the engine's components:

```cypher run name=use-system
USE system CALL dbms.components() YIELD name, versions
RETURN name, versions
```

```table
| name           | versions           |
|----------------|--------------------|
| "Neo4j Kernel" | ["2026.10-relate"] |
| "Cypher"       | ["5", "25"]        |
| "Relate"       | ["1.0.1"]          |
3 rows
```

A name the store does not have fails while the statement is planned, so nothing runs, even a `RETURN 1`:

```cypher run name=use-unknown expect=error
USE movies MATCH (n) RETURN count(n) AS n
```

```table
error: semantic error: DatabaseNotFound: Graph not found: movies
```

The restricted namespaces refuse what they cannot answer. `system` takes no `MATCH`:

```cypher run name=match-system expect=error
USE system MATCH (n) RETURN count(n) AS n
```

```table
error: semantic error: SemanticError: The following unsupported clauses were used: MATCH. 
The system database supports a restricted set of Cypher clauses. The supported clause structure for procedure calls is: CALL, YIELD, RETURN. YIELD and RETURN clauses are optional. The order of the clauses is fixed and each can only occur once.
```

and `system_ontologies` refuses every statement except the administration commands:

```cypher run name=match-ontologies expect=error
USE system_ontologies MATCH (n) RETURN count(n) AS n
```

```table
error: semantic error: SemanticError: This database is not queryable. Use the db.ontology.* procedures on the user database 'neo4j' instead.
```

One statement reads one graph. Two different `USE` targets in one statement, across the arms of a `UNION` or inside a `CALL` subquery, fail with `Multiple graphs in the same query not allowed here`: Neo4j allows that only on composite databases, which relate does not have.

properties.heading: Several graphs in one application
properties.text:
An application with several graphs keeps one store per graph and opens each one. Two stores in one process are independent: each has its own `neo4j` graph, and neither sees the other. This Python program opens two in-memory stores side by side, then moves one connection's session to `system`:

```python run name=two-stores title="two_stores.py"
import relate

team = relate.connect(":memory:")
deps = relate.connect(":memory:")
team.execute("CREATE (:Person {name: 'Ada'})")
deps.execute("CREATE (:Version {key: 'NPM/route-kit@2.3.1'})")

print("team:", team.execute("MATCH (n) RETURN labels(n)[0] AS label, count(*) AS n").data())
print("deps:", deps.execute("MATCH (n) RETURN labels(n)[0] AS label, count(*) AS n").data())

team.set_namespace("system")
cur = team.execute("SHOW DATABASES YIELD name")
names = [row["name"] for row in cur.data()]
print(cur.consume().namespace, names)

try:
    relate.connect(":memory:", namespace="movies")
except relate.OperationalError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e)
```

```text
team: [{'label': 'Person', 'n': 1}]
deps: [{'label': 'Version', 'n': 1}]
system ['neo4j', 'system', 'system_ontologies']
OperationalError semantic error: DatabaseNotFound: Graph not found: movies
```

A statement cannot join the two. To combine them, an application queries each and joins the rows itself, or copies one graph into the other store with `MERGE` statements; `relate clone` copies a whole store to a new path. When the graphs share people, places or keys, one store with a label per source keeps them joinable in a single statement, and that is usually the better shape.

properties.heading: Three names, one graph
properties.text:
A Neo4j server hosts many databases and a catalog of them, named `system`. relate runs inside your process and opens one store, so the store is the unit a graph lives in, and its catalog is fixed. It keeps the three names a Neo4j Community Edition 2026.09 server reports, so a tool built for Neo4j that lists databases or opens a `system` session finds the names it expects:

| Namespace           | Holds                                                      | What runs there                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `neo4j`             | The graph: every node, relationship, index, and constraint | Every statement. The default for every session and the only namespace that holds data                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `system`            | No graph data                                              | `SHOW` commands, the supported database administration commands, and procedure calls in the shape `CALL`, `YIELD`, `RETURN`                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `system_ontologies` | Nothing queryable; listed for compatibility                | Only the database administration commands, such as `SHOW DATABASES`, from a session set to it; a `USE system_ontologies` on one fails with [`UseClauseWithAdministrationCommand`](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/#engine-use-on-administration-command). Every other statement fails, reads included |

The store's [ontology](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#ontology) document, where one is set, belongs to the `neo4j` graph and is read and written with the `db.ontology.*` procedures on `neo4j`, a preview feature ([Use an ontology](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/ontology/)). `system_ontologies` gives no view of it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: How a statement reaches a namespace
  accDescr {
    Each statement runs against the session namespace, neo4j unless the session chose another, or against the namespace its USE clause names.
    neo4j holds the graph; system answers SHOW commands, administration commands and procedure calls; system_ontologies answers only the administration commands, and only from a session set to it.
    Any other name fails with Graph not found before the statement runs.
  }
  S["Statement"] --> R{"USE clause or session namespace"}
  R -->|"neo4j (default)"| N["neo4j: the graph"]
  R -->|"system"| Y["system: SHOW, administration, CALL"]
  R -->|"system_ontologies (session)"| O["system_ontologies: administration only"]
  R -->|"any other name"| E["Graph not found, nothing runs"]
```

Each statement runs against the session namespace, neo4j unless the session chose another, or against the namespace its USE clause names. neo4j holds the graph; system answers SHOW commands, administration commands and procedure calls; system_ontologies answers only the administration commands, and only from a session set to it. Any other name fails with Graph not found before the statement runs.

`SHOW DATABASES` lists the three rows on every store, with `neo4j` as the default and home namespace:

```cypher run name=show
SHOW DATABASES YIELD name, type, access, default, home
RETURN name, type, access, default, home
```

```table
| name                | type       | access       | default | home  |
|---------------------|------------|--------------|---------|-------|
| "neo4j"             | "standard" | "read-write" | true    | true  |
| "system"            | "system"   | "read-write" | false   | false |
| "system_ontologies" | "standard" | "read-only"  | false   | false |
3 rows
```

properties.heading: Trade-offs
properties.text:
Fixed namespaces keep the engine's catalog trivial: there is nothing to create, drop, attach or route, and every store opens the same way. Tools that expect Neo4j's `system` and `SHOW DATABASES` keep working, and a statement written with a database name fails at once with a message naming it, instead of reading the wrong graph.

The cost is that a cross-graph question is two statements. Neo4j's composite databases, `USE graph.byName(…)` and several `USE` targets in one statement have no equivalent. Where many tenants or graphs must be queried together, a server database fits better; [Where relate fits](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/where-relate-fits/) lists that condition with the others.

properties.heading: Where this shows up
properties.text:
- [Differences from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/differences-from-neo4j/): `CREATE DATABASE` and `USE` with a database name, with the errors they produce.
- [Limitations](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/limitations/): one graph per statement, and the administration commands that run.
- [CLI flags](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/flags/): `--namespace`.
- [Bolt server](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/server/bolt/): how a driver's database name selects a namespace.
- [Use an ontology](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/ontology/): the document `system_ontologies` does not expose.
- [Errors](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/#engine-database-not-found): `Graph not found` and the other namespace errors, with their codes.

properties.heading: Why a store holds one graph
properties.text:
In a server, a database is the unit an operator creates, backs up, secures, and moves. In relate those jobs belong to the store, and a store is a directory or a file. Creating one is opening a new path; backing it up is `relate clone`; access control is file permissions, `--read-only`, and the credentials of `relate serve`; moving it is copying it. A second database inside the same store would add a catalog and a second set of every one of those jobs, with nothing gained over a second store.

So relate follows Neo4j Community Edition for database administration and stops there: `SHOW DATABASES`, `SHOW DEFAULT DATABASE`, `SHOW HOME DATABASE` and `ALTER DATABASE … SET DEFAULT LANGUAGE CYPHER 5` or `CYPHER 25` run, and every other database administration command, `CREATE DATABASE` included, fails with `Unsupported administration command: <statement>`.

properties.heading: Problems relate solves
properties.text: Which problems is relate the right database for? A database is best chosen by the problem at hand rather than by its feature list, so each entry on this page starts from a problem in the words people use for it, names the relate capability that solves it, links the guides, recipes and reference that cover it, and cites the recorded run that shows it working, or says that none does yet. Every entry shares relate's shape: the graph belongs to one application, agent or tool, lives on one machine, and fits in that machine's memory. [Where relate fits](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/where-relate-fits/) lists the conditions under which another kind of database fits better.

properties.heading: Agent memory
properties.text:
An agent's context ends with its session. Memory that outlives the session has to live somewhere the next one can query: the people and things the agent knows about, where it learned each fact, and which facts a later message corrected. That is a graph: entities are nodes, an episode links to the entities it mentions, and a fact links to its subject and to its evidence. relate keeps that graph in a store the agent's own process opens, a `.rl` file or a directory beside the agent, with no server to run. Uniqueness constraints and `MERGE` keep one node per entity across sessions. A correction closes the old fact and links it from the new one with `SUPERSEDES` instead of deleting it, so recall can show what is true now and what it replaced. A vector index and the `SEARCH` clause recall facts by meaning, and a property declared on the index lets the search skip closed facts before it counts its results. [Model agent memory](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/model-agent-memory/) builds this model cell by cell, and the [agent memory recipe](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/agent-memory/) runs two sessions against it. ```mermaid flowchart LR accTitle: Recommended data model for agent memory: entities, the episodes that mention them, and facts with their evidence accDescr { An Episode MENTIONS the Entity nodes it names. A Fact is ABOUT one or more entities and comes FROM the Episode that is its evidence. A newer Fact SUPERSEDES the one it replaced in the same slot, so a correction keeps the history. } Episode(("Episode
id · session · at · text")) -- "MENTIONS" --> Entity(("Entity
key · name")) Fact(("Fact
text · slot · embedding
validFrom · validTo")) -- "ABOUT" --> Entity Fact -- "FROM" --> Episode Fact -- "SUPERSEDES" --> Fact class Entity l3 class Episode l2 class Fact l4 ``` An Episode MENTIONS the Entity nodes it names. A Fact is ABOUT one or more entities and comes FROM the Episode that is its evidence. A newer Fact SUPERSEDES the one it replaced in the same slot, so a correction keeps the history. - **Problem:** Give an agent memory that survives restarts, which a later session can recall by meaning and by connection. - **Capability:** A durable store the agent's process opens itself, with uniqueness constraints and `MERGE` for one node per entity, `SUPERSEDES` chains for corrections, and vector `SEARCH` for recall. - **Surfaces:** `python`, `node`, `cli`, `mcp`, `agents`, `cypher` - **Guides:** [Model agent memory](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/model-agent-memory/), [Give an agent a memory](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/agent-memory/), [Use relate with LangGraph](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/integrations/langgraph/), [Use relate with the Claude Agent SDK](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/integrations/claude-agent-sdk/), [Use relate with LangChain](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/integrations/langchain/) - **Recipes:** [Pick up where the last session left off](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/agent-memory/) - **Reference:** [Search](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/search/), [Storage formats](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/storage/formats/) - **Verified by:** cell `recall` of the recipe [Pick up where the last session left off](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/agent-memory/#cell-recall), replayed against its recorded result on every build

properties.heading: Agent trajectory timeline
properties.text:
An agent runtime that appends one step per tool call reads its timeline on every turn: the last few steps, the page before those, everything since a cutoff, and for a supervisor the newest steps across all sessions. Those reads are only as good as the sort key under them, and one runtime that copies a timestamp in another type puts every page that follows out of order. In the [agent trajectory timeline recipe](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/agent-trajectory-timeline/) each step hangs off its session by a `STEP` relationship whose `ts` is an integer, and four constraints make that hold: one node per session, one per tool, and every `STEP` with a `ts` that is not null and is an `INTEGER`. An append that copies a datetime fails with an error instead of corrupting the order. Token counts sit on the relationship, so a budget read never touches the step nodes, and one statement migrates a timeline written with datetimes. ```mermaid flowchart LR accTitle: Recommended data model for an agent trajectory: a session's steps, each calling one tool accDescr { A Session links to each of its Step nodes by a STEP relationship that carries an integer timestamp, a sequence number and a token count. Each Step has a kind, text and time, and a CALLED relationship to the Tool it used. } Session(("Session
id")) -- "STEP
ts (integer) · seq · tokens" --> Step(("Step
id · kind · text · at")) Step -- "CALLED" --> Tool(("Tool
name")) class Session l1 class Step l2 class Tool l3 ``` A Session links to each of its Step nodes by a STEP relationship that carries an integer timestamp, a sequence number and a token count. Each Step has a kind, text and time, and a CALLED relationship to the Tool it used. - **Problem:** Log every step an agent takes and read the last few, the page before them, and everything since a cutoff, in the right order every time. - **Capability:** Steps on a timestamped relationship whose integer sort key relationship property type and existence constraints enforce, read newest first with `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT` and `SKIP`. - **Surfaces:** `cypher`, `agents` - **Recipes:** [Let an agent look back at its own steps](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/agent-trajectory-timeline/) - **Reference:** [Cypher overview](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/overview/) - **Verified by:** cell `latest` of the recipe [Let an agent look back at its own steps](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/agent-trajectory-timeline/#cell-latest), replayed against its recorded result on every build

properties.heading: Bi-temporal facts
properties.text:
News reaches an agent late. A decision that took effect on one date is logged a week later, a reviewer rejects another, and a change is planned ahead. With one timestamp per fact, the log can say what it believes now but not what it believed then, and an audit of a past action needs exactly that. The [bi-temporal decisions recipe](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/bitemporal-decisions/) gives every decision two intervals. Valid time, `validFrom` to `validTo`, is when the decision held in the world; record time, `recordedAt` and `closedAt`, is when the log wrote it and when it closed it. Nothing is deleted: a correction closes the old decision and links the new one with `SUPERSEDES`, and a retried session changes nothing because its writes use `MERGE`. One graph then answers "what was true on 20 January" and "what did the log believe on 20 January", and the two answers differ. [Model agent memory](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/model-agent-memory/) applies the same two axes to an agent's facts. ```mermaid flowchart LR accTitle: Recommended data model for bi-temporal facts: decisions about entities, the decisions they replace, and reviews accDescr { A Decision is ABOUT an Entity and carries two time ranges: validFrom and validTo for when it held, recordedAt and closedAt for when it was believed. A Decision SUPERSEDES the one it replaces, and a Review REJECTS a Decision. } Decision(("Decision
id · text · validFrom · validTo
recordedAt · closedAt")) -- "ABOUT" --> Entity(("Entity
name")) Decision -- "SUPERSEDES" --> Decision Review(("Review
by · at · reason")) -- "REJECTS" --> Decision class Decision l1 class Entity l2 class Review l3 ``` A Decision is ABOUT an Entity and carries two time ranges: validFrom and validTo for when it held, recordedAt and closedAt for when it was believed. A Decision SUPERSEDES the one it replaces, and a Review REJECTS a Decision. - **Problem:** Answer both what was true on a date and what the agent believed on that date, after late corrections and rejected decisions. - **Capability:** Two time ranges on every fact, valid time and record time, written with `datetime()` and `MERGE` so nothing is deleted, and queried with chained comparisons. - **Surfaces:** `cypher`, `agents` - **Guides:** [Model agent memory](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/model-agent-memory/) - **Recipes:** [Know what an agent believed, and when](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/bitemporal-decisions/) - **Reference:** [Cypher overview](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/overview/), [Types and values (`#temporal-types`)](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/types-and-values/#temporal-types) - **Verified by:** cell `as-of` of the recipe [Know what an agent believed, and when](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/bitemporal-decisions/#cell-as-of), replayed against its recorded result on every build

properties.heading: Codebase context graph
properties.text:
A coding agent asks what replaced a design decision, or which modules build on the parser. The paragraph that best matches the question rarely holds the answer; the links between documents and modules do. Text search alone returns the paragraph and stops there. The [codebase context graph recipe](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/codebase-context-graph/) loads a real repository, relate's own, into one graph: its crates and their dependencies, its README, and every design record with its status and citations, the most-cited split into sections. IDF-weighted full-text `SEARCH` picks where each question starts, and short, bounded graph hops bring in the rest: supersessions between records, dependencies between crates, and the citations that connect them. Served over MCP with `--read-only`, the same graph is a tool the agent queries while it works ([Connect over MCP](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/connect-over-mcp/)). ```mermaid flowchart TB accTitle: Recommended data model for a codebase context graph: crates, design records and their sections accDescr { A Crate DEPENDS_ON other crates and CITES design records (Doc). Each Doc HAS_CHUNK sections; a Chunk MENTIONS crates and CITES docs, and a Doc SUPERSEDES an earlier one. } Crate(("Crate
name · description")) -- "DEPENDS_ON" --> Crate Crate -- "CITES" --> Doc(("Doc
path · title · status")) Doc -- "HAS_CHUNK" --> Chunk(("Chunk
id · heading · text")) Chunk -- "MENTIONS" --> Crate Chunk -- "CITES" --> Doc Doc -- "SUPERSEDES" --> Doc class Crate l1 class Doc l2 class Chunk l3 ``` A Crate DEPENDS_ON other crates and CITES design records (Doc). Each Doc HAS_CHUNK sections; a Chunk MENTIONS crates and CITES docs, and a Doc SUPERSEDES an earlier one. - **Problem:** Give a coding agent answers to multi-hop questions about a codebase, such as what replaced a design decision or what builds on a module. - **Capability:** Crates, design records and their sections as one graph, IDF-weighted full-text `SEARCH` to find where to start, and bounded quantified path patterns to follow the links. - **Surfaces:** `cypher`, `agents`, `mcp` - **Guides:** [Connect over MCP](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/connect-over-mcp/), [Import git history with git-to-graph](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/extensions/git-to-graph/), [Import a directory tree with fs-to-graph](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/extensions/fs-to-graph/) - **Recipes:** [Answer codebase questions text search can't](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/codebase-context-graph/) - **Reference:** [Search](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/search/), [Patterns (`#quantified-path-patterns`)](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/patterns/#quantified-path-patterns) - **Verified by:** cell `storage` of the recipe [Answer codebase questions text search can't](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/codebase-context-graph/#cell-storage), replayed against its recorded result on every build

properties.heading: Dependency analysis
properties.text:
A lockfile lists what a project installs, not why. Whether an advisory matters depends on whether a package can reach the affected version, along which chain, and what else would disappear with the dependency that brings it in. Those are path questions, and a flat list cannot answer them. The [dependency blast radius recipe](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/dependency-blast-radius/) loads the resolved dependency graphs of three packages, with the advisories listed for every version, as `Version` nodes linked by `DEPENDS_ON`. Quantified path patterns find every advisory each package can reach, `SHORTEST` shows the chain, and `COUNT` and `EXISTS` subqueries measure what a dropped dependency takes with it. The last step turns the answer into a build check: a statement that returns no rows when the build may pass. [Script the CLI](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cli/scripting/) covers running statements from a script, with output a program can parse and exit codes to branch on. ```mermaid flowchart LR accTitle: Recommended data model for dependency analysis: package versions, what they depend on, and the advisories that affect them accDescr { A Version DEPENDS_ON other Version nodes, and each DEPENDS_ON relationship records its version requirement. Any Version can be AFFECTED_BY an Advisory, which has an id, a title and a score. } Version(("Version
key · name · version")) -- "DEPENDS_ON
requirement" --> Version Version -- "AFFECTED_BY" --> Advisory(("Advisory
id · title · cvss3")) class Version l2 class Advisory l5 ``` A Version DEPENDS_ON other Version nodes, and each DEPENDS_ON relationship records its version requirement. Any Version can be AFFECTED_BY an Advisory, which has an id, a title and a score. - **Problem:** Find which known advisories a package can reach and through which chain, and what goes away when a dependency is dropped. - **Capability:** Resolved dependency graphs as nodes and relationships, quantified path patterns and `SHORTEST` for reachability and chains, and `COUNT` and `EXISTS` subqueries for blast radius. - **Surfaces:** `cypher`, `cli` - **Guides:** [Script the CLI](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cli/scripting/), [Use relate in CI](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/use-in-ci/) - **Recipes:** [Trace how vulnerabilities reach your app](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/dependency-blast-radius/) - **Reference:** [Cypher overview](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/overview/), [Exit codes and errors](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/exit-codes-and-errors/), [Patterns (`#quantified-path-patterns`)](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/patterns/#quantified-path-patterns), [Composing clauses (`#subquery-expressions`)](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/composing-clauses/#subquery-expressions) - **Verified by:** cell `reachable` of the recipe [Trace how vulnerabilities reach your app](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/dependency-blast-radius/#cell-reachable), replayed against its recorded result on every build

properties.heading: Diffable memory
properties.text:
An agent that changes its memory during a task makes a change nobody reviews. Kept in the repository as readable text, the same memory goes through review like code: each session's writes appear in a pull request, and a bad fact is caught, reverted or corrected before it is merged.

A directory store created with `--snapshot-format json` writes its checkpoint as one readable `graph.json`, every node and relationship with its labels or type and properties, then the index and constraint catalog, so a code review can diff it. The `markdown` codec writes one note per node, with properties and outgoing relationships in YAML frontmatter. Each checkpoint also rewrites the schema as text under `.cypherlite/schema/` ([Schema as files](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/problems-relate-solves/#schema-as-files)), and `relate clone --to-snapshot-format json` converts an existing store. Writes built on `MERGE` keep the diff to real changes: in the [bi-temporal decisions recipe](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/bitemporal-decisions/) a retried session matches every node and relationship and writes nothing.

- **Problem:** Keep an agent's memory in the repository, so each session's changes show up in a pull request as a diff a person can review.
- **Capability:** A directory store whose checkpoint writes the graph as text, one `graph.json` with the `json` codec or one note per node with `markdown`, and `MERGE` writes that replay to no change.
- **Surfaces:** `cli`, `agents`
- **Guides:** [Keep a diffable memory in the repo](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/diffable-memory/), [Choose a store layout](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/choose-a-store-layout/), [Open a store as an Obsidian vault](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/obsidian-vault/)
- **Recipes:** [Know what an agent believed, and when](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/bitemporal-decisions/)
- **Reference:** [Storage formats (`#codecs`)](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/storage/formats/#codecs), [WAL and checkpoints](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/storage/wal-and-checkpoints/)
- **Verified by:** cell `retry` of the recipe [Know what an agent believed, and when](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/bitemporal-decisions/#cell-retry), replayed against its recorded result on every build

properties.heading: Embedded graph in an app
properties.text:
An application that needs relationships, paths or pattern queries often reaches for a graph database server: another process to deploy, configure, secure and keep running, and a network round trip on every query. For a graph that belongs to one application and fits in one machine's memory, the server is overhead.

relate is an embedded graph database: the engine runs inside the application's process, holds the whole graph in memory, and answers Cypher statements with nothing to deploy. The same engine sits behind every front door: the Python, Node.js, Rust, Java, Go and Swift clients, the C ABI and a WebAssembly build for the browser. A store is `:memory:`, a directory or a single `.rl` file, which the client opens and creates when it is missing. [Where relate fits](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/where-relate-fits/) lists the conditions under which a server database fits better.

- **Problem:** Add a graph database to an application without running, securing or paying for a database server.
- **Capability:** The engine as a library in the application's process, through the Python, Node.js, Rust, Java, Go and Swift clients, the C ABI or the WebAssembly build.
- **Surfaces:** `python`, `node`, `browser`, `rust`, `java`, `go`, `swift`, `c`
