- **Guides:** [Embed relate in a Python app](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/python/), [Embed relate in a Node.js app](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/node/), [Embed relate in a Rust program](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/rust/), [Embed relate in a Java app](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/java/), [Embed relate in a Go program](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/go/), [Embed relate in a Swift app](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/swift/), [Run relate in the browser](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/browser/), [Use the Python client](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/embed/python/), [Use the Node.js client](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/embed/node/), [Use the Rust crate](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/embed/rust/), [Use the C ABI](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/embed/c/), [Use the Java client](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/embed/java/), [Use the Go client](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/embed/go/), [Use the Swift package](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/embed/swift/), [Use relate from a web page](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/embed/browser/), [Choose a store layout](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/choose-a-store-layout/), [Migrate from SQLite](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/migrate/from-sqlite/), [Migrate from Kuzu](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/migrate/from-kuzu/)
- **Reference:** [API reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/api/), [Python API](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/api/python/), [Node.js API](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/api/javascript/), [Rust API](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/api/rust/), [C ABI](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/api/c/), [Java API](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/api/java/), [Go API](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/api/go/), [Swift API](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/api/swift/), [WebAssembly API](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/api/wasm/), [Storage formats](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/storage/formats/), [Limitations](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/limitations/)
- **Verified by:** the Python sample `program` on [Embed relate in a Python app](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/python/#put-it-together), whose output is recorded from a run against the Python client

properties.heading: Entity resolution
properties.text:
A CRM export and a billing export name the same customers differently: one in capitals with a suffix, one with a typo. Matching them row by row in application code means a fuzzy-matching library, a pairwise loop and thresholds tuned by eye, and the evidence for each merge is gone once the loop ends. The [entity resolution recipe](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/entity-resolution/) does the matching inside the store, in Cypher. Each row becomes a `Record` that resolves to an `Entity` per normalized name; the words of the names become `Token` nodes weighted by rarity, and `SIMILAR` links words that look like typos of each other by bigram similarity. Strong candidate pairs become `SAME_AS` and doubtful ones `POSSIBLE_MATCH`, a queue for a person to check. On the recipe's data it resolves 396 records into 211 companies and, against the generator's ground truth, finds 216 of 218 duplicate pairs with no false merges. [Import a CSV](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/import-csv/) loads exports like these from files. ```mermaid flowchart LR accTitle: Recommended data model for entity resolution: records, the entities they resolve to, and the words that match them accDescr { A Record from either export RESOLVES_TO an Entity. An Entity HAS_TOKEN the words of its name, and tokens are SIMILAR to one another. Between two entities, SAME_AS holds a scored match and POSSIBLE_MATCH a doubtful pair left for review. } Record(("Record
id · name · domain
city · key")) -- "RESOLVES_TO" --> Entity(("Entity
key · cluster")) Entity -- "HAS_TOKEN" --> Token(("Token
text · idf")) Token -- "SIMILAR
dice" --> Token Entity -- "SAME_AS
score" --> Other(("Entity
another entity")) Entity -- "POSSIBLE_MATCH
score · reason" --> Other class Record l1 class Entity,Other l3 class Token l4 ``` A Record from either export RESOLVES_TO an Entity. An Entity HAS_TOKEN the words of its name, and tokens are SIMILAR to one another. Between two entities, SAME_AS holds a scored match and POSSIBLE_MATCH a doubtful pair left for review. - **Problem:** Merge two messy exports that list the same customers spelled differently into one record per company, with doubtful pairs left for a person. - **Capability:** Normalized keys, bigram similarity and IDF-weighted scores computed in Cypher over records, entities and tokens, with `SAME_AS` and `POSSIBLE_MATCH` relationships for the decisions. - **Surfaces:** `cypher`, `cli` - **Guides:** [Import a CSV](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/import-csv/) - **Recipes:** [Merge duplicate customers across systems](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/entity-resolution/) - **Reference:** [Cypher overview](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/overview/) - **Verified by:** cell `score` of the recipe [Merge duplicate customers across systems](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/entity-resolution/#cell-score), replayed against its recorded result on every build

properties.heading: Fresh graph per test run
properties.text:
A test that shares a database with the previous run inherits its state, and a test suite that needs a database server needs that server in CI too. Each run should start from a known graph, check what it needs to, and leave nothing behind.

With no `--database`, a statement runs against an in-memory store that is gone when the process exits, and the clients open the same store as `:memory:`. A fixture kept as a `.rl` file loads with `--load` into an in-memory copy, which is read-only, so a test cannot change the fixture; `--load ./fixture.rl --database ./scratch.rl` copies it and opens the copy for writing. `--mode envelope` prints one JSON object per result, and the exit code names the class of a failure, so a CI step can branch on both ([Script the CLI](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cli/scripting/)). The [dependency blast radius recipe](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/dependency-blast-radius/) ends with a statement that returns no rows when the build may pass.

- **Problem:** Give every test or CI run its own graph, built from a fixture and thrown away afterwards, with results a script can check.
- **Capability:** The in-memory store, the default, gone when the process exits; `--load` to read a fixture store into memory; envelope output and typed exit codes for the script that checks it.
- **Surfaces:** `cli`, `python`, `node`
- **Guides:** [Script the CLI](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cli/scripting/), [Choose a store layout (`#start-in-memory`)](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/choose-a-store-layout/#start-in-memory), [Embed relate in a Python app](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/python/), [Use relate in CI](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/use-in-ci/)
- **Recipes:** [Trace how vulnerabilities reach your app](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/dependency-blast-radius/), [Catch a migration that quietly loses data](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/migration-rehearsal/)
- **Reference:** [Exit codes and errors](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/exit-codes-and-errors/), [CLI flags](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/flags/)
- **Verified by:** cell `gate` of the recipe [Trace how vulnerabilities reach your app](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/dependency-blast-radius/#cell-gate), replayed against its recorded result on every build

properties.heading: Geospatial memory
properties.text:
A travel or field agent remembers places: the ones its users mention and the ones it visited. The useful questions about them are spatial (what is within 2 km, what is nearest, what is inside the map the user is looking at), and they often mix with the rest of memory, such as where this agent went recently near here. relate stores a location as a point property and answers those questions in Cypher. In the [nearby places recipe](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/nearby-places/) each place's `loc` is a WGS-84 point, so `point.distance` returns metres; `point.withinBBox` answers the map-box question, and a `POINT` index serves the lookups. Visits are `VISITED` relationships with a timestamp and a sequence number, so "recently, near here" is one statement that filters by distance and orders by time. relate does not reject a distance between points in different coordinate systems, so the recipe's query checks the caller's position before it compares distances. ```mermaid flowchart LR accTitle: Recommended data model for geospatial memory: agents visit places, and places are in cities accDescr { An Agent VISITED a Place, and each visit records a timestamp and a sequence number. A Place has a name, a kind and a location point, and is IN a City. } Agent(("Agent
id")) -- "VISITED
ts · seq" --> Place(("Place
name · kind · loc")) Place -- "IN" --> City(("City
name")) class Agent l1 class Place l2 class City l3 ``` An Agent VISITED a Place, and each visit records a timestamp and a sequence number. A Place has a name, a kind and a location point, and is IN a City. - **Problem:** Let an agent answer what is near here, what is nearest, what is inside this map box, and where it went recently near a place. - **Capability:** WGS-84 points stored as properties, distances in metres with `point.distance`, map boxes with `point.withinBBox`, and a `POINT` index, in the same graph as the rest of the memory. - **Surfaces:** `cypher`, `agents` - **Guides:** [Geospatial queries](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/geospatial/) - **Recipes:** [Answer "what's nearby?" from memory](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/nearby-places/) - **Reference:** [Cypher overview](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/overview/), [Functions (`#spatial-functions`)](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/functions/#spatial-functions) - **Verified by:** cell `within` of the recipe [Answer "what's nearby?" from memory](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/nearby-places/#cell-within), replayed against its recorded result on every build

properties.heading: Graph queries over MCP
properties.text:
An agent host such as Claude Code, Cursor or Codex reaches outside data through MCP servers it starts itself. A graph the agent can query that way becomes a tool it calls during a task, and a tool that can write is a tool that can damage the data it was meant to read.

`relate serve --mcp stdio --database <store> --read-only` starts a server on the host's standard input and output. Opened read-only it lists two tools, `read_cypher` and `get_schema`, takes no writer lease and leaves out `write_cypher`; `read_cypher` refuses writes and schema changes either way. Every host's configuration block in [Connect over MCP](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/connect-over-mcp/) starts the same command. For several clients or a host that connects to a URL, `relate serve --mcp <port>` serves over HTTP and asks for HTTP Basic authentication by default.

- **Problem:** Give a coding agent or an agent framework a graph it can query through MCP, without letting it change the data.
- **Capability:** `relate serve --mcp stdio` on a store opened `--read-only`, which lists the `read_cypher` and `get_schema` tools and leaves out `write_cypher`.
- **Surfaces:** `mcp`, `agents`, `cli`
- **Guides:** [Connect over MCP](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/connect-over-mcp/), [Serve a store over MCP](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/serve/mcp/), [Use relate with the Claude Agent SDK](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/integrations/claude-agent-sdk/), [Keep an agent safe](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/agent-safety/), [Use relate with PydanticAI](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/integrations/pydantic-ai/), [Use relate with the OpenAI Agents SDK](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/integrations/openai-agents-sdk/)
- **Reference:** [MCP server](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/server/mcp/), [relate serve](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/serve/), [CLI flags (`#relate-serve`)](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/flags/#relate-serve), [Errors (`#mcp-read-query-only`)](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/#mcp-read-query-only)
- **Verified by:** the Python sample `options` on [Use relate with the Claude Agent SDK](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/integrations/claude-agent-sdk/#register-the-server-with-the-sdk), whose output is recorded from a run against the Python client

properties.heading: How an entry is built
properties.text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: How an entry connects a problem to its proof
  accDescr {
    A problem, in the reader's words, is solved by a capability, in relate's
    words. The capability is covered by guides, recipes and reference pages,
    and verified by one recorded run: a cell on a recipe or a docs page, a
    language sample, or a CLI step, which the checks replay against its
    recording.
  }
  Problem -->|solved by| Capability
  Capability --> Guides
  Capability --> Recipes
  Capability --> Reference
  Capability -->|verified by| Run[Recorded run]
```

A problem, in the reader's words, is solved by a capability, in relate's words. The capability is covered by guides, recipes and reference pages, and verified by one recorded run: a cell on a recipe or a docs page, a language sample, or a CLI step, which the checks replay against its recording.

Each entry is one heading whose anchor is the capability's id, so `/docs/concepts/problems-relate-solves#agent-memory` names the agent memory entry wherever it is cited. Under the heading, two to four paragraphs explain the problem and how relate solves it; where the problem has a data model, a diagram shows the recommended one, with [labels](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#label) as circles and [relationship types](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#relationship-type) as arrows; and a list gives the problem, the capability, the [surfaces](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#surface) it applies to (the same names as every page's `surfaces`), the links, and the recorded run that verifies it.

A cookbook cell is replayed against its recorded result on every build of the site, and a docs cell by the docs checks on every pull request. A language sample's output is recorded from a run against its client library (Python, Node.js, Rust, Java, Go, Swift or the C ABI), and a CLI step's output from a run of the relate binary, which the CLI check repeats. An entry whose capability no recorded run exercises yet, such as one that needs a Neo4j server, says so in its list. A capability without a guide yet cites the recipe or reference pages that cover it today.

The same entries are data at [/docs/capabilities.json](https://relatedb.ai/docs/capabilities.json): each with the intents an agent might phrase the problem as, its data model as mermaid source, and the canonical URL of everything it cites.

properties.heading: Hybrid retrieval for RAG
properties.text:
Vector search finds passages that mean something close to the question and misses exact names and codes; full-text search finds the words and misses paraphrases. A retrieval step for a model needs both lists, merged into one ranking, and then the context the best passage does not hold itself, such as the decision that later replaced what it says. relate keeps the embeddings, the text and the links in one store. Embeddings come from the application's model and are stored as typed vectors; a vector index and a full-text index are both queried with the `SEARCH` clause, which can filter inside the search rather than after it. The [hybrid recall recipe](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/hybrid-recall/) fuses the two ranked lists by reciprocal rank in one statement, then hops from each recalled note to its topic and that topic's latest decision. [Search by vector similarity](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/vector-search/) covers the vector half, and the [search reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/search/) the index options and the hybrid form. ```mermaid flowchart LR accTitle: Recommended data model for hybrid retrieval: notes about topics, some of which record a decision accDescr { A Note has text, a timestamp and an embedding, and is ABOUT a Topic. A Note that records a decision also has a DECIDED relationship to the Topic, carrying the decision's text and timestamp. } Note(("Note
id · text · ts
embedding")) -- "ABOUT" --> Topic(("Topic
name")) Note -- "DECIDED
text · ts" --> Topic class Note l1 class Topic l2 ``` A Note has text, a timestamp and an embedding, and is ABOUT a Topic. A Note that records a decision also has a DECIDED relationship to the Topic, carrying the decision's text and timestamp. - **Problem:** Retrieve the passages that answer a question by meaning and by keyword at once, then follow links to the context around them. - **Capability:** Vector and full-text indexes queried with the `SEARCH` clause, fused by reciprocal rank in one Cypher statement, with a graph hop from each hit to its related nodes. - **Surfaces:** `cypher`, `python`, `node`, `agents` - **Guides:** [Search by vector similarity](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/vector-search/), [Full-text and hybrid search](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/full-text-and-hybrid-search/), [Migrate from a vector store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/migrate/from-a-vector-store/), [Use relate with LlamaIndex](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/integrations/llamaindex/) - **Recipes:** [Find a note, then what was decided since](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/hybrid-recall/), [Answer codebase questions text search can't](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/codebase-context-graph/) - **Reference:** [Search](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/search/) - **Verified by:** cell `fuse-vector` of the recipe [Find a note, then what was decided since](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/hybrid-recall/#cell-fuse-vector), replayed against its recorded result on every build

properties.heading: Migration rehearsal
properties.text:
A migration can keep every node count right and every intended change in place and still destroy data. Counting nodes before and after misses it, and so does checking the changes the migration was written to make.

The [migration rehearsal recipe](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/migration-rehearsal/) fingerprints the graph in Cypher before the migration runs, writes down what the migration is allowed to change, and compares afterwards. A probe on each organization's relationships catches a bug that deletes 352 city links across 61 organizations, and the fingerprint puts the links back. The rehearsal belongs on a copy: `relate clone` writes one from a store, a directory store even while its writer runs ([Back up and restore a store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/backup-and-restore/)), and `--load` gives an in-memory copy to try a statement against.

- **Problem:** Check that a data migration changed only what it was meant to, before it runs on the real graph.
- **Capability:** A fingerprint of the graph taken in Cypher before the migration, probes that compare it afterwards, and `relate clone` or `--load` to run the migration on a copy.
- **Surfaces:** `cypher`, `cli`
- **Guides:** [Back up and restore a store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/backup-and-restore/), [Keep an agent safe (`#back-up-before-a-write`)](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/agent-safety/#back-up-before-a-write), [Migrate from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/migrate/from-neo4j/)
- **Recipes:** [Catch a migration that quietly loses data](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/migration-rehearsal/)
- **Reference:** [Cypher overview](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/overview/), [relate clone](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/clone/)
- **Verified by:** cell `verdict` of the recipe [Catch a migration that quietly loses data](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/migration-rehearsal/#cell-verdict), replayed against its recorded result on every build

properties.heading: Neo4j subgraph mirror
properties.text:
A team with data in Neo4j or Aura often wants part of it local: for an agent to query without network access, as a test fixture, or for an experiment that must not touch the shared database. Exporting to files and importing them again needs a file format and a converter in each direction.

`relate pull` copies a subgraph over the Neo4j HTTP Query API into a local directory or `.rl` store. Every statement given with `--query` returns graph elements; the statements run in one process with one checkpoint at the end, and the credentials come from an env file named with `--from` or from `NEO4J_URI`, `NEO4J_USERNAME`, `NEO4J_PASSWORD` and `NEO4J_DATABASE`. `relate push` copies a scoped subgraph back, merging on keys from the store's constraints unless `--merge-key` names others, and `--dry-run` prints the plan without touching the remote. [Differences from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/differences-from-neo4j/) lists the constructs a query written for Neo4j may use that relate does not have, such as APOC, with what to write instead, and `relate serve` speaks Bolt and the HTTP Query API, so Neo4j tools can reach the local copy. Pull and push need a running Neo4j or Aura database, which the docs checks do not have; the recorded run is the push plan from `--dry-run`, which reads only the local store.

- **Problem:** Work on a slice of a Neo4j or Aura graph locally, offline or in a test, and copy changes back when they are ready.
- **Capability:** `relate pull`, which copies the graph elements a query returns from Neo4j or Aura into a local store, and `relate push`, which copies a scoped subgraph back with a `--dry-run` plan.
- **Surfaces:** `cli`, `bolt`, `http`
- **Guides:** [Pull a subgraph from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/neo4j/pull-from-neo4j/), [Push a subgraph to Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/neo4j/push-to-neo4j/), [Migrate from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/migrate/from-neo4j/)
- **Reference:** [relate pull](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/pull/), [relate push](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/push/), [Differences from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/differences-from-neo4j/), [Where relate fits](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/where-relate-fits/)
- **Verified by:** the `bash verify` step 3 on [Push a subgraph to Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/neo4j/push-to-neo4j/#give-each-label-a-merge-key), whose recorded output begins `{"columnTypes":[],"columns":[],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":1.072917000000000`; the CLI check replays it against a relate binary

properties.heading: Offline and sandboxed use
properties.text:
Agents increasingly run in sandboxes: Claude Code's sandbox, Codex, Cursor cloud agents, E2B, Vercel Sandbox, Daytona or a plain container, each limiting what a command may write and which hosts it may reach. A database that needs a server process or a network connection does not fit there.

Once relate is installed and usage metrics are off, it needs no network, so most sandboxes need egress only while the image is built. `DO_NOT_TRACK=1` sends nothing and prints no first-run notice. A store is a file in the workspace, such as `--database ./work.rl`, that can be committed with the change and opened `--read-only` for reads. The commands and flags that do reach the network, `--load` from a URL, `--fetch-params`, `pull`, `push`, `upgrade` and extension installs, each appear on the command line the agent runs. The guide [Run relate in a sandbox](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/run-in-a-sandbox/) lists the hosts to allow and the setup for each harness. The step that verifies this entry shows `relate telemetry status` reporting usage metrics disabled by `DO_NOT_TRACK`; that no network is needed after installation rests on the sandbox guide and the privacy reference, not on a recorded run.

- **Problem:** Run a graph database where an agent works isolated, with no network after setup and nothing sent anywhere.
- **Capability:** A single binary that needs no network once installed with usage metrics off (`DO_NOT_TRACK=1`), stores that are files in the workspace, and network access visible on the command line.
- **Surfaces:** `cli`, `docker`, `agents`
- **Guides:** [Run relate in a sandbox](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/run-in-a-sandbox/), [Keep an agent safe](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/agent-safety/)
- **Reference:** [Privacy and telemetry](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/privacy-and-telemetry/), [Security](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/security/), [relate telemetry](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/telemetry/), [relate upgrade](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/upgrade/), [relate extension](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/extension/)
- **Verified by:** the `bash verify` step 1 on [Run relate in a sandbox](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/run-in-a-sandbox/#verify), whose recorded output begins `disabled (DO_NOT_TRACK)`; the CLI check replays it against a relate binary

properties.heading: Schema as files
properties.text:
The schema of a database usually lives inside it: to learn which indexes and constraints exist, an agent or a reviewer has to open the store and run a `SHOW` statement, and a schema change in a pull request is invisible next to the code that relies on it.

Every checkpoint of a durable store writes its schema as text under `.cypherlite/schema/` inside the store. `schema.cypher` holds one `CREATE INDEX` or `CREATE CONSTRAINT` statement per entry, with the graph type beside it when the store has one, so one file read answers what the schema is and a schema change shows up as an ordinary diff. The text is a copy, not the source: an open compares it with the schema the checkpoint persisted, and a hand-edited file fails the open with an error naming the file, which says that deleting the folder and reopening regenerates it. Schema changes are made with Cypher statements, and the next checkpoint rewrites the files.

- **Problem:** Let an agent or a reviewer read a store's indexes and constraints from a file instead of opening the database, and see a schema change as a text diff.
- **Capability:** A text copy of the schema under `.cypherlite/schema/`, with `schema.cypher` holding one `CREATE` statement per index and constraint, rewritten at every checkpoint and checked at every open.
- **Surfaces:** `cli`, `agents`
- **Guides:** [Choose a store layout](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/choose-a-store-layout/), [Keep the schema as files](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/schema-as-files/)
- **Reference:** [Storage formats](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/storage/formats/), [WAL and checkpoints](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/storage/wal-and-checkpoints/), [Schema clauses](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/schema-clauses/)
- **Verified by:** the `bash verify` step 2 on [Storage formats](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/storage/formats/#parquet-data-files), whose recorded output begins `layout: native directory`; the CLI check replays it against a relate binary

properties.heading: Shared store across processes
properties.text:
An embedded database belongs to the process that opens it, but real setups have more than one process: an application that writes the graph and an agent that reads it, or several workers reading the same data. Two writers on one set of files would corrupt it, so the database has to say who may write and what everyone else gets.

A relate store has one writer: the first process that opens it for writing owns it until it exits, and a second writable open fails with `storage locked: <path>` and exit code 5. A directory store can be opened `--read-only` beside its writer by several readers, and `--read-only=live` follows the writer's commits; a `.rl` file allows no second opener while a writer holds it. For clients that must all write, one `relate serve` process hosts the store for Bolt, HTTP Query API and MCP clients. [Share one store between two processes](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/two-processes-one-store/) shows each case, and inside one process concurrent transactions that write the same data get a retryable write-write conflict ([Transactions and concurrency](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/transactions-and-concurrency/)).

- **Problem:** Let an agent and an application, or several readers, use the same graph without corrupting it or blocking each other.
- **Capability:** One writer per store, enforced by a lock; `--read-only` opens beside the writer on a directory store; `--read-only=live` to follow its commits; or one `relate serve` process.
- **Surfaces:** `cli`, `http`, `bolt`, `mcp`
- **Guides:** [Share one store between two processes](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/two-processes-one-store/), [Choose a store layout](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/choose-a-store-layout/), [Open a store read-only and follow a writer](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/read-only-and-follow/), [Serve the HTTP Query API](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/serve/http-query-api/), [Serve a store over Bolt](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/serve/bolt/), [Use relate with CrewAI](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/integrations/crewai/)
- **Reference:** [Storage formats](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/storage/formats/), [Exit codes and errors](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/exit-codes-and-errors/), [relate serve](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/serve/)
- **Verified by:** the `bash verify` step 2 on [Share one store between two processes](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/two-processes-one-store/#see-what-the-second-process-gets), whose recorded output begins `Failed to open Relate: storage locked: <dir>/team.rl`; the CLI check replays it against a relate binary

properties.heading: Single-file graph
properties.text:
A graph that travels, attached to an issue, shipped with an application, handed from one agent run to the next, is easier to handle as one file than as a folder of data files and logs. The file has to hold everything, including commits not yet checkpointed, so a copy is never missing its newest writes.

A store whose path ends in `.rl` is one file holding the same tree as a directory store, its write-ahead log included. relate creates it on the first writable open, and every client spells it the same way. A plain copy taken while no process has the file open is a complete backup, and `relate clone` writes a compact copy holding only the current state, since a `.rl` file keeps the most space it has needed. `--load` reads the file into an in-memory copy, which is read-only, without holding the file. One writer locks the whole file, so a reader cannot open it beside a running writer; [Choose a store layout](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/choose-a-store-layout/) compares it with the directory store, which allows that.

- **Problem:** Keep a whole graph in one file that can be copied, attached, checked in or handed to another program.
- **Capability:** The `.rl` store: one file holding the snapshot and the write-ahead log, created on the first open, compacted by `relate clone`, and read into memory with `--load`.
- **Surfaces:** `cli`, `python`, `node`
- **Guides:** [Choose a store layout](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/choose-a-store-layout/), [Back up and restore a store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/backup-and-restore/), [Clone and convert a store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/clone-and-convert/)
- **Reference:** [Storage formats](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/storage/formats/), [relate clone](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/clone/)
- **Verified by:** the Python sample `open-layouts` on [Choose a store layout](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/choose-a-store-layout/#open-a-store-from-python-or-nodejs), whose output is recorded from a run against the Python client

properties.heading: Text-to-Cypher
properties.text:
A model that writes Cypher needs three things it cannot guess: the labels, relationship types and properties of this graph, the dialect this engine accepts, and a way to find out that a statement is wrong before it changes anything. Without them it writes plausible statements for a schema it imagined, often in a dialect from its training data.

relate supplies each from the engine itself. `CALL db.schema.nodeTypeProperties()` returns every label's properties and their types, and over MCP the `get_schema` tool returns the labels, properties and relationship types for the model's context. `EXPLAIN` plans a statement without running it, so a write, a procedure or a `LOAD CSV` is only planned, and the plan comes back with the planner's notifications. A store opened `--read-only` refuses any write the model produces. [Differences from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/differences-from-neo4j/) lists the constructs a model trained on Neo4j examples reaches for that relate does not have, with the error each produces and what to write instead.

- **Problem:** Let a model turn a question into a Cypher statement over a graph whose schema it can read, and check the statement before it runs.
- **Capability:** The schema as data from the `db.schema` procedures and the MCP `get_schema` tool, `EXPLAIN` to plan a statement without running it, and read-only opens that refuse writes.
- **Surfaces:** `cypher`, `mcp`, `cli`, `agents`
- **Guides:** [Turn questions into Cypher with an LLM](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/text-to-cypher/), [Tune a query](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/tune-a-query/), [Connect over MCP](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/connect-over-mcp/), [Use relate with the OpenAI Agents SDK](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/integrations/openai-agents-sdk/), [Use relate with Mastra](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/integrations/mastra/)
- **Recipes:** [Answer codebase questions text search can't](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/codebase-context-graph/)
- **Reference:** [Differences from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/differences-from-neo4j/), [Cypher overview](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/overview/), [Errors](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/), [Schema clauses (`#schema-procedures`)](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/schema-clauses/#schema-procedures), [Procedures (`#schema-procedures`)](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/procedures/#schema-procedures), [EXPLAIN and PROFILE](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/explain-and-profile/)
- **Verified by:** cell `schema` on [Differences from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/differences-from-neo4j/#cell-schema), replayed against its recorded result by the docs checks on every pull request

properties.heading: Tool-call provenance
properties.text:
When an agent's memory holds something wrong, the questions are about history: which call wrote the fact, which calls have read it since, and what the calls that failed left behind. A log kept in a separate system answers them only after a join across two stores, and only if both recorded the same identifiers. In the [tool-call provenance recipe](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/tool-call-provenance/) the trace lives in the memory graph itself. Every call becomes a `ToolCall` node, written by the same statement as the call, and `TOUCHED` relationships link it to each node the call wrote or returned. NODE KEY and relationship property constraints refuse an audit row that repeats a sequence number or carries a timestamp of the wrong type. An audit is then a graph read: the lineage of one fact, what each tool cost, and which calls rolled back. ```mermaid flowchart TB accTitle: Recommended data model for tool-call provenance: the agent's memory and the trace of every call beside it accDescr { A Session HAS_CALL each of its ToolCall nodes, with a timestamp. A ToolCall records its sequence number, tool name, status and row count, and TOUCHED the Entity and Fact nodes it wrote or returned. A Fact is ABOUT an Entity. } Session(("Session
id")) -- "HAS_CALL
ts" --> ToolCall(("ToolCall
seq · name · status
rows · error")) ToolCall -- "TOUCHED" --> Entity(("Entity
key · kind")) ToolCall -- "TOUCHED" --> Fact(("Fact
text")) Fact -- "ABOUT" --> Entity class Session l1 class ToolCall l2 class Entity l3 class Fact l4 ``` A Session HAS_CALL each of its ToolCall nodes, with a timestamp. A ToolCall records its sequence number, tool name, status and row count, and TOUCHED the Entity and Fact nodes it wrote or returned. A Fact is ABOUT an Entity. - **Problem:** Find out which tool call wrote a fact in an agent's memory, which calls read it since, and what failed calls left behind. - **Capability:** Each tool call recorded as a node in the same graph, by the same statement as the call, linked to every node it wrote or returned and guarded by `NODE KEY` and relationship property constraints. - **Surfaces:** `cypher`, `agents` - **Guides:** [Model agent memory](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/model-agent-memory/) - **Recipes:** [Audit where an agent's memories came from](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/tool-call-provenance/) - **Reference:** [Cypher overview](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/overview/) - **Verified by:** cell `lineage` of the recipe [Audit where an agent's memories came from](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/tool-call-provenance/#cell-lineage), replayed against its recorded result on every build

properties.heading: What the catalog leaves out
properties.text: An entry exists only where a published page or recipe shows the capability, so the catalog is shorter than the list of things relate can do. It also leaves out the problems relate's shape does not fit: a graph larger than one machine's memory, several processes writing one [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store), a service that must survive a machine failure, users and roles kept apart inside one database, and statements that join several graphs. Each of those comes from a limit, and the [limitations reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/limitations/) gives the error each one produces.

properties.heading: Where this shows up
properties.text:
- [/docs/capabilities.json](https://relatedb.ai/docs/capabilities.json): the entries on this page as data, with intents and canonical URLs.
- [Where relate fits](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/where-relate-fits/): the shape every entry shares, and when to use something else.
- [Model agent memory](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/model-agent-memory/): the data model the agent memory entry recommends, built cell by cell.
- [The cookbook](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/): every recipe an entry cites, runnable in the browser.
- [Limitations](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/limitations/): the limits behind the problems this page leaves out.

properties.heading: Security and trust
properties.text: What does relate trust, and why are its defaults where they are? relate runs with the authority of the process that starts it, so it cannot protect a store from the person who owns the file. What it can do is decide what reaches that process without anyone choosing it: a write from a statement an agent produced, a connection from another machine, a file outside the working directory, a binary or a package from the network, a page of documentation read as an order. Each default keeps one of those out, and each way to let it in is a flag or a command that shows on the command line, where a person, a reviewer or a sandbox policy can see it.

properties.heading: Code from elsewhere is checked before it lands
properties.text:
A release is trusted because of a key, not a download location. Every release's `SHA256SUMS` is signed with one Ed25519 key, and `install.sh` and `relate upgrade` check that signature against a copy of the key they carry, never one fetched from the release. The signed manifest's first line names its release, so an older, validly signed manifest cannot be replayed as a newer one, and the binary must match its line. Any failure installs nothing. A pinned install in CI makes the same checks ([Use relate in CI](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/use-in-ci/)).

[Extensions](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#extension), the packages `relate run` starts, come in tiers, each matched to what can be known about the source. The first-party channel's index is signed with the same release key. A package from someone else's GitHub release has no key to check, so its pin is the trust: the first install records the commit its tag resolved to and the asset's SHA-256, and a later install that resolves differently is refused before anything is downloaded. A package from a URL or a local directory carries no signature at all, and naming that source on the command line is the act of trusting it. Nothing installs itself, and `relate run` starts only what is installed.

properties.heading: Documentation is data
properties.text: An agent reads these docs, and the [skill bundle](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#skill-bundle) as input to its task, so that input must not be able to steer it. Every twin, skill file and tool result is reference text: outside a fenced prompt a person chooses to paste, nothing addresses the agent as an order. The skill is copied from the engine repository at a recorded commit, with the SHA-256 of each file, and each refresh is reviewed before it is published.

properties.heading: Files and the network appear on the command line
properties.text:
`LOAD CSV` reads no local file until `--load-csv-dir` names a directory, and then only regular files under it. A path that escapes the directory, a symlink out of it and a special file fail with the same message, which names no path, so a probing statement learns nothing about the filesystem. The default is closed because a statement is data an agent may have assembled from text it read, and a file read is the first step toward sending a file somewhere.

The commands and flags that reach the network, `--load` from a URL, `--fetch-params`, [pull](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#pull) and [push](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#push), `upgrade` and `extension install`, reach the network only when they run, and none is triggered by a statement. Each reaches a known place: `--load` and `--fetch-params` the URL on their command line; `pull` the Neo4j URI in the env file `--from` names, or in the `NEO4J_URI` environment variable; `push` the URI or env file `--to` names; `upgrade` relatedb.ai's `releases.json` and the release assets it lists; `extension install` the signed first-party channel, unless `--github` or `--url` names another source. So a sandbox can allow exactly the hosts a task needs ([Run relate in a sandbox](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/run-in-a-sandbox/) lists them). A store published at a URL is safest downloaded, checked against its published SHA-256, and loaded from the local copy, which is why `--safe` refuses the remote form.

Usage metrics are the one thing the CLI sends on its own. They carry no query text, store paths or parameter values, because the events have no fields for them, and `DO_NOT_TRACK=1` turns them off ([Privacy and telemetry](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/privacy-and-telemetry/)).

properties.heading: One principal, widened on purpose
properties.text:
An embedded engine has one principal: the process. There are no users, roles or grants inside a store, because everything that could hold them, the file, the process and the host, already belongs to someone. relate's controls therefore act at the boundaries of the process, and the default at each boundary is the narrow one.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: The boundaries of a relate process and their defaults
  accDescr {
    A relate process has five boundaries.
    Statements reach the store and can be limited with read-only and safe mode; network clients reach it only on loopback with a generated credential; local files reach LOAD CSV only from a named directory.
    Releases and extensions come in only after a signature or a pinned checksum is checked, and documentation comes in as reference text, never as instructions.
  }
  P(["relate process and its store"])
  A["Statements: read-only, safe mode"] --> P
  N["Network clients: loopback, generated credential"] --> P
  F["Local files: LOAD CSV from one named directory"] --> P
  R["Releases and extensions: signature or pinned checksum"] --> P
  D["Docs and skill: reference text, not instructions"] --> P
```

A relate process has five boundaries. Statements reach the store and can be limited with read-only and safe mode; network clients reach it only on loopback with a generated credential; local files reach LOAD CSV only from a named directory. Releases and extensions come in only after a signature or a pinned checksum is checked, and documentation comes in as reference text, never as instructions.

The defaults bias toward the case that is hard to undo: an unwanted write, an open port or an unchecked binary costs more to discover later than a flag costs to type now, and the flag stays visible in the command an agent runs.

properties.heading: Read-only is a guarantee, safe mode is a policy
properties.text:
`--read-only` is structural. The engine opens the store without a writer: no write is applied, no checkpoint runs, no migration happens, and a write statement fails before it changes anything. Because no statement can talk its way around it, it is the control these docs put on every block an agent can copy, with one line saying how to allow writes. For an agent that answers questions, read-only turns a wrong statement into an error message instead of a damaged graph.

[Safe mode](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#safe-mode) works differently. `--safe` refuses statement shapes agents commonly get wrong, such as a new named node without a label or a `MATCH` read with neither a `LIMIT` nor a reducing aggregate, and a remote `--load`. It judges the shape of a statement, not its effect, so it is off unless asked for: it refuses an unbounded read of a ten-node store, and a labeled `DETACH DELETE` passes it. It keeps a writing agent's reads bounded; it does not stand in for read-only.

properties.heading: Servers listen on loopback, with a credential
properties.text:
`relate serve` hosts Bolt, the HTTP Query API, and MCP on one store. None of them has TLS, so anything a client sends crosses the wire in plaintext. That is why the server binds `127.0.0.1` unless told otherwise, and why a non-loopback `--host` prints a warning at startup: exposing a plaintext surface is a decision the operator makes out loud, with a TLS proxy, or a private network, in front.

The same reasoning sets authentication. A server started without `--auth` generates a token, prints it, and keeps it beside the store in a file only its owner can read, so a server is never open by accident, even on loopback, where every local process can connect. Turning authentication off takes `--auth none`, written out. There is one credential for every surface, not a user list, because the store has one principal. MCP over stdio asks for none: the host that started the process is its only client, and holds its pipes.

properties.heading: What the defaults leave to you
properties.text: The model stops at the process. relate's surfaces have no TLS and the store has no user accounts; a store is as private as its file permissions. No release publishes a software bill of materials. The npm packages carry npm provenance and the PyPI files trusted-publishing attestations, and vulnerabilities are reported to `security@neo4j.com` under the engine's security policy ([Security](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/security/#reporting-a-vulnerability)). Inside those lines, the defaults let an agent work with the least it needs, and a person widen that one visible flag at a time.

properties.heading: Where this shows up
properties.text:
- [Security](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/security/): the signing key, what each install check proves, and the served surfaces' defaults.
- [Keep an agent safe](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/agent-safety/): read-only, safe mode, backups and the permission matrix across the CLI and MCP.
- [Privacy and telemetry](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/privacy-and-telemetry/): what the CLI sends and how to turn it off.
- [Run relate in a sandbox](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/run-in-a-sandbox/): the hosts to allow, and why the network is needed only to install.
- [Agent-native by design](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/agent-native/): the envelope, typed errors, and the row cap.

properties.heading: Storage and durability
properties.text: What happens to a write between the statement and the disk, and what can a crash take back? In relate, every commit takes one path: its changes are appended to the [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store)'s [write-ahead log](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#wal) (WAL), then applied to the graph in memory, which is where every query reads. Disk is for recovery, not for answering queries. Under the default durability mode the log is synced to disk before a commit is acknowledged, so a crash loses no acknowledged write; the two relaxed modes skip that wait and accept a stated loss window instead.

properties.heading: Checkpoints
properties.text:
A [checkpoint](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#checkpoint) turns the log into a snapshot. It pins a position in the log, writes the committed state up to it through the store's codec, then recycles the closed WAL segments the snapshot now covers. Writers do not stop: new commits go to the next segment while the snapshot is written.

A checkpoint runs when the current segment reaches 64 MiB or 10,000 commits, every 300 seconds by default (`--checkpoint-interval-secs`, or `RELATE_CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL_SECS` for `relate serve`), and when a writable store closes cleanly. The CLI closes cleanly on every exit from a writable run, so a store last written from the CLI has its state in the snapshot. A process that keeps a store open, such as an application or `relate serve`, carries recent commits in the WAL until the next checkpoint. That is why a backup copies the WAL along with the snapshot, or uses `relate clone`.

An in-memory store has no files, so its checkpoints only recycle the WAL.

properties.heading: Codecs
properties.text:
A [codec](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#codec) is the encoding a checkpoint writes the snapshot in. `parquet`, the default, writes compact columnar files and rewrites only the id ranges that changed. `json` rewrites one readable `graph.json` every time. `markdown` writes one note per node. The WAL's format is the same under every codec.

Queries never read the snapshot files, so the codec decides size on disk, checkpoint cost and how long an open takes to load, not how fast a statement runs. A store keeps the codec it was created with; `relate clone --to-snapshot-format` makes a copy in another.

properties.heading: Durability modes and their loss windows
properties.text:
The durability mode decides when a commit is acknowledged relative to the WAL sync. It is chosen per open with `--durability-mode` or `RELATE_DURABILITY_MODE`, and is not stored in the store.

| Mode             | A commit is acknowledged                                     | A crash can lose                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `full` (default) | After the WAL is synced to disk                              | No acknowledged write                                                                                                                |
| `everysecond`    | After it is applied; the WAL is synced about once per second | About the last second of acknowledged writes; slow scheduling or storage can widen the window                                        |
| `snapshot`       | Without a WAL sync                                           | Every write since the last completed checkpoint: up to 300 seconds of writes under the default timer, fewer when the WAL fills first |

The relaxed modes exist for work that can be rebuilt: a bulk load from a file that still exists, or a scratch store an agent fills and throws away. [Choose a durability mode](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/durability-modes/) covers when each fits and how to set it.

properties.heading: One write path
properties.text:
The write path step by step, what each durability mode can lose in a crash, and the parts of one `.rl` file.

**The write path**, under the default durability mode, `full`. One commit:

1. The statement runs and collects its changes privately; nothing is written yet.
2. At commit, the changes become one record, numbered by its log sequence number (LSN). It holds physical changes to nodes, relationships, labels and properties, not Cypher text.
3. The record is appended to the open WAL segment, `wal/NNNNNNNN.log`.
4. The WAL is synced to disk before the commit returns; commits waiting together share one sync.
5. The changes are applied to the in-memory graph, where every query reads.
6. The commit is acknowledged.

A checkpoint:

1. The open segment closes, and new commits go to the next one, so writers do not stop.
2. The checkpoint pins the LSN of the newest closed segment's last record.
3. The committed state up to that LSN goes through the store's codec into snapshot files, under temporary names.
4. The files are renamed into place, `manifest.json` last. A crash before the renames leaves the previous snapshot in force.
5. Closed segments whose last record is at or below the pinned LSN are deleted.

A checkpoint runs when the open segment reaches 64 MiB or 10,000 commits, every 300 seconds by default, when a writable store closes cleanly, and on `.checkpoint`.

After a crash, the next open:

1. Loads the latest snapshot: the state at its checkpoint LSN.
2. Replays every WAL record with a higher LSN, in LSN order.
3. Drops a record the crash cut short at the very end of the WAL. Under `full` that commit was never acknowledged, so every acknowledged commit is back.

**What a crash can lose.** The durability mode decides when a commit is acknowledged relative to the WAL sync. It is a setting of the process that opens the store (`--durability-mode` or `RELATE_DURABILITY_MODE`, default `full`), not of the store.

The picture's timeline: 8 writes are acknowledged in the 4.6 s after a completed checkpoint, then the process crashes. A killed process can lose the window as well as a power cut.

| Mode          | The WAL is synced                                        | Acknowledged writes the crash at 4.6 s can lose |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `full`        | Before each commit, or group of commits, is acknowledged | None: all 8 come back                           |
| `everysecond` | About once a second, in the background                   | The 2 writes after the last sync, at 4 s        |
| `snapshot`    | Never on commit; only a completed checkpoint is durable  | All 8, every write since the checkpoint         |

Under `everysecond`, slow storage or a delayed sync makes the window longer than about a second. Under `snapshot`, the window runs until the next completed checkpoint: up to 300 seconds of writes under the default timer, fewer when a WAL segment fills first.

**One `.rl` file.** A single-file store keeps in one file the same tree a directory store spreads over a folder, WAL included. Its parts, in logical order rather than by byte position:

| Part            | Holds                                                                                                                                                     |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Superblock      | The container's version marker: magic `MDBCLB01`, version `1` (`relate info` prints `superblock version: 1`)                                              |
| Snapshot        | `manifest.json` and the codec's files (with the default `parquet` codec, the files under `nodes/` and `relationships/`): the state at the last checkpoint |
| WAL             | `wal/NNNNNNNN.log` segments: every commit since the last checkpoint                                                                                       |
| Space it reuses | The most space the snapshot and WAL have needed at once; later writes reuse what they no longer hold, and the file does not shrink                        |

A commit appends its record to the open segment inside the file. A checkpoint writes the new snapshot files inside it, publishes them with `manifest.json` last, and deletes the segments the snapshot covers. A writer holds the file itself, with no lock files beside it, so a `--read-only` open is refused while a writer has it, and `--wal-dir` is refused for a `.rl` path. `relate clone` writes a compact copy that holds only the current state.

Live: Commit, Checkpoint and Crash step through what relate does with the WAL, the in-memory graph and the snapshot (inside one `.rl` file in the file view), and a mode switch with a crash slider shades what `full`, `everysecond` and `snapshot` can lose; under reduced motion each step waits for Next. It is a diagram of documented behaviour: no engine runs.

![The write path, what each durability mode can lose in a crash and the parts of one .rl file, as relate documents them](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/storage-and-durability/element-write-path-light.svg)

A statement collects its changes privately while it runs. At commit they become one record of physical changes: a node or relationship created or deleted, a property set or removed, or a label added or removed. The record is not Cypher text, so replaying it never re-runs a query. relate appends the record to the WAL first and applies it to the in-memory graph second; the graph in memory is never the source of a commit.

A single statement outside a transaction is one commit. An explicit transaction collects all its statements and appends one record at `COMMIT`; a rollback appends nothing. [Transactions and concurrency](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/transactions-and-concurrency/) covers isolation and conflicts.

properties.heading: The write-ahead log
properties.text:
The WAL is a series of segment files, `wal/NNNNNNNN.log` in a directory store (`.cypherlite/wal/` under the `markdown` codec) and the same tree inside a `.rl` file. Each record carries a checksum. One commit's record can be at most 64 MiB; a larger commit is refused before anything is written, and splitting it into smaller transactions clears it.

On open, relate loads the latest [snapshot](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#snapshot) and replays every WAL record written after the snapshot's position in the log. Committed writes that never reached a snapshot survive this way. A crash can leave a final record cut short, which recovery does not count as a commit; [Recover from a crash](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/crash-and-recovery/) covers what recovery does and the errors it can report.

properties.heading: Trade-offs against a page cache design
properties.text:
Many databases keep their data in files on disk and cache recently used pages in memory. Their working set can be larger than RAM, at the cost of reads that sometimes wait on disk and a cache that needs warming and tuning. relate takes the other side of that trade:

| relate's choice                 | What it gives                                                                                               | What it costs                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The whole graph in memory       | Reads never wait on disk; there is no cache to size or warm                                                 | The graph and its indexes must fit in memory; there is no paging to disk                                        |
| Disk holds a snapshot and a log | Recovery is load-then-replay, the same path as every open                                                   | An open reads the whole snapshot, so startup grows with the graph rather than with what the first query touches |
| Snapshots in open formats       | `graph.json`, markdown notes and Parquet files can be read by other tools, and JSON can be diffed in review | A `json` checkpoint rewrites the whole file, so large stores favor `parquet`                                    |
| One process owns the store      | No shared cache or lock manager between processes                                                           | A second process reads a directory store with `--read-only`, or goes through `relate serve`                     |

The reason for this shape is the job relate is built for: an embedded graph that one application or agent owns, small enough to hold in memory, where the slow part should never be a cache miss. The disk remembers the graph; memory answers the questions.

- [Back up and restore a store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/backup-and-restore/): why a backup needs the WAL, and `relate clone`.
