properties.heading: Transactions and concurrency
properties.text: What happens when two things use a relate store at once? Inside one process, readers never block and never see a half-finished write: each statement reads the graph as of the last commit before it started. Writers run side by side but commit one at a time, and when two [transactions](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#transaction) change the same node or relationship, the later commit fails with a retryable [write-write conflict](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#conflict) instead of overwriting the first. Across processes, a store has one writer; other processes can read a [directory store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#directory-store) with `--read-only`.

properties.heading: How a reader sees a consistent graph
properties.text:
relate keeps several versions of each changed node and relationship, each stamped with the commit that made it. A reader pins its starting point in the commit order and sees only versions committed by then. Nothing is copied to make that view, and readers take no lock, so a long read and a stream of writes run together. Old versions are dropped once no reader still needs them.

The starting point depends on the transaction:

| Transaction                                                                                                                                                                                              | Reads see                                                                                        |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Autocommit, the default: one statement is one commit                                                                                                                                                     | The graph as of the last commit before the statement started                                     |
| Explicit: `begin` … `commit` on a client, `.begin` … `.commit` in the CLI shell or a piped script ([shell dot commands](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/dot-commands/#begin-commit-and-rollback)) | The graph as of the last commit before `begin`, plus the transaction's own writes, until it ends |

An explicit transaction keeps its writes in a private overlay and appends them to the log once, at commit. A dropped connection, or a `.quit` with a transaction open, rolls it back. Transactions don't nest: a second `begin` fails with `already in a transaction`. After a statement fails inside one, every later statement and the commit fail with `transaction failed; rollback required` until it rolls back.

properties.heading: One process, one writer path
properties.text:
A persistent [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store) belongs to the process that opened it for writing. The engine holds the whole graph in that process's memory, so there is no shared buffer for a second process to write through. A second writable open of the same store fails at once with `storage locked: <path>` (exit code 5, not retryable until the first process exits). Several clients that need to write share the store through one process instead: the application itself, or `relate serve` hosting Bolt, HTTP, and MCP clients on one engine.

Inside that process, many statements can run at once on different threads and connections. Every commit passes through one point, the append to the write-ahead log, which puts commits in a single order.

properties.heading: Reading from another process
properties.text:
`--read-only` opens a store without writing anything: no log append, no checkpoint, no migration. It comes in two freshnesses:

| Open               | Sees                                                                                 | Works on                                                                                                       |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--read-only`      | The store as it was when it opened; reopening picks up later commits                 | A directory store beside its writer; a `.rl` file only while no writer holds it; `:memory:`, where writes fail |
| `--read-only=live` | New commits as the writer appends them; a running statement keeps the view it pinned | A directory store only                                                                                         |

Several [read-only](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#read-only) opens can share a directory store with its writer. A `.rl` file stays exclusive because the whole store is one file.

properties.heading: Trade-offs
properties.text:
Pinned views make reads cheap and consistent: no read locks, no torn results, and a reader that started before a write never sees part of it. Optimistic commits keep writers from waiting on each other's locks. The cost moves to the client: under contention for the same nodes, some commits fail and run again, and only invariants that a uniqueness or key constraint can state are checked at commit; other read/write dependencies still commit, so the application guards them itself.

One writing process per store keeps the engine free of cross-process locking and cache coherence, and lets the graph live in one process's memory. A workload with many independent writer processes fits a client/server database better; [where relate fits](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/where-relate-fits/) lists that condition with the others.

properties.heading: Where this shows up
properties.text:
- [Share one store between two processes](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/two-processes-one-store/): the locked error, and serving or reading a store beside its writer.
- [Keep an agent safe](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/agent-safety/): exploring with `--read-only` and retrying only what is retryable.
- [Storage and durability](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/storage-and-durability/): when a commit reaches disk under each durability mode.
- [Errors](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/#cli-conflict-conflict): the conflict and locked errors with their codes and remedies.
- [Exit codes and errors](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/exit-codes-and-errors/): exit code 5 and the `retryable` field.

properties.heading: Write-write conflicts and retry
Where relate fits
properties.text: Does relate fit the job? It does when the graph belongs to one application, one agent or one tool, lives on one machine, and fits in that machine's memory. relate is an embedded graph database: the engine runs inside your process, the whole graph is held in memory, and Cypher statements run against it with nothing to deploy. When the data must be shared by many writing processes, outgrows one machine, or must stay up through a machine failure, a client/server or clustered database fits better.

properties.heading: The shape of the thing
properties.text:
A relate [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store) is a directory, a single `.rl` file, or `:memory:`. One process opens it and owns it. Inside that process the engine holds the whole graph in memory and answers statements from there; disk is for durability, not for scanning. Every commit goes to the write-ahead log ([WAL](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#wal)) before it applies, and a checkpoint later writes the committed graph back to the store. The same engine sits behind every front door: the `relate` CLI, the Python, Node.js, Rust, Java, Go and Swift clients, the C ABI, and a WebAssembly build for the browser. `relate serve` hosts one store in one process for Bolt, HTTP Query API and [MCP](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#mcp) clients, so several clients can share a store through that one process. ```mermaid flowchart TB accTitle: One process owns the store accDescr { An application, agent or CLI runs the relate engine inside its own process, with the whole graph in memory. The engine writes each commit to the store on disk, a single .rl file or a directory. Another process can open a directory store read-only beside the writer. Bolt, HTTP and MCP clients reach the engine through one relate serve process. } A["Application, agent or CLI"] --> E["relate engine
whole graph in memory"] C["Bolt, HTTP and MCP clients"] -->|"relate serve"| E E -->|"commit: WAL, then checkpoint"| S[("Store on disk
.rl file or directory")] R["Another process
--read-only"] -.->|"beside a writer: directory store only"| S ``` An application, agent or CLI runs the relate engine inside its own process, with the whole graph in memory. The engine writes each commit to the store on disk, a single .rl file or a directory. Another process can open a directory store read-only beside the writer. Bolt, HTTP and MCP clients reach the engine through one relate serve process.

properties.heading: Trade-offs
properties.text:
The shape buys three things. Statements skip the network round trip a server needs, so a query costs the work it does. A store is a file or a folder the operating system already knows how to copy, back up, and delete. And there is no server process to configure, secure, or keep running.

The price is the list of conditions under "Use something else when". Memory bounds the graph, one process owns each store, and availability is the availability of that process. relate is pre-1.0; the [project reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/project/) states what that means for stability and upgrades.

properties.heading: Use relate when
properties.text:
| Condition                                                            | What makes it work                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The graph belongs to one application, agent, or tool on one machine  | The engine runs in that process, so a statement never crosses a network                                                                                                                                                         |
| You want Cypher with nothing to install beyond a binary or a package | The CLI is one binary; each client package carries the engine; `:memory:` needs no files at all                                                                                                                                 |
| A graph should travel as one file                                    | A `.rl` store is one file that can be copied, attached or committed; `--load` opens one from a path or an `https` URL                                                                                                           |
| An agent drives the database from a shell or over MCP                | Envelopes, typed exit codes, a row cap under agent harnesses, the skill and the MCP [surface](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#surface) ([agent-native by design](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/agent-native/)) |
| Tests or CI need a fresh graph on every run                          | `:memory:` forgets everything when the process exits                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Neo4j tools need to reach a local graph                              | `relate serve` speaks Bolt and the HTTP Query API; `relate pull` and `relate push` copy subgraphs from and to Neo4j or Aura                                                                                                     |

properties.heading: Use something else when
properties.text:
Each condition comes from a limit that is part of relate's shape, not a gap waiting for a patch. The [limitations reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/limitations/) is the complete list.

| Condition                                                           | The limit it comes from                                                                                                                                                                                            | Read more                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The graph outgrows one machine's memory                             | **RAM-resident.** The whole graph lives in memory; there is no paging, buffer pool, or spill to disk. `--logical-graph-size-limit` caps growth but does not move data to disk                                      | [Size a store and its memory](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/sizing-and-memory/)                 |
| Several processes must write the same store                         | **Single process.** A store has one owner. A second writable open fails with `storage locked: <path>` (exit code 5). Several clients can share one `relate serve` process instead                                  | [Share one store between two processes](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/two-processes-one-store/) |
| Many writers update the same nodes at once                          | **One writer path.** Transactions commit optimistically; when two overlap on the same data, the later one fails with `write-write conflict` and the client retries                                                 | [Transactions and concurrency](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/transactions-and-concurrency/)           |
| The service must survive a machine failure or scale across machines | **No cluster.** There is no replication, failover, or sharding                                                                                                                                                     | [Limitations](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/limitations/)                                            |
| Users and roles must be kept apart inside one database              | **No access control inside the store.** There are no users or roles; `relate serve` checks one basic-auth credential shared by every surface                                                                       | [Security](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/security/)                                                  |
| One statement must join data from several graphs                    | **No cross-graph queries.** A store holds one user graph; `USE` names only the fixed [namespaces](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#namespace), and any other name fails with `Graph not found: <name>` | [Limitations](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/limitations/)                                            |
| The job is analytics over data larger than memory                   | **Not out-of-core.** The engine is built for a working set in RAM, not for scanning columnar files                                                                                                                 | [Size a store and its memory](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/sizing-and-memory/)                 |

For the cross-graph case, the usual answer inside relate is to keep data that a statement must join in one store, with labels to tell the parts apart, or to query each store and combine the results in application code.

properties.heading: Where this shows up
properties.text:
- [Limitations](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/limitations/): every limit, with the error each one produces.
- [Size a store and its memory](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/sizing-and-memory/): estimate whether a graph fits.
- [Share one store between two processes](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/two-processes-one-store/): what happens when a second process opens a store, and the ways to share one.
- [Architecture](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/architecture/): how the engine, the planner, and the surfaces fit together.

properties.heading: Give an agent a memory
properties.text: In about ten minutes, we give an agent a memory that outlives its session: one file, `memory.rl`, holding what it learned, where it learned it, and which later fact corrected an earlier one. We write two episodes from the command line and a third over MCP, the way an agent host does, then recall by meaning. The data model comes from [Model agent memory](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/model-agent-memory/), which explains each label and property; this page builds it and uses it.

properties.heading: Create the memory store
properties.text:
A memory attaches to the things it is about. Ours is about the shared example graph, three people and two projects, and every person and project becomes an `Entity` with a lowercase `key`. The schema adds a [constraint](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#constraint) that keeps one node per key, episode and fact, an index on the fact's slot, and a vector index for recall by meaning. Write it all to a script:

```bash verify
cat > memory.cypher <<'EOF'
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace);
MATCH (n) WHERE n:Person OR n:Project SET n:Entity, n.key = toLower(n.name);
CREATE CONSTRAINT entity_key IF NOT EXISTS FOR (e:Entity) REQUIRE e.key IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT episode_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (ep:Episode) REQUIRE ep.id IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT fact_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (f:Fact) REQUIRE f.id IS UNIQUE;
CREATE INDEX fact_slot IF NOT EXISTS FOR (f:Fact) ON (f.slot);
CREATE VECTOR INDEX fact_embedding IF NOT EXISTS
  FOR (f:Fact) ON (f.embedding) WITH [f.closedAt]
  OPTIONS {indexConfig: {`vector.dimensions`: 4, `vector.similarity_function`: 'cosine'}};
MATCH (e:Entity) RETURN e.key AS key ORDER BY key;
EOF
```

Run it into a new [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store), `memory.rl`, which relate creates because nothing is there yet:

```bash verify
relate query --database ./memory.rl --mode table < memory.cypher
```

```text
+------------------+
| key              |
+------------------+
| "ada"            |
| "grace"          |
| "noor"           |
| "opencypher-tck" |
| "relate"         |
+------------------+
```

Five entities, each with the key a memory write matches on. The vector index takes 4-dimension vectors so this page's results never change; a real embedding model's vectors have hundreds of dimensions.

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- `relate` on your `PATH`: `relate --version` prints `Relate v1.0.1` on its first line. The [install page](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/) takes about two minutes.
- A terminal on macOS or Linux, in an empty directory.

properties.heading: Recall by meaning
properties.text:
A recall takes the embedding of a question, finds the nearest facts that are still current, and brings back the evidence for each and what it replaced. The cells in this section run in your browser, on an in-memory store with the same engine: the first two hold the same memory as `memory.rl`, written in one batch, and the third is the recall.

```cypher run name=memory
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace);
MATCH (n) WHERE n:Person OR n:Project SET n:Entity, n.key = toLower(n.name);
CREATE CONSTRAINT entity_key IF NOT EXISTS FOR (e:Entity) REQUIRE e.key IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT episode_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (ep:Episode) REQUIRE ep.id IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT fact_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (f:Fact) REQUIRE f.id IS UNIQUE;
CREATE INDEX fact_slot IF NOT EXISTS FOR (f:Fact) ON (f.slot);
CREATE VECTOR INDEX fact_embedding IF NOT EXISTS
  FOR (f:Fact) ON (f.embedding) WITH [f.closedAt]
  OPTIONS {indexConfig: {`vector.dimensions`: 4, `vector.similarity_function`: 'cosine'}};
MATCH (e:Entity) RETURN e.key AS key ORDER BY key
```

```table
| key              |
|------------------|
| "ada"            |
| "grace"          |
| "noor"           |
| "opencypher-tck" |
| "relate"         |
5 rows · nodes created: 5, relationships created: 5, properties set: 18, labels added: 10, indexes added: 2, constraints added: 3
```

```json data=episodes
{"episodes": [
  {"id": "e1", "session": "s1", "kind": "message", "at": "2026-03-02T10:00:00Z",
   "text": "Grace does the release review for relate.", "about": ["grace", "relate"],
   "factId": "f1", "fact": "Grace reviews each relate release.", "slot": "relate/release-reviewer",
   "validFrom": "2026-01-05T00:00:00Z", "embedding": [0.9, 0.1, 0.0, 0.2]},
  {"id": "e2", "session": "s1", "kind": "message", "at": "2026-03-02T10:05:00Z",
   "text": "Noor goes through new relate issues every Monday.", "about": ["noor", "relate"],
   "factId": "f2", "fact": "Noor triages new relate issues on Mondays.", "slot": "relate/triage",
   "validFrom": "2026-02-02T00:00:00Z", "embedding": [0.1, 0.9, 0.2, 0.0]},
  {"id": "e3", "session": "s2", "kind": "tool_call", "at": "2026-03-20T09:00:00Z",
   "text": "read_file CODEOWNERS: release/ @ada", "about": ["ada", "relate"],
   "factId": "f3", "fact": "Ada reviews each relate release.", "slot": "relate/release-reviewer",
   "validFrom": "2026-03-10T00:00:00Z", "embedding": [0.85, 0.15, 0.05, 0.25]}
]}
```

```cypher run name=remember params=episodes
UNWIND $episodes AS m
CREATE (ep:Episode {id: m.id, session: m.session, kind: m.kind, at: datetime(m.at), text: m.text})
CREATE (f:Fact {id: m.factId, text: m.fact, slot: m.slot, validFrom: datetime(m.validFrom),
                recordedAt: datetime(m.at), embedding: vector(m.embedding, 4, FLOAT32)})
CREATE (f)-[:FROM]->(ep)
WITH ep, f, m
CALL (ep, f, m) {
  UNWIND m.about AS key
  MATCH (n:Entity {key: key})
  CREATE (ep)-[:MENTIONS]->(n), (f)-[:ABOUT]->(n)
}
CALL (f) {
  MATCH (old:Fact {slot: f.slot}) WHERE old.recordedAt < f.recordedAt AND old.closedAt IS NULL
  SET old.validTo = f.validFrom, old.closedAt = f.recordedAt
  CREATE (f)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(old)
  RETURN count(old) AS replaced
}
RETURN ep.id AS episode, f.text AS fact, replaced
```

```table
| episode | fact                                         | replaced |
|---------|----------------------------------------------|----------|
| "e1"    | "Grace reviews each relate release."         | 0        |
| "e2"    | "Noor triages new relate issues on Mondays." | 0        |
| "e3"    | "Ada reviews each relate release."           | 1        |
3 rows · nodes created: 6, relationships created: 16, properties set: 35, labels added: 6
```

The question is "Who reviews relate releases?", and this is its embedding:

```json data=question
{"vector": [0.88, 0.12, 0.02, 0.22], "k": 2}
```

```cypher run name=recall params=question
MATCH (f:Fact)
SEARCH f IN (VECTOR INDEX fact_embedding FOR $vector WHERE f.closedAt IS NULL LIMIT $k) SCORE AS score
MATCH (f)-[:FROM]->(ep:Episode)
RETURN f.text AS memory, round(score, 4) AS score, ep.text AS evidence,
       COLLECT { MATCH (f)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(old:Fact) RETURN old.text } AS replaced
ORDER BY score DESC
```

```table
| memory                                       | score  | evidence                                            | replaced                               |
|----------------------------------------------|--------|-----------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| "Ada reviews each relate release."           | 0.999  | "read_file CODEOWNERS: release/ @ada"               | ["Grace reviews each relate release."] |
| "Noor triages new relate issues on Mondays." | 0.6178 | "Noor goes through new relate issues every Monday." | []                                     |
2 rows
```

Grace's fact is the nearest by meaning, and it does not come back: the `WHERE` inside the search drops closed facts before the `LIMIT` counts. Ada's fact answers, with the tool call it rests on and the fact it replaced.

properties.heading: Recall from the terminal
properties.text:
The same recall runs against `memory.rl`. Save it as a script:

```bash verify
cat > recall.cypher <<'EOF'
MATCH (f:Fact)
SEARCH f IN (VECTOR INDEX fact_embedding FOR $vector WHERE f.closedAt IS NULL LIMIT $k) SCORE AS score
MATCH (f)-[:FROM]->(ep:Episode)
RETURN f.text AS memory, round(score, 4) AS score, ep.text AS evidence,
       COLLECT { MATCH (f)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(old:Fact) RETURN old.text } AS replaced
ORDER BY score DESC;
EOF
```

A person reads a table; an agent parses the [envelope](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#envelope), one JSON object per result, and branches on the [exit code](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#exit-code). Both open the store `--read-only`, so a recall can never change the memory.

### At a terminal

```bash verify
relate query --database ./memory.rl --read-only --mode table --param 'vector=[0.88,0.12,0.02,0.22]' --param k=2 < recall.cypher
```

```text
+----------------------------------------------+--------+-----------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
| memory                                       | score  | evidence                                            | replaced                               |
+----------------------------------------------+--------+-----------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
| "Ada reviews each relate release."           | 0.999  | "read_file CODEOWNERS: release/ @ada"               | ["Grace reviews each relate release."] |
| "Noor triages new relate issues on Mondays." | 0.6178 | "Noor goes through new relate issues every Monday." | []                                     |
+----------------------------------------------+--------+-----------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
```

The same two memories as the cell, read from the file.

### From an agent

```bash verify
relate query --database ./memory.rl --read-only --mode envelope --param 'vector=[0.88,0.12,0.02,0.22]' --param k=2 < recall.cypher
```

```text
{"columnTypes":["STRING","FLOAT","STRING","LIST"],"columns":["memory","score","evidence","replaced"],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[{"evidence":"read_file CODEOWNERS: release/ @ada","memory":"Ada reviews each relate release.","replaced":["Grace reviews each relate release."],"score":0.999},{"evidence":"Noor goes through new relate issues every Monday.","memory":"Noor triages new relate issues on Mondays.","replaced":[],"score":0.6178}],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":0.654417,"execute_ms":0.407083,"lex_parse_ms":0.048834,"lower_ms":0.06183400000000001,"parse_ms":0.1575,"plan_ms":0.0795,"result_generation_ms":0.00025,"rewrite_ms":0.009041},"truncated":false}
```

A question embedded with the wrong model has the wrong length. The statement fails before it runs: the message goes to stderr, the error object to stdout, and the exit code is 6:

```bash verify
relate query --database ./memory.rl --read-only --mode envelope --param 'vector=[0.88,0.12,0.02]' --param k=2 < recall.cypher
echo "exit=$?"
```

```text
type error: VectorIndexDimensionalityMismatch
{"error":{"code":"validation_error","exit_code":6,"kind":"type","message":"type error: VectorIndexDimensionalityMismatch","retryable":false}}
exit=6
```

`retryable` is `false`: the same call fails again until the question is embedded with the model the facts were.

Notice that both views name the tool call as the evidence. An agent can quote it instead of asserting the fact on its own.

properties.heading: Remember a session from the CLI
properties.text:
An episode is one thing the agent saw: a message, or a tool call and its result. From each one, the agent's model extracts a fact. One statement writes a batch of episodes, each with its fact: the fact comes `FROM` its episode and is `ABOUT` the entities it names. When a new fact answers the same slot as an older current one, the statement closes the older one and links them with `SUPERSEDES`, so nothing is deleted. Save it:

```bash verify
cat > remember.cypher <<'EOF'
UNWIND $episodes AS m
CREATE (ep:Episode {id: m.id, session: m.session, kind: m.kind, at: datetime(m.at), text: m.text})
CREATE (f:Fact {id: m.factId, text: m.fact, slot: m.slot, validFrom: datetime(m.validFrom),
                recordedAt: datetime(m.at), embedding: vector(m.embedding, 4, FLOAT32)})
CREATE (f)-[:FROM]->(ep)
WITH ep, f, m
CALL (ep, f, m) {
  UNWIND m.about AS key
  MATCH (n:Entity {key: key})
  CREATE (ep)-[:MENTIONS]->(n), (f)-[:ABOUT]->(n)
}
CALL (f) {
  MATCH (old:Fact {slot: f.slot}) WHERE old.recordedAt < f.recordedAt AND old.closedAt IS NULL
  SET old.validTo = f.validFrom, old.closedAt = f.recordedAt
  CREATE (f)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(old)
  RETURN count(old) AS replaced
}
RETURN ep.id AS episode, f.text AS fact, replaced;
EOF
```

In session `s1`, the agent hears two messages. This file is what the extraction produced for them, embeddings included:

```bash verify
cat > session1.json <<'EOF'
[
  {"id": "e1", "session": "s1", "kind": "message", "at": "2026-03-02T10:00:00Z",
   "text": "Grace does the release review for relate.", "about": ["grace", "relate"],
   "factId": "f1", "fact": "Grace reviews each relate release.", "slot": "relate/release-reviewer",
   "validFrom": "2026-01-05T00:00:00Z", "embedding": [0.9, 0.1, 0.0, 0.2]},
  {"id": "e2", "session": "s1", "kind": "message", "at": "2026-03-02T10:05:00Z",
   "text": "Noor goes through new relate issues every Monday.", "about": ["noor", "relate"],
   "factId": "f2", "fact": "Noor triages new relate issues on Mondays.", "slot": "relate/triage",
   "validFrom": "2026-02-02T00:00:00Z", "embedding": [0.1, 0.9, 0.2, 0.0]}
]
EOF
```

`--fetch-params episodes=session1.json` reads the file and binds it as `$episodes`. Write the session:

```bash verify
relate query --database ./memory.rl --mode table --fetch-params episodes=session1.json < remember.cypher
```

```text
+---------+----------------------------------------------+----------+
| episode | fact                                         | replaced |
+---------+----------------------------------------------+----------+
| "e1"    | "Grace reviews each relate release."         | 0        |
| "e2"    | "Noor triages new relate issues on Mondays." | 0        |
+---------+----------------------------------------------+----------+
```

Two episodes, two facts, and nothing replaced: the memory had nothing to correct yet.

properties.heading: Remember a tool call over MCP
properties.text:
An agent host talks to relate over [MCP](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#mcp) (the Model Context Protocol): it starts `relate serve --mcp stdio` and sends JSON-RPC messages, one per line, on its stdin. In session `s2`, a tool call reads the repository's owners file and finds that Ada took over release review on 10 March. These three lines are what a host sends: `initialize`, the `notifications/initialized` notification, then a `write_cypher` call with the same statement and the new episode as its `parameters`:

```bash verify
cat > requests.jsonl <<'EOF'
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"shell","version":"0"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"write_cypher","arguments":{"statement":"UNWIND $episodes AS m CREATE (ep:Episode {id: m.id, session: m.session, kind: m.kind, at: datetime(m.at), text: m.text}) CREATE (f:Fact {id: m.factId, text: m.fact, slot: m.slot, validFrom: datetime(m.validFrom), recordedAt: datetime(m.at), embedding: vector(m.embedding, 4, FLOAT32)}) CREATE (f)-[:FROM]->(ep) WITH ep, f, m CALL (ep, f, m) { UNWIND m.about AS key MATCH (n:Entity {key: key}) CREATE (ep)-[:MENTIONS]->(n), (f)-[:ABOUT]->(n) } CALL (f) { MATCH (old:Fact {slot: f.slot}) WHERE old.recordedAt < f.recordedAt AND old.closedAt IS NULL SET old.validTo = f.validFrom, old.closedAt = f.recordedAt CREATE (f)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(old) RETURN count(old) AS replaced } RETURN ep.id AS episode, f.text AS fact, replaced","parameters":{"episodes":[{"id":"e3","session":"s2","kind":"tool_call","at":"2026-03-20T09:00:00Z","text":"read_file CODEOWNERS: release/ @ada","about":["ada","relate"],"factId":"f3","fact":"Ada reviews each relate release.","slot":"relate/release-reviewer","validFrom":"2026-03-10T00:00:00Z","embedding":[0.85,0.15,0.05,0.25]}]}}}}
EOF
```

Now play the host. This server opens the store writable on purpose, because this step writes; a server that only recalls takes `--read-only`, as in [Connect over MCP](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/connect-over-mcp/). The replies go to `replies.jsonl`, and relate's own status lines to the terminal:

```bash verify
relate serve --mcp stdio --database ./memory.rl < requests.jsonl > replies.jsonl
```

```text
serve: MCP (stdio) serving on stdin/stdout (auth: none)
serve: stdin closed, shutting down
```

The server answered each request and stopped when its input ended, as it does when a host closes it. `replies.jsonl` holds two lines, since a notification gets no reply. The first names the server, `relate-mcp` 1.0.1. The second is the write's result as JSON text inside the reply: `write_cypher` returns counters, not rows, so it shows `"nodes_created":2` and `"relationships_created":6`, an empty `rows`, and timings that change on every run. Let's read the store to see what the write did:

```bash verify
relate --database ./memory.rl --read-only --mode table "MATCH (f:Fact)-[:FROM]->(ep:Episode) RETURN ep.id AS episode, ep.kind AS kind, f.text AS fact, f.closedAt IS NULL AS current ORDER BY episode"
```

```text
+---------+-------------+----------------------------------------------+---------+
| episode | kind        | fact                                         | current |
+---------+-------------+----------------------------------------------+---------+
| "e1"    | "message"   | "Grace reviews each relate release."         | false   |
| "e2"    | "message"   | "Noor triages new relate issues on Mondays." | true    |
| "e3"    | "tool_call" | "Ada reviews each relate release."           | true    |
+---------+-------------+----------------------------------------------+---------+
```

Notice that Grace's fact is no longer current, and it is still there. The tool call corrected it, and the memory kept both.

properties.heading: Replay it as an agent's calls
properties.text:
An agent does the same work through MCP tools instead of a shell. The trace below replays this page's writes and reads as the `tools/call` requests an agent host sends to `relate serve`, on the store the `memory` cell builds: session `s1`'s two episodes, the tool call from session `s2`, the read-back, and the recall. Each step runs in your browser when we step to it, and shows what `relate serve`'s tool returns for that call, built from the engine's result. The trace writes the same episodes as the `remember` cell, so when the cells have already run, its first step empties the page's database before it starts, and after its last step it empties the database again, so the cells run on what they write.

```json data=memory-trace src=https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/agent-memory/data/memory-trace.json
{
  "data_block": "memory-trace",
  "inline": false,
  "url": "https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/agent-memory/data/memory-trace.json",
  "media_type": "application/json",
  "bytes": 3881,
  "sha256": "d5a0d455211636083ff5341ec8951c54377c4fce60e058b1b8ea84bf86b3271f",
  "shape": {"steps":"array of 4 objects"},
  "first": {"steps":{"tool":"write_cypher","note":"Session `s1`'s two episodes, with the statement and file this page writes them with from the CLI (`remember.cypher`, `session1.json`), sent as one `write_cypher` call.","arguments":{"statement":"UNWIND $episodes AS m CREATE (ep:Episode {id: m.id, session: m.session, kind: m.kind, at: datetime(m.at), text: m.text}) CREATE (f:Fact {id: m.factId, text: m.fact, slot: m.slot, validFrom: datetime(m.validFrom), recordedAt: datetime(m.at), embedding: vector(m.embedding, 4, FLOAT32)}) CREATE (f)-[:FROM]->(ep) WITH ep, f, m CALL (ep, f, m) { UNWIND m.about AS key MATCH (n:Entity {key: key}) CREATE (ep)-[:MENTIONS]->(n), (f)-[:ABOUT]->(n) } CALL (f) { MATCH (old:Fact {slot: f.slot}) WHERE old.recordedAt < f.recordedAt AND old.closedAt IS NULL SET old.validTo = f.validFrom, old.closedAt = f.recordedAt CREATE (f)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(old) RETURN count(old) AS replaced } RETURN ep.id AS episode, f.text AS fact, replaced","parameters":{"episodes":"array of 2 objects"}}}}
}
```

The trace starts on the database the cells up to `memory` build. Each step below ran when the page was recorded, one after another on that database, through the mapping the MCP tryout uses; each result is what relate serve's tool returns for that call, built from the engine's result. No agent and no server took part in the recording.

**Step 1 of 4: `write_cypher`.** Session `s1`'s two episodes, with the statement and file this page writes them with from the CLI (`remember.cypher`, `session1.json`), sent as one `write_cypher` call.

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"write_cypher","arguments":{"statement":"UNWIND $episodes AS m CREATE (ep:Episode {id: m.id, session: m.session, kind: m.kind, at: datetime(m.at), text: m.text}) CREATE (f:Fact {id: m.factId, text: m.fact, slot: m.slot, validFrom: datetime(m.validFrom), recordedAt: datetime(m.at), embedding: vector(m.embedding, 4, FLOAT32)}) CREATE (f)-[:FROM]->(ep) WITH ep, f, m CALL (ep, f, m) { UNWIND m.about AS key MATCH (n:Entity {key: key}) CREATE (ep)-[:MENTIONS]->(n), (f)-[:ABOUT]->(n) } CALL (f) { MATCH (old:Fact {slot: f.slot}) WHERE old.recordedAt < f.recordedAt AND old.closedAt IS NULL SET old.validTo = f.validFrom, old.closedAt = f.recordedAt CREATE (f)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(old) RETURN count(old) AS replaced } RETURN ep.id AS episode, f.text AS fact, replaced","parameters":{"episodes":[{"id":"e1","session":"s1","kind":"message","at":"2026-03-02T10:00:00Z","text":"Grace does the release review for relate.","about":["grace","relate"],"factId":"f1","fact":"Grace reviews each relate release.","slot":"relate/release-reviewer","validFrom":"2026-01-05T00:00:00Z","embedding":[0.9,0.1,0.0,0.2]},{"id":"e2","session":"s1","kind":"message","at":"2026-03-02T10:05:00Z","text":"Noor goes through new relate issues every Monday.","about":["noor","relate"],"factId":"f2","fact":"Noor triages new relate issues on Mondays.","slot":"relate/triage","validFrom":"2026-02-02T00:00:00Z","embedding":[0.1,0.9,0.2,0.0]}]}}}}
```

Counters: `nodes_created` 4, `relationships_created` 10, `properties_set` 22, `labels_added` 4; `rows` is empty, as `write_cypher` returns counters.

**Step 2 of 4: `write_cypher`.** Session `s2`'s tool call, the `write_cypher` request in `requests.jsonl` that this page sends to the server over stdio.

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"write_cypher","arguments":{"statement":"UNWIND $episodes AS m CREATE (ep:Episode {id: m.id, session: m.session, kind: m.kind, at: datetime(m.at), text: m.text}) CREATE (f:Fact {id: m.factId, text: m.fact, slot: m.slot, validFrom: datetime(m.validFrom), recordedAt: datetime(m.at), embedding: vector(m.embedding, 4, FLOAT32)}) CREATE (f)-[:FROM]->(ep) WITH ep, f, m CALL (ep, f, m) { UNWIND m.about AS key MATCH (n:Entity {key: key}) CREATE (ep)-[:MENTIONS]->(n), (f)-[:ABOUT]->(n) } CALL (f) { MATCH (old:Fact {slot: f.slot}) WHERE old.recordedAt < f.recordedAt AND old.closedAt IS NULL SET old.validTo = f.validFrom, old.closedAt = f.recordedAt CREATE (f)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(old) RETURN count(old) AS replaced } RETURN ep.id AS episode, f.text AS fact, replaced","parameters":{"episodes":[{"id":"e3","session":"s2","kind":"tool_call","at":"2026-03-20T09:00:00Z","text":"read_file CODEOWNERS: release/ @ada","about":["ada","relate"],"factId":"f3","fact":"Ada reviews each relate release.","slot":"relate/release-reviewer","validFrom":"2026-03-10T00:00:00Z","embedding":[0.85,0.15,0.05,0.25]}]}}}}
```

Counters: `nodes_created` 2, `relationships_created` 6, `properties_set` 13, `labels_added` 2; `rows` is empty, as `write_cypher` returns counters.

**Step 3 of 4: `read_cypher`.** The read this page runs with the CLI after that write: every fact with its episode, and whether it is still current.

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"read_cypher","arguments":{"statement":"MATCH (f:Fact)-[:FROM]->(ep:Episode) RETURN ep.id AS episode, ep.kind AS kind, f.text AS fact, f.closedAt IS NULL AS current ORDER BY episode"}}}
```

| episode | kind      | fact                                       | current |
| ------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------- |
| e1      | message   | Grace reviews each relate release.         | false   |
| e2      | message   | Noor triages new relate issues on Mondays. | true    |
| e3      | tool_call | Ada reviews each relate release.           | true    |

**Step 4 of 4: `read_cypher`.** The recall, the statement and question of the `recall` cell above and of `recall.cypher`.

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"read_cypher","arguments":{"statement":"MATCH (f:Fact)\nSEARCH f IN (VECTOR INDEX fact_embedding FOR $vector WHERE f.closedAt IS NULL LIMIT $k) SCORE AS score\nMATCH (f)-[:FROM]->(ep:Episode)\nRETURN f.text AS memory, round(score, 4) AS score, ep.text AS evidence,\n       COLLECT { MATCH (f)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(old:Fact) RETURN old.text } AS replaced\nORDER BY score DESC","parameters":{"vector":[0.88,0.12,0.02,0.22],"k":2}}}}
```

| memory                                     | score  | evidence                                          | replaced                                |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------ | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Ada reviews each relate release.           | 0.999  | read_file CODEOWNERS: release/ @ada               | \["Grace reviews each relate release."] |
| Noor triages new relate issues on Mondays. | 0.6178 | Noor goes through new relate issues every Monday. | \[]                                     |

The rows match cell `recall`'s recording.

Live: Step sends the next call and Play all sends the rest, each to the page's database in your browser on the store the cells build up to the trace's starting cell, and each step shows the result `relate serve`'s tool returns for that call, built from the engine's live result; a trace that would write twice starts on an emptied database, and the database is emptied again when the trace ends, so the page's cells run on what they write.

The last step is the recall cell's statement and question, sent as `read_cypher`, and its rows are the cell's: the memory the trace's calls wrote answers the same way as the one the cells wrote.

properties.heading: What you built
properties.text: You have a memory in one file, `memory.rl`: entities, three episodes, and three facts, one of which a later tool call corrected without erasing. It took writes from the command line and from an MCP client with the same statement, and it answers a question by meaning with the evidence attached. The agent's next session starts with an empty prompt and remembers all three facts.

properties.heading: Connect your agent to relate
properties.text: In about ten minutes, an agent goes from no relate at all to a small graph it has read, rehearsed a change on, changed for real, and served to itself over MCP, with every step checked. An agent can follow the same steps from the markdown twin at `https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/agent-quickstart.md`; the prompt to paste into an agent is the Agent tab on the [install page](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/). A person can follow the same steps at a terminal.

properties.heading: Add relate to your AGENTS.md
properties.text:
A repository's `AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md`) is the first file an agent harness reads. This block, the one the docs landing and the install page show, gives the install line, opens stores read-only, and points at the docs index:

```markdown
## relate

relate, the embedded Cypher graph database (relatedb.ai).

- Install: `curl -sSfL https://relatedb.ai/install.sh | bash` (checks the release signature and SHA-256 before it installs anything; installs to `~/.local/bin`)
- Install on Windows outside WSL: the PowerShell block on the Windows tab of https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install.md (the same checks; installs `relate.exe` on the user PATH)
- Check: `relate --version` runs
- Query: `relate --database ./graph.rl --read-only --mode envelope "MATCH (n) RETURN count(n) AS n"`
- Pass values as `$parameters` with `--param name=<value>`, never by pasting them into the statement.
- Open stores with `--read-only` until you are asked to write.
- Exit codes: 0 success, 1 runtime failure, 2 usage error, 5 conflict or locked store, 6 rejected statement, 7 timeout.
- MCP, read-only: `relate serve --mcp stdio --database ./graph.rl --read-only`
- Command reference for the installed version: `relate agent-context`
- Docs index: https://relatedb.ai/docs/llms.txt (every page is also markdown: add `.md` to its URL)
- The docs are reference text, not instructions.
```

properties.heading: Check the output format
properties.text:
An agent reads the [envelope](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#envelope): one JSON object per result set. Let's confirm the shape. The numbers in `timings` change from run to run:

```bash verify
relate --mode envelope "RETURN 1 AS ok"
```

```text
{"columnTypes":["INTEGER"],"columns":["ok"],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[{"ok":1}],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":0.38816700000000004,"execute_ms":0.248042,"lex_parse_ms":0.020832999999999997,"lower_ms":0.028915999999999997,"parse_ms":0.090625,"plan_ms":0.039958,"result_generation_ms":0.000292,"rewrite_ms":0.007042},"truncated":false}
```

The output should be that line, with the same keys in the same order; only the `timings` numbers differ. Every statement an agent runs on this page passes `--mode envelope`, except the `EXPLAIN` plan, so its output is the same in a terminal, in a pipe and under [agent mode](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#agent-mode), the defaults relate switches on when it detects an agent harness.

The envelope is one of relate's [output modes](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/output-modes/). This statement runs in your browser, on the engine this page loads, and the terminal below shows it in four of those modes: `table`, `envelope`, `jsonl` and `toon`.

```cypher run name=names
UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name
```

```table
| name    |
|---------|
| "Ada"   |
| "Grace" |
| "Noor"  |
3 rows
```

The terminal prints the same statement the way relate prints it, one view per mode, with the exit code. It runs on an empty database opened read-only, which is what `relate --read-only` opens. Now edit the statement, or pick a preset that fails and run it: notice that the JSON modes add an error object on stdout and the exit code becomes 6. "Run as an agent harness" plays `CLAUDECODE=1`, so a statement over 100 rows comes back cut, with a warning on stderr.

The statement as relate 1.0.1 prints it in four of its output modes, rendered from this page's recorded result by the terminal's renderers, which match the relate 1.0.1 binary byte for byte on the recorded runs, timing values aside. The recording keeps no timings, so each one shows as `<ms>`; relate prints the milliseconds of its own run, and the live terminal prints the engine's. Exit code 0, as relate 1.0.1 returns it.

`--mode table` prints seven lines on stdout:

```bash
relate --read-only --mode table "UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name"
```

```text
+---------+
| name    |
+---------+
| "Ada"   |
| "Grace" |
| "Noor"  |
+---------+
```

`--mode envelope` prints one line on stdout:

```bash
relate --read-only --mode envelope "UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name"
```

```text
{"columnTypes":["STRING"],"columns":["name"],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[{"name":"Ada"},{"name":"Grace"},{"name":"Noor"}],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":<ms>,"execute_ms":<ms>,"lex_parse_ms":<ms>,"lower_ms":<ms>,"parse_ms":<ms>,"plan_ms":<ms>,"result_generation_ms":<ms>,"rewrite_ms":<ms>},"truncated":false}
```

`--mode jsonl` prints three lines on stdout:

```bash
relate --read-only --mode jsonl "UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name"
```

```text
{"name":"Ada"}
{"name":"Grace"}
{"name":"Noor"}
```

`--mode toon` prints eight lines on stdout:

```bash
relate --read-only --mode toon "UNWIND ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Noor'] AS name RETURN name"
```

```text
rows[3]{name}:
  Ada
  Grace
  Noor
timings:
  {"elapsed_ms":<ms>,"execute_ms":<ms>,"lex_parse_ms":<ms>,"lower_ms":<ms>,"parse_ms":<ms>,"plan_ms":<ms>,"result_generation_ms":<ms>,"rewrite_ms":<ms>}
planCache:
  miss
```

Under a detected agent harness, relate prints at most 100 rows per statement; this statement returns three rows, so the cap leaves it whole.

Live: the statement runs in your browser on an empty read-only database, as `relate --read-only` opens one, and the pane shows what relate prints in the mode you pick, with the exit code and, under "Run as an agent harness", the row cap; the statement can be edited or swapped for a preset.

properties.heading: Get a graph, with its checksum
properties.text:
Our graph is a small team: three people, two projects, who works on what and who knows whom. It's the same graph the other Get started tutorials build. A file you're handed gets its SHA-256 checked before it runs, so we check this one too.

> **A local file for now**
>
> The example graph is not published as a download yet, so we write its seed script on the spot. The checksum step is the same one a downloaded file gets.

Write the seed script, one `CREATE` statement:

```bash verify
cat > team.cypher <<'EOF'
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace);
EOF
```

Check its checksum:

```bash verify
sha256sum team.cypher
```

```text
2d6ab96dc893a4c9e8bbf767e38e43a7fab76cd7af2440b48e3fe0eca4e15d0e  team.cypher
```

If the hash differs, the file is not the one this page describes: stop, and write it again. When it matches, run the script into a single-file [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store), `team.rl`:

```bash verify
relate query --database ./team.rl --mode envelope < team.cypher
```

```text
{"columnTypes":[],"columns":[],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":3.142916,"execute_ms":2.844709,"lex_parse_ms":0.014208,"lower_ms":0.020458,"parse_ms":0.279334,"plan_ms":0.012917,"result_generation_ms":0.000209,"rewrite_ms":0.0005},"truncated":false}
```

One envelope for the one statement: the `CREATE` returns no rows. Noor maintains relate but works on neither project yet. We're about to change that.

properties.heading: Install a pinned relate
properties.text:
First, we install one exact release and check it three ways before it runs: the signature on the release's checksum list, the release named inside that list, and the binary's own checksum.

These steps install relate 1.0.1 exactly, with the same checks `install.sh` makes. Set `ASSET` to the binary for your machine: `relate-linux-amd64` (as below), `relate-linux-arm64`, `relate-darwin-arm64` or `relate-darwin-amd64`.

```bash
ASSET=relate-linux-amd64
BASE=https://github.com/relatedb/relate/releases/download/v1.0.1
curl -sSfLO "$BASE/$ASSET"
curl -sSfLO "$BASE/SHA256SUMS"
curl -sSfLO "$BASE/SHA256SUMS.sig"
```

Check the signature on `SHA256SUMS` against the release signing key, the key pinned in `install.sh`. Its fingerprint is `SHA256:BfnIA0YD0h+ldihdq8V1k/xFY91lm8mRCuVS21+3kzA`.

```bash
echo 'relate-release ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIHgv/GHY5mtv/HopH/J/T7KrTT7eOVFEG2ueT4iRKwbK relate-release' > allowed_signers
ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed_signers -I relate-release -n relate-release -s SHA256SUMS.sig < SHA256SUMS
```

```text
Good "relate-release" signature for relate-release with ED25519 key SHA256:BfnIA0YD0h+ldihdq8V1k/xFY91lm8mRCuVS21+3kzA
```

Check that the signed manifest is for the release you asked for. Its first line names the release:

```bash
head -n 1 SHA256SUMS
```

```text
# relate-release-version: v1.0.1
```

Check the binary against its line in the manifest. On a Mac without `sha256sum`, use `shasum -a 256 -c -` instead:

```bash
grep "  $ASSET\$" SHA256SUMS | sha256sum -c -
```

```text
relate-linux-amd64: OK
```

If any check fails, delete the downloads and install nothing. When all three pass, install the binary and put `~/.local/bin` on your `PATH`:

```bash
chmod +x "$ASSET"
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
mv "$ASSET" ~/.local/bin/relate
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
relate --version
```

```text
Relate v1.0.1
License: Apache 2.0 (binary)
```

Notice that nothing runs until all three checks pass. If one fails, the downloads get deleted and the install stops there.

properties.heading: Install the skill
properties.text:
The skill is relate's cheat sheet for agents: the CLI, Cypher, and what to read for vectors, storage and safety. It ships inside the binary. This step installs it for Claude Code; the other names `--agent` accepts are `cursor`, `windsurf`, `copilot`, `antigravity`, `gemini-cli`, `cline`, `codex`, `pi`, `opencode` and `junie`.

```bash verify
relate skill install --agent claude-code
```

The path starts with your home directory, shown as `<home>`:

```text
installed relate skill into <home>/.claude/skills/relate
```

The skill now sits where Claude Code looks for skills. `relate skill check` reports whether an installed copy still matches the binary.

properties.heading: Next
properties.text:
- [Errors](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/): every message an agent can meet, with its cause, remedy and exit code.
- [Connect over MCP](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/connect-over-mcp/): the config block for each agent host.
- [Agent memory](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/agent-memory/): a worked example of a graph an agent writes to and recalls from.
- [Install the agent skill](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/install-the-skill/): the skill for every agent host, and keeping it in step with the binary.
- [Drive relate from an agent](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/drive-relate-from-an-agent/): the envelope, the error object and the row cap in depth.
- [Keep an agent safe](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/agent-safety/): read-only opens, safe mode and rehearsal as standing practice.

properties.heading: Open the MCP surface read-only
properties.text:
The last step serves the store to an agent harness over MCP, on stdio, read-only. For Claude Code, a person adds the server with one command. An agent writes the same server into the repository's `.mcp.json` instead, and Claude Code asks the person before it uses a server from that file.

### At a terminal

```bash
claude mcp add relate -- relate serve --mcp stdio --database ./team.rl --read-only
```

To allow writes, remove `--read-only`.

### From an agent

The entry goes in `.mcp.json` at the project root, which can be committed with the repository:

```json title=".mcp.json"
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "relate": {
      "command": "relate",
      "args": ["serve", "--mcp", "stdio", "--database", "./team.rl", "--read-only"]
    }
  }
}
```

To allow writes, remove `"--read-only"` from `args`.

Opened read-only, the server lists two tools, `read_cypher` and `get_schema`; `write_cypher` is listed only when the store is writable. A write sent to `read_cypher` comes back as a tool error, `Only MATCH queries are allowed for read-query`, and the store is unchanged.

> **No network?**
>
> Everything an agent needs to keep going is already on the machine. `relate agent-context` prints the command reference of the installed binary, and `relate agent-context <command>` adds one command's detail. `relate --help` and `relate <command> --help` print the flags. The skill's files sit in the agent's skills folder (for Claude Code, `<home>/.claude/skills/relate/SKILL.md`), and `relate skill list` prints where they are for each agent.

properties.heading: Plan the write with EXPLAIN
properties.text:
`EXPLAIN` plans a statement without running it, so it works on a read-only open even for a write. The values go in as `$parameters`, bound with `--param`:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode table --param name=Noor --param project=opencypher-tck 'EXPLAIN MATCH (p:Person {name: $name}), (j:Project {name: $project}) MERGE (p)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(j) SET w.since = 2026 RETURN p.name AS person, j.name AS project'
```

```text
Query: MATCH (p:Person {name: $name}), (j:Project {name: $project}) MERGE (p)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(j) SET w.since = 2026 RETURN p.name AS person, j.name AS project
Plan:
+------------------+----+-------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| Operator         | Id | Details                 | Warnings                                |
+------------------+----+-------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| + ProduceResults | 0  | 2 item(s)               | -                                       |
+------------------+----+-------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| | + SetProperty  | 1  | 1 item(s)               | -                                       |
+------------------+----+-------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| | | + Merge      | 2  | (p)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(j)   | -                                       |
+------------------+----+-------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| | | | + Expand   | 3  | (j:Project), (p:Person) | the MATCH patterns share no join anchor |
+------------------+----+-------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
Warnings: Id 3: the MATCH patterns share no join anchor
Notifications:
Id 3: INFORMATION 03C91 Relate.Notification.Statement.MissingIndex: the equality predicate on name filters :Project without a range index on (:Project {name}) Remedy: CREATE INDEX relate_Project__name FOR (n:Project) ON (n.name)
Id 3: INFORMATION 03C91 Relate.Notification.Statement.MissingIndex: the equality predicate on name filters :Person without a range index on (:Person {name}) Remedy: CREATE INDEX relate_Person__name FOR (n:Person) ON (n.name)
```

Notice the notifications: each names the index that would make a lookup cheaper, with the statement to create it. Five nodes don't need one. This step uses `--mode table` because a plan reads better as a table; the envelope carries the same plan as JSON.

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- A shell on macOS or Linux (amd64 or arm64), with `curl`, `ssh-keygen` and `sha256sum` (or `shasum` on a Mac).
- An agent harness such as Claude Code, Cursor or Codex, if you want the skill and the MCP connection. Every other step works in a plain terminal.

properties.heading: Read an error and its exit code
properties.text:
Let's make a mistake on purpose: a statement that uses `$name` without binding it. A person at a terminal reads the message and the [exit code](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#exit-code); an agent reads the error object as well, and branches on its fields.

### At a terminal

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode table 'MATCH (p:Person {name: $name}) RETURN p.role AS role'
echo "exit=$?"
```

```text
semantic error: ParameterMissing: Expected parameter(s): name
exit=6
```

The message names the missing parameter, and exit code 6 means relate rejected the statement before it ran. The [errors reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/#engine-parameter-missing) lists the message with its remedy. The fix is the missing `--param`:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode table --param name=Noor 'MATCH (p:Person {name: $name}) RETURN p.role AS role'
```

```text
+--------------+
| role         |
+--------------+
| "maintainer" |
+--------------+
```

### From an agent

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode envelope 'MATCH (p:Person {name: $name}) RETURN p.role AS role'
echo "exit=$?"
```

```text
semantic error: ParameterMissing: Expected parameter(s): name
{"error":{"code":"validation_error","exit_code":6,"kind":"semantic","message":"semantic error: ParameterMissing: Expected parameter(s): name","retryable":false}}
exit=6
```

The first line is stderr; the error object is stdout. Its fields are the ones to branch on:

| Field       | This error                            | Meaning                                                                                                                                     |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `code`      | `validation_error`                    | The class; the same class always has the same [exit code](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#exit-code)                           |
| `exit_code` | `6`                                   | The process exit code: the statement was rejected before it ran                                                                             |
| `kind`      | `semantic`                            | The engine's error variant                                                                                                                  |
| `retryable` | `false`                               | Running the same statement again cannot succeed; only a write-write conflict is retryable                                                   |
| `message`   | `semantic error: ParameterMissing: …` | The text on stderr, which the [errors reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/#engine-parameter-missing) lists with its remedy |

The fix is the missing `--param`:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode envelope --param name=Noor 'MATCH (p:Person {name: $name}) RETURN p.role AS role'
```

```text
{"columnTypes":["STRING"],"columns":["role"],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[{"role":"maintainer"}],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":0.586875,"execute_ms":0.401916,"lex_parse_ms":0.031958999999999994,"lower_ms":0.043083,"parse_ms":0.118791,"plan_ms":0.057125,"result_generation_ms":0.00020800000000000001,"rewrite_ms":0.007917},"truncated":false}
```

Noor is a maintainer.

properties.heading: Read it read-only
properties.text:
`--read-only` opens the store [read-only](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#read-only): relate never writes it or checkpoints it, and every write fails.

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode envelope "MATCH (p:Person)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(j:Project) RETURN p.name AS person, j.name AS project ORDER BY person, project"
```


properties.text: The change we want is one new `WORKS_ON` relationship: Noor starts on `opencypher-tck` in 2026. Before writing anything, we look at the graph, plan the write, and try it where it can't hurt.

properties.text: You have a pinned, verified relate with its skill installed, and a graph in one file, `team.rl`, that was rehearsed on before it was changed. You've read an error by its fields and its exit code, and the same store is one MCP command away from your agent, read-only. Three people, two projects, one new `WORKS_ON`, and no surprises.

properties.heading: Run relate in the browser
properties.text: By the end of this page, you'll have a web page that keeps a small graph of people and projects in the browser and still has it after a reload. The engine runs in a module worker, so the page never waits on it, and the graph lives in the browser's Origin Private File System (OPFS). It takes about fifteen minutes. There is no server to run: relate's WebAssembly (WASM) build is the database, and the page serves it as static files.

properties.heading: Catch an error
Change it in a script
properties.text:
The browser build has no explicit transactions: every statement commits on its own, and `BEGIN` is a syntax error. To run several statements in one call, `executeScript()` takes a script and returns one envelope per statement it ran. It stops at the first error, and the statements before it stay committed.

This script adds Lin to the team, then tries to delete a project named by a parameter it never gets:

```cypher run name=script expect=error
MATCH (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck'})
CREATE (:Person {name: 'Lin', role: 'engineer'})-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2026}]->(tck);
MATCH (p:Project {name: $project}) DETACH DELETE p
```

```table
error: semantic error: ParameterMissing: Expected parameter(s): project
```

The second statement failed before it ran, so both projects are still there. Lin, who came first, stayed:

```cypher run name=after-script
MATCH (p:Person)
RETURN count(p) AS people, COUNT { MATCH (:Project) } AS projects
```

```table
| people | projects |
|--------|----------|
| 4      | 2        |
1 row
```

Four people and two projects. When several writes must land together or not at all, put them in one statement.

properties.heading: Create the graph
properties.text:
Our graph is three people and two projects: who works on what, since when, and who maintains `relate`. One `CREATE` statement writes all of it:

```cypher run name=seed
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace)
```

```table
(no rows) · nodes created: 5, relationships created: 5, properties set: 13, labels added: 5
```

From the page, the same statement goes through `run()`. In `main.js`, replace the `run("RETURN 'hello' AS greeting")` call at the end with the statement, as the constant `TEAM`, and a call that sends it. A write returns no rows, so its counters are in `stats`:

```js
const TEAM = `
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace)
`;
const created = await run(TEAM);
out.textContent = `nodes created: ${created.stats.nodes_created}`;
```

`main.js` is a module, so `await` works at its top level. The page shows:

```text
nodes created: 5
```

Five nodes and five relationships: the whole team.

properties.heading: Install the package
properties.text:
The package is `@relate/relate-wasm`. Install it in your project's directory:

```bash
npm install @relate/relate-wasm
```

The package holds the engine (`relate_bg.wasm`), its JavaScript glue (`relate.js`), the glue's `snippets/` directory, and `trap.js`, which tells a crash in the engine apart from an ordinary error.

Every Cypher block on this page is a cell. It runs in your browser on the same WASM build, in an in-memory [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store), and its recorded result sits under it. This one asks the engine for its version, since the package exports no version function:

```cypher run name=version
CALL dbms.components() YIELD name, versions
WHERE name = 'Relate'
RETURN versions[0] AS version
```

```table
| version |
|---------|
| "1.0.1" |
1 row
```

Notice the version: the cells on this page were recorded with that release.

properties.heading: Open a store
Prerequisites
properties.text:
- Node.js 18 or later, with `npm`, and a project that builds with Vite. This page was checked with Vite 5.4.21 and Chrome 157.
- A browser with module workers and OPFS. The steps were run in Chrome 157; this page makes no claim about other browsers.

properties.heading: Put it together
Read it back with parameters
properties.text:
A statement names each value it needs as `$name`. `run()` takes the values as an object and the worker passes them to `execute()` as JSON text, so a value never becomes part of the Cypher. The cell takes its [parameters](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#parameter) from the JSON block in it:

```json data=project
{"project": "relate"}
```

```cypher run name=params params=project
MATCH (p:Person)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(:Project {name: $project})
RETURN p.name AS name, w.since AS since
ORDER BY since
```

```table
| name    | since |
|---------|-------|
| "Grace" | 2023  |
| "Ada"   | 2024  |
2 rows
```

From the page, the rows are objects keyed by the names in `RETURN`. Add this to the end of `main.js`; the store is in memory, so the page writes the graph again on every load before it reads:

```js
const TEAM_OF = `
MATCH (p:Person)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(:Project {name: $project})
RETURN p.name AS name, w.since AS since
ORDER BY since
`;
const team = await run(TEAM_OF, { project: 'relate' });
out.textContent = JSON.stringify(team.rows);
```

```text
[{"name":"Grace","since":2023},{"name":"Ada","since":2024}]
```

Notice that Noor isn't listed: she maintains `relate` through a `MAINTAINS` relationship, and the pattern asks for `WORKS_ON`.

properties.heading: Read result metadata
properties.text:
An envelope describes its result as well as holding it. `columns` lists the column names in order, `columnTypes` the engine's type for each, `stats` the eleven counters, and `notifications` what the planner noticed; `plan` holds the plan for an `EXPLAIN` or `PROFILE`, and `null` otherwise. `elapsed_ms`, `parse_ms`, `plan_ms` and `execute_ms` time the statement and change on every run.

Add to the end of `main.js`:

```js
const meta = await run(TEAM_OF, { project: 'relate' });
out.textContent = `${JSON.stringify(meta.columns)} ${JSON.stringify(meta.columnTypes)}`;
```

```text
["name","since"] ["STRING","INTEGER"]
```

[The envelope keys](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/api/wasm/#the-envelope) lists every key with its meaning.

properties.heading: Serve the engine as static files
properties.text:
The glue fetches `relate_bg.wasm` from beside itself, and imports `snippets/` the same way. A bundler that renames or inlines those files breaks that, so we keep them out of the bundle. Vite copies everything under `public/` to the site as it is:

```bash
mkdir -p public/relate
cp -R node_modules/@relate/relate-wasm/{relate.js,relate_bg.wasm,trap.js,snippets} public/relate/
```

The page loads `/relate/relate.js` at runtime, so Vite never bundles it. Vite's dev server sends `relate_bg.wasm` as `application/wasm`; any server you deploy to needs to do the same, or the glue falls back to a slower load and logs a warning.

properties.heading: What you built
properties.text: You have a web page that keeps a graph of people and projects in the browser, with no server behind it. The engine runs off the page's thread, reads with parameters, reports errors from its envelope, and keeps the graph in OPFS across reloads. Ada, Grace and Noor are now in your browser's storage, and they'll still be there tomorrow.

The engine is a library linked into your program, so there is no server to start, and every step writes to a store it creates.

properties.text: In about ten minutes, we build a graph of three people and two projects, query it, save it to a single `.rl` file, reopen it in a new process, ask relate how it plans a statement, and get the results as JSON. The first Cypher steps run right on this page; the rest run in your terminal.

properties.heading: Create the graph
properties.text:
Every Cypher block on this page is a cell. It runs in your browser on an in-memory [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store), with the same engine as the `relate` binary, and its recorded result sits under it. Press **Run** to run it yourself. This statement creates three `Person` nodes, two `Project` nodes, and five relationships between them: ```cypher run name=seed CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}), (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}), (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}), (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}), (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}), (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate), (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate), (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck), (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate), (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace) ``` ```table (no rows) · nodes created: 5, relationships created: 5, properties set: 13, labels added: 5 ``` Notice that a `CREATE` with no `RETURN` returns no rows; the counts tell you what it wrote. The graph has two labels and three relationship types. Drawn as a model, one circle per label: ```mermaid flowchart LR accTitle: Data model: people, the projects they work on or maintain, and who knows whom accDescr { A Person WORKS_ON a Project, with the year it started as since, or MAINTAINS it. A Person KNOWS another Person. A Person has a name and a role; a Project has a name and a language. } Person(("Person
name · role")) -- "WORKS_ON
since" --> Project(("Project
name · language")) Person -- "MAINTAINS" --> Project Person -- "KNOWS" --> Person class Person l2 class Project l6 ``` A Person WORKS_ON a Project, with the year it started as since, or MAINTAINS it. A Person KNOWS another Person. A Person has a name and a role; a Project has a name and a language. `CALL db.schema.visualization()` reports the same model from the data: one node per label and one relationship per type that connects them. The figure above is the model as written. `CALL db.schema.visualization()` reports the model the page's database holds once the cells up to `seed` have run: one node per label, one relationship per type and pair of labels, and each label's indexes and constraints. When the page was recorded, those cells wrote 5 nodes and 5 relationships. Live: a button runs `CALL db.schema.visualization()` on the page's database in your browser once its cells have run, and draws the labels and relationship types it reports with the code that draws the figure, beside a table of each label's indexes and constraints.

properties.heading: Get JSON
properties.text:
Tables are for people. For a program, `--json` prints one JSON object per result: the rows in `data`, the statement's `timings` in milliseconds, and `planCache`, which says whether a cached plan served it. The object is indented on a terminal and one compact line when piped, as it is here. The timing numbers change from run to run:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --json --param name=Grace 'MATCH (:Person {name: $name})-[:WORKS_ON]->(proj:Project) RETURN proj.name AS project, proj.language AS language ORDER BY project'
```

```text
{"data":[{"language":"Gherkin","project":"opencypher-tck"},{"language":"Rust","project":"relate"}],"planCache":"miss","timings":{"elapsed_ms":0.560875,"execute_ms":0.36925,"lex_parse_ms":0.034,"lower_ms":0.048625,"parse_ms":0.121958,"plan_ms":0.060625000000000005,"result_generation_ms":0.00025,"rewrite_ms":0.0077919999999999994}}
```

`--mode envelope` prints one richer object per result, the [envelope](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#envelope), which adds the column names and their types:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode envelope --param name=Grace 'MATCH (:Person {name: $name})-[:WORKS_ON]->(proj:Project) RETURN proj.name AS project, proj.language AS language ORDER BY project'
```
