properties.heading: Full-text and hybrid search
properties.text: This guide shows you how to find nodes by the words in their text with a [full-text index](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#full-text-index) and the [SEARCH clause](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#search), how the index splits text into terms and ranks a match, and how to fuse a full-text search with a vector search into one ranking. The cells run in page order on one in-memory [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store), in your browser and in the docs build.

properties.heading: Combine words with operators
properties.text: The words of a query are alternatives: any note holding one of them matches. `AND`, `OR` and `NOT`, written in capitals, are operators, and parentheses group them. `wal AND tests` matches only `n6`, and `wal NOT tests` only `n1`. A lowercase `and` is one more term. `&&` and `||` work as `AND` and `OR`; `+`, `-` and `!` before a word change nothing. `text:wal` matches `wal` in the `text` property only, which matters for an index over several properties. The [search reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/search/#full-text-matching) lists every rule.

properties.heading: Create a full-text index
properties.text:
Name the index, the label, and the string properties it covers after `ON EACH`:

```cypher run name=create-fulltext
CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX note_text IF NOT EXISTS
FOR (n:Note) ON EACH [n.text]
```

```table
(no rows) · indexes added: 1
```

`ON EACH [n.title, n.text]` indexes several properties, and `FOR ()-[r:<TYPE>]-()` indexes relationships instead of nodes. Without `IF NOT EXISTS`, a second index of the same name fails with `semantic error: IndexAlreadyExists`. The [search reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/search/#index-statements) has every form.

properties.heading: Fuse with a vector search
properties.text:
A full-text search finds the exact words and misses paraphrases; a vector search finds what is near in meaning and misses exact names. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) merges the two ranked lists without comparing their scores: a note earns `1 / (60 + rank)` from each list it appears in, and the shares add up. First, a vector index on the embeddings:

```cypher run name=create-vector
CREATE VECTOR INDEX note_embedding IF NOT EXISTS
FOR (n:Note) ON (n.embedding)
OPTIONS {indexConfig: {`vector.dimensions`: 3, `vector.similarity_function`: 'cosine'}}
```

```table
(no rows) · indexes added: 1
```

The question is `wal tests` again, with its embedding. On its own, each search returns a ranked list of `$k` notes:

```json data=question
{"q": "wal tests", "v": [0.5, 0.8, 0.1], "k": 3}
```

```cypher run name=vector-list params=question
MATCH (n:Note)
SEARCH n IN (VECTOR INDEX note_embedding FOR $v LIMIT $k) SCORE AS score
RETURN n.id AS id, score
ORDER BY score DESC, id
```

```table
| id   | score              |
|------|--------------------|
| "n6" | 0.9944459199905396 |
| "n3" | 0.9512366056442261 |
| "n2" | 0.8602553606033325 |
3 rows
```

```cypher run name=fulltext-list params=question
MATCH (n:Note)
SEARCH n IN (FULLTEXT INDEX note_text FOR $q LIMIT $k) SCORE AS score
RETURN n.id AS id, score
ORDER BY score DESC, id
```

```table
| id   | score              |
|------|--------------------|
| "n6" | 1.1371966628886316 |
| "n1" | 0.4118477668724633 |
2 rows
```

`CALL () { … UNION ALL … }` runs both searches in one statement; each branch numbers its results by position, and the outer query adds up the shares and walks from each note to its project:

```cypher run name=fuse params=question
CALL () {
  MATCH (n:Note)
  SEARCH n IN (VECTOR INDEX note_embedding FOR $v LIMIT $k) SCORE AS score
  WITH n ORDER BY score DESC, n.id
  WITH collect(n) AS ns
  UNWIND range(0, size(ns) - 1) AS i
  RETURN ns[i] AS n, 'vector' AS list, i + 1 AS rank
  UNION ALL
  MATCH (n:Note)
  SEARCH n IN (FULLTEXT INDEX note_text FOR $q LIMIT $k) SCORE AS score
  WITH n ORDER BY score DESC, n.id
  WITH collect(n) AS ns
  UNWIND range(0, size(ns) - 1) AS i
  RETURN ns[i] AS n, 'fulltext' AS list, i + 1 AS rank
}
WITH n, sum(1.0 / (60 + rank)) AS rrf,
     min(CASE list WHEN 'vector' THEN rank END) AS vector_rank,
     min(CASE list WHEN 'fulltext' THEN rank END) AS fulltext_rank
ORDER BY rrf DESC, n.id LIMIT $k
MATCH (n)-[:ABOUT]->(p:Project)
RETURN n.id AS id, vector_rank, fulltext_rank, round(rrf, 4) AS rrf, p.name AS project
```

```table
| id   | vector_rank | fulltext_rank | rrf    | project          |
|------|-------------|---------------|--------|------------------|
| "n6" | 1           | 1             | 0.0328 | "opencypher-tck" |
| "n1" | null        | 2             | 0.0161 | "relate"         |
| "n3" | 2           | null          | 0.0161 | "opencypher-tck" |
3 rows
```

The view runs the two lists and the fused statement with the chosen `k`, up to the six notes the page holds, and shows the arithmetic beside the engine's fused score:

The 2 ranked lists for "wal tests", as recorded with k = 3:

| Rank | `vector-list` | `fulltext-list` |
| ---- | ------------- | --------------- |
| 1    | `n6`          | `n6`            |
| 2    | `n3`          | `n1`            |
| 3    | `n2`          |                 |

Fused by reciprocal rank: each list gives an id 1 / (60 + its rank there), and the shares add up. 4 ids, best first:

| id   | Rank in `vector-list` | Rank in `fulltext-list` | Arithmetic          | Fused score |
| ---- | --------------------- | ----------------------- | ------------------- | ----------- |
| `n6` | 1                     | 1                       | 1/(60+1) + 1/(60+1) | 0.0328      |
| `n1` |                       | 2                       | 1/(60+2)            | 0.0161      |
| `n3` | 2                     |                         | 1/(60+2)            | 0.0161      |
| `n2` | 3                     |                         | 1/(60+3)            | 0.0159      |

Live: a k slider runs the page's search statements on its database in your browser with that k, and the view marks the ids the engine returns.

`n6` leads both lists. `n1` holds the word `wal` but is not among the nearest vectors, and `n3` is near in meaning but holds neither word; the fusion keeps both, tied, with `n.id` breaking the tie. The constant 60 keeps one list's first place from outweighing the other list.

[Hybrid recall](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/hybrid-recall/) builds the same fusion over 40 notes, with a time filter inside the vector search. Two other forms combine the indexes: the intersection, which runs the second search only over what the first returned, and `COMBINE … USING WRRF`, a preview that fuses inside `SEARCH` itself; the [search reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/search/#hybrid-search) has both.

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
| Message or symptom                                                                       | Cause                                                                                                    | Remedy                                                           |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `syntax error: InvalidUseOfCommand: WHERE cannot be used together with 'FULLTEXT INDEX'` | A `WHERE` inside the full-text search's parentheses.                                                     | Move the filter after the `SEARCH` clause and raise its `LIMIT`. |
| `syntax error: parse error: expected LIMIT, got ")" (RightParen)`                        | The search has no `LIMIT`.                                                                               | Add `LIMIT <k>` inside the parentheses.                          |
| `syntax error: UndefinedVariable: variable 'score' not defined`                          | The query reads `score` without `SCORE AS`.                                                              | Add `SCORE AS score` after the closing parenthesis.              |
| `IndexDoesNotExist: <name>` or `WrongIndexType: <name>`                                  | The index name is misspelled, or names a vector index after `FULLTEXT INDEX`.                            | Check the name and type in `SHOW INDEXES`.                       |
| No rows for a word the text holds in another form                                        | The index has no stemming and no accent folding; `WITH ANALYZER 'english'` stems the query's words only. | Search for the form the text holds, or index a normalized copy.  |
| A query with `and` or `not` returns more notes, not fewer                                | Lowercase `and` and `not` are terms, and a query's terms are alternatives.                               | Write the operators in capitals: `wal AND tests`.                |

properties.heading: Know how text becomes terms
properties.text:
The index lowercases text and splits it into words of letters and digits. A query goes through the same split, and its operators are read ([Combine words with operators](#combine-words-with-operators)); nothing else happens to either. This cell runs one search per query string and lists the notes each one finds:

```cypher run name=terms
UNWIND ['wal', 'replay', 'replays', 'test', 'the', 'pull-request', '"torn tail"', 'tor*'] AS q
CALL (q) {
  MATCH (n:Note)
  SEARCH n IN (FULLTEXT INDEX note_text FOR q LIMIT 10) SCORE AS score
  RETURN collect(n.id) AS ids
}
RETURN q AS query, ids
```

```table
| query           | ids                            |
|-----------------|--------------------------------|
| "wal"           | ["n6", "n1"]                   |
| "replay"        | []                             |
| "replays"       | ["n5", "n1"]                   |
| "test"          | []                             |
| "the"           | ["n5", "n3", "n2", "n6", "n1"] |
| "pull-request"  | ["n3"]                         |
| "\"torn tail\"" | ["n1"]                         |
| "tor*"          | []                             |
8 rows
```

| Query            | What the result shows                                                     |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `wal`            | Case is ignored: it matches `WAL` in the text                             |
| `replay`, `test` | No stemming: `replay` does not match `replays`, nor `test` `tests`        |
| `the`            | No stop words: common words are terms like any other                      |
| `pull-request`   | Punctuation splits words: the query is the two terms `pull` and `request` |
| `"torn tail"`    | No phrase search: quotes are dropped, and the two words match separately  |
| `tor*`           | No wildcards: the query is the term `tor`, which no note holds            |

Accented letters are letters, and nothing folds them: `cafe` does not match `café`. To match word variants, store a normalized copy of the text in a second indexed property and search that. `WITH ANALYZER 'english'` after the query stems the query's words and drops English stop words, but the indexed text keeps its written form: with it, `replays` searches for `replay` and `tests` for `test`, which no note holds.

properties.heading: Load the notes
properties.text:
This cell writes the two example projects and six short notes about them. Each note has a `text`, an `embedding` vector, and an `ABOUT` relationship to its project.

```cypher run name=seed
CREATE (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (:Note {id: 'n1', text: 'The WAL replays on open and trims a torn tail.', embedding: vector([0.9, 0.1, 0.1], 3, FLOAT32)})-[:ABOUT]->(relate),
       (:Note {id: 'n2', text: 'A checkpoint writes the graph to a snapshot.', embedding: vector([0.8, 0.2, 0.2], 3, FLOAT32)})-[:ABOUT]->(relate),
       (:Note {id: 'n3', text: 'The scenarios run on every pull request.', embedding: vector([0.1, 0.9, 0.1], 3, FLOAT32)})-[:ABOUT]->(tck),
       (:Note {id: 'n4', text: 'Release notes list every fixed scenario.', embedding: vector([0.2, 0.5, 0.7], 3, FLOAT32)})-[:ABOUT]->(relate),
       (:Note {id: 'n5', text: 'The docs build replays every cell.', embedding: vector([0.1, 0.4, 0.9], 3, FLOAT32)})-[:ABOUT]->(relate),
       (:Note {id: 'n6', text: 'Recovery tests cut the WAL at every byte.', embedding: vector([0.6, 0.7, 0.1], 3, FLOAT32)})-[:ABOUT]->(tck)
```

```table
(no rows) · nodes created: 8, relationships created: 6, properties set: 22, labels added: 8
```

properties.heading: Page through and narrow the results
properties.text:
`SKIP` (or `OFFSET`) inside the search skips that many results before `LIMIT`:

```cypher run name=page
MATCH (n:Note)
SEARCH n IN (FULLTEXT INDEX note_text FOR 'every' SKIP 2 LIMIT 2) SCORE AS score
RETURN n.id AS id, score
```

```table
| id   | score               |
|------|---------------------|
| "n3" | 0.2064639029341305  |
| "n6" | 0.19550121782258376 |
2 rows
```

A full-text search takes no `WHERE` inside its parentheses. A filter or a pattern after the `SEARCH` clause keeps only the rows the search already returned, so ask the search for more than you need and limit afterwards. This cell keeps the notes about `relate`:

```cypher run name=narrow
MATCH (n:Note)
SEARCH n IN (FULLTEXT INDEX note_text FOR 'every' LIMIT 6) SCORE AS score
MATCH (n)-[:ABOUT]->(:Project {name: 'relate'})
RETURN n.id AS id, n.text AS text, score
ORDER BY score DESC, id
LIMIT 2
```

```table
| id   | text                                       | score               |
|------|--------------------------------------------|---------------------|
| "n4" | "Release notes list every fixed scenario." | 0.21872908528665308 |
| "n5" | "The docs build replays every cell."       | 0.21872908528665308 |
2 rows
```

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- A first look at Cypher, such as [your first graph](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/first-graph/).
- For the hybrid step, embeddings from the model of your choice. This guide uses three-dimensional vectors so the numbers stay readable; [search by vector similarity](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/vector-search/) covers the vector half on its own.

properties.heading: Read the score
properties.text: The score is BM25, the relevance score Neo4j's full-text index gives: each matching term adds more when few notes hold it, and a short note scores higher than a long one. `n6` holds both `wal` and `tests` and scores about `1.14`; `n1` holds only `wal` and scores about `0.41`. The score is not normalized, so it ranks results within one search and means nothing next to a vector score. Equal scores have no documented order, so sort on a second key, as the cell does with `id`.

properties.heading: Related
properties.text:
- [Search](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/search/): index statements, every `SEARCH` rule, the full-text matching table, and hybrid search.
- [Search by vector similarity](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/vector-search/): the vector half, with filters inside the search.
- [Hybrid recall](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/hybrid-recall/): reciprocal rank fusion over 40 notes, then a hop to each note's topic.
- [Problems relate solves](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/problems-relate-solves/#hybrid-retrieval-for-rag): hybrid retrieval for retrieval-augmented generation, and its data model.

properties.heading: Search by words
properties.text:
`SEARCH` restricts the `MATCH` to the index's top results. `LIMIT` is required, and `SCORE AS` names the score:

```json data=words
{"q": "wal tests"}
```

```cypher run name=search params=words
MATCH (n:Note)
SEARCH n IN (FULLTEXT INDEX note_text FOR $q LIMIT 5) SCORE AS score
RETURN n.id AS id, n.text AS text, score
ORDER BY score DESC, id
```

```table
| id   | text                                             | score              |
|------|--------------------------------------------------|--------------------|
| "n6" | "Recovery tests cut the WAL at every byte."      | 1.1371966628886316 |
| "n1" | "The WAL replays on open and trims a torn tail." | 0.4118477668724633 |
2 rows
```

Each word of the query is a term, and a note holding any of the terms matches. `n6` holds both `wal` and `tests`, `n1` only `wal`. The query can be a parameter, as in this cell, or a string literal; any other type fails with `type error: InvalidValueType: fulltext SEARCH requires a STRING query`.

properties.heading: Verify
properties.text:
`SHOW INDEXES` lists both indexes, the properties they cover, and their state:

```cypher run name=verify
SHOW INDEXES YIELD name, type, labelsOrTypes, properties, state
WHERE type IN ['FULLTEXT', 'VECTOR']
RETURN name, type, labelsOrTypes, properties, state
ORDER BY name
```

```table
| name             | type       | labelsOrTypes | properties    | state    |
|------------------|------------|---------------|---------------|----------|
| "note_embedding" | "VECTOR"   | ["Note"]      | ["embedding"] | "ONLINE" |
| "note_text"      | "FULLTEXT" | ["Note"]      | ["text"]      | "ONLINE" |
2 rows
```

Two `ONLINE` indexes and three fused rows mean both searches serve the statement.

properties.heading: Geospatial queries
properties.text: This guide shows you how to store locations as `point` values, measure the distance between them, find the places within a radius or inside a map box, and add a [point index](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#point-index) that narrows those searches. The cells run in page order on one in-memory [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store), in your browser and in the docs build; the index steps also run in a terminal, where the plan and its counters are visible.

properties.heading: Add a point index
properties.text:
A point index keeps the points of one label and property in an R-tree, so a radius or box predicate reads only the nearby nodes:

```cypher run name=create-index
CREATE POINT INDEX place_loc IF NOT EXISTS FOR (p:Place) ON (p.loc)
```

```table
(no rows) · indexes added: 1
```

The plan does not name the index: `EXPLAIN` shows the same `NodeByLabelScan` with a `WHERE` filter before and after it, because the index works inside that filter. `PROFILE` shows the difference in the scan's database hits. To see it in a terminal, write the same places to a new store, `places.rl`. This command writes:

```bash verify
relate --database ./places.rl "CREATE (:Place {name: 'Riverside Office', kind: 'office', loc: point({latitude: 45.5231, longitude: -122.6765})}),
       (:Place {name: 'Bean There', kind: 'cafe', loc: point({latitude: 45.5262, longitude: -122.6789})}),
       (:Place {name: 'Ferry Cafe', kind: 'cafe', loc: point({latitude: 45.5122, longitude: -122.6587})}),
       (:Place {name: 'Hilltop Roasters', kind: 'cafe', loc: point({latitude: 45.5428, longitude: -122.7011})}),
       (:Place {name: 'Harbor Library', kind: 'library', loc: point({latitude: 45.5190, longitude: -122.6730})}),
       (:Place {name: 'Eastside Cafe', kind: 'cafe', loc: point({latitude: 45.5155, longitude: -122.6205})}),
       (:Place {name: 'Pier Cafe', kind: 'cafe', loc: point({latitude: 47.6097, longitude: -122.3331})}),
       (:Place {name: 'North Library', kind: 'library', loc: point({latitude: 47.6205, longitude: -122.3493})})"
```

Profile the radius search, read-only, and print only the scan's `DbHits` counter from the plan in the [envelope](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#envelope). Without an index, the scan reads all eight places:

```bash verify
relate --database ./places.rl --read-only --mode envelope "PROFILE MATCH (p:Place) WHERE point.distance(p.loc, point({latitude: 45.5231, longitude: -122.6765})) < 2000 RETURN p.name AS name" | grep -o '"DbHits":[0-9]*' | tail -n 1
```

```text
"DbHits":8
```

Create the index. This command writes it to `places.rl`:

```bash verify
relate --database ./places.rl "CREATE POINT INDEX place_loc IF NOT EXISTS FOR (p:Place) ON (p.loc)"
```

The same search now reads only the four places the index returns:

```bash verify
relate --database ./places.rl --read-only --mode envelope "PROFILE MATCH (p:Place) WHERE point.distance(p.loc, point({latitude: 45.5231, longitude: -122.6765})) < 2000 RETURN p.name AS name" | grep -o '"DbHits":[0-9]*' | tail -n 1
```

```text
"DbHits":4
```

The index serves `point.withinBBox(<property>, …)` and `point.distance(<property>, <center>) < <bound>` (or `<=`) in a `WHERE`, with the center a literal, a parameter or a variable bound before the `MATCH`. Ordering by distance with `LIMIT` and no radius reads every node of the label. [Tune a query](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/tune-a-query/) covers reading a profile.

properties.heading: Find places inside a map box
properties.text:
`point.withinBBox(<point>, <lower-left>, <upper-right>)` is true when the point lies inside the box the two corners span. For geographic points, the corners are latitude and longitude pairs, so the box is a latitude and longitude rectangle. Its south, west, north and east limits are parameters:

```json data=box
{"south": 45.50, "west": -122.70, "north": 45.53, "east": -122.65}
```

```cypher run name=bbox params=box
MATCH (p:Place)
WHERE point.withinBBox(p.loc, point({latitude: $south, longitude: $west}), point({latitude: $north, longitude: $east}))
RETURN p.name AS name
ORDER BY name
```

```table
| name               |
|--------------------|
| "Bean There"       |
| "Ferry Cafe"       |
| "Harbor Library"   |
| "Riverside Office" |
4 rows
```

A box whose lower-left longitude is greater than its upper-right longitude crosses the antimeridian, at longitude 180. Mixing coordinate systems among the three points returns `null`.

properties.heading: Find places within a radius
properties.text:
Compare the distance from a center with the radius in meters. The center and the radius are parameters, so the same statement serves any position:

```json data=here
{"lat": 45.5231, "lon": -122.6765, "radius": 2000}
```

```cypher run name=radius params=here
MATCH (p:Place)
WHERE point.distance(p.loc, point({latitude: $lat, longitude: $lon})) < $radius
RETURN p.name AS name, p.kind AS kind,
       round(point.distance(p.loc, point({latitude: $lat, longitude: $lon}))) AS meters
ORDER BY meters
```

```table
| name               | kind      | meters |
|--------------------|-----------|--------|
| "Riverside Office" | "office"  | 0.0    |
| "Bean There"       | "cafe"    | 393.0  |
| "Harbor Library"   | "library" | 532.0  |
| "Ferry Cafe"       | "cafe"    | 1844.0 |
4 rows
```

Keep `point.distance(<property>, <center>)` on the left of the comparison, inside the `WHERE`, as the cell does. That is the shape a point index serves; a distance computed in a `WITH` and filtered later is checked on every place instead.

properties.heading: Find the nearest places
properties.text:
Order by distance and take the first few. Bounding the search with a radius first lets a point index narrow it, and keeps the result near:

```cypher run name=nearest params=here
MATCH (p:Place {kind: 'cafe'})
WHERE point.distance(p.loc, point({latitude: $lat, longitude: $lon})) < 5000
RETURN p.name AS cafe, round(point.distance(p.loc, point({latitude: $lat, longitude: $lon})) / 1000, 1) AS km
ORDER BY km
LIMIT 3
```

```table
| cafe               | km  |
|--------------------|-----|
| "Bean There"       | 0.4 |
| "Ferry Cafe"       | 1.8 |
| "Hilltop Roasters" | 2.9 |
3 rows
```

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
| Message or symptom                                                                                                                                    | Cause                                                                                 | Remedy                                                                              |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `semantic error: InvalidArgumentValue: point() latitude must be in the range [-90, 90]`                                                               | The latitude is out of range, often because latitude and longitude are swapped.       | Pass `{latitude: <lat>, longitude: <lon>}` by name.                                 |
| `syntax error: InvalidPoint: the map is not a valid POINT. Use either Cartesian ('x' and 'y') or geographic ('latitude' and 'longitude') coordinates` | The map lacks one of the two keys of a kind, as in `{x: 1, latitude: 2}`.             | Give `x` and `y`, or `latitude` and `longitude`.                                    |
| A distance or `withinBBox` returns `null`                                                                                                             | The points use different coordinate systems, or one is `null`.                        | Compare `p.loc.srid` on both sides, and build every point the same way.             |
| `syntax error: UnknownFunction: unknown function distance()`                                                                                          | The older Neo4j name.                                                                 | Use `point.distance()`.                                                             |
| `PROFILE` reads every node after the index exists                                                                                                     | The distance is computed in a `WITH` and filtered later, or the search has no radius. | Put `point.distance(<property>, <center>) < <bound>` in the `WHERE` of the `MATCH`. |

properties.heading: Load some places
properties.text:
This cell writes eight places: six near a riverside office in Portland, Oregon, and two in Seattle, Washington, to the north. Each place has a `loc` [property](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#property) built with `point()` from a latitude and a longitude.

```cypher run name=seed
CREATE (:Place {name: 'Riverside Office', kind: 'office', loc: point({latitude: 45.5231, longitude: -122.6765})}),
       (:Place {name: 'Bean There', kind: 'cafe', loc: point({latitude: 45.5262, longitude: -122.6789})}),
       (:Place {name: 'Ferry Cafe', kind: 'cafe', loc: point({latitude: 45.5122, longitude: -122.6587})}),
       (:Place {name: 'Hilltop Roasters', kind: 'cafe', loc: point({latitude: 45.5428, longitude: -122.7011})}),
       (:Place {name: 'Harbor Library', kind: 'library', loc: point({latitude: 45.5190, longitude: -122.6730})}),
       (:Place {name: 'Eastside Cafe', kind: 'cafe', loc: point({latitude: 45.5155, longitude: -122.6205})}),
       (:Place {name: 'Pier Cafe', kind: 'cafe', loc: point({latitude: 47.6097, longitude: -122.3331})}),
       (:Place {name: 'North Library', kind: 'library', loc: point({latitude: 47.6205, longitude: -122.3493})})
```

```table
(no rows) · nodes created: 8, properties set: 24, labels added: 8
```

List them with their coordinates to check the load:

```cypher run name=places
MATCH (p:Place)
RETURN p.name AS name, p.kind AS kind, p.loc.latitude AS latitude, p.loc.longitude AS longitude
ORDER BY name
```

```table

|--------------------|-----------|----------|-----------|
| "Bean There"       | "cafe"    | 45.5262  | -122.6789 |
| "Eastside Cafe"    | "cafe"    | 45.5155  | -122.6205 |
| "Ferry Cafe"       | "cafe"    | 45.5122  | -122.6587 |
| "Harbor Library"   | "library" | 45.519   | -122.673  |
| "Hilltop Roasters" | "cafe"    | 45.5428  | -122.7011 |
| "North Library"    | "library" | 47.6205  | -122.3493 |
| "Pier Cafe"        | "cafe"    | 47.6097  | -122.3331 |
| "Riverside Office" | "office"  | 45.5231  | -122.6765 |
8 rows
```

properties.heading: Measure a distance
properties.text:
`point.distance(a, b)` between two geographic points returns meters, by the haversine formula with an Earth radius of 6,378,140 m:

```cypher run name=distance
MATCH (a:Place {name: 'Riverside Office'}), (b:Place {name: 'Pier Cafe'})
RETURN round(point.distance(a.loc, b.loc) / 1000, 1) AS km
```

```table
| km    |
|-------|
| 233.8 |
1 row
```

Between two cartesian points it returns the straight-line distance: `point.distance(point({x: 0, y: 0}), point({x: 3, y: 4}))` is `5.0`. Between points of two different coordinate systems it returns `null`, with no error.

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- A first look at Cypher, such as [your first graph](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/first-graph/).
- For the terminal steps, relate on your `PATH` ([install](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).

properties.heading: Read a point
properties.text:
A point built from `latitude` and `longitude` is a geographic point on the WGS-84 coordinate system, spatial reference id (SRID) 4326. Its parts are properties of the value:

```cypher run name=read-point
MATCH (p:Place {name: 'Riverside Office'})
RETURN p.loc.srid AS srid, p.loc.crs AS crs, p.loc.latitude AS latitude, p.loc.longitude AS longitude
```

```table
| srid | crs      | latitude | longitude |
|------|----------|----------|-----------|
| 4326 | "wgs-84" | 45.5231  | -122.6765 |
1 row
```

| `point()` map                   | Coordinate system | SRID | Distance unit                                 |
| ------------------------------- | ----------------- | ---- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `{latitude, longitude}`         | `wgs-84`          | 4326 | meters, along the Earth's surface             |
| `{latitude, longitude, height}` | `wgs-84-3d`       | 4979 | meters                                        |
| `{x, y}`                        | `cartesian`       | 7203 | the coordinates' own unit, as a straight line |
| `{x, y, z}`                     | `cartesian-3d`    | 9157 | the coordinates' own unit                     |

On a geographic point, `x` is the longitude and `y` the latitude. A latitude outside -90 to 90 fails with `InvalidArgumentValue: point() latitude must be in the range [-90, 90]`, after `type error:` in the cells and `semantic error:` on the CLI. The check also catches a latitude and longitude passed the wrong way round wherever the longitude is beyond 90 degrees either way, as in Portland. Points are the whole geospatial surface: there are no polygons or lines, so store a shape as an ordinary property and do the geometry in your program.

properties.text:

- [Problems relate solves](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/problems-relate-solves/#geospatial-memory): geospatial memory for an agent, and its data model.

properties.heading: Search an area on a plane
properties.text:
The explorer draws the places on a plane, longitude across and latitude up, and searches them with two cells on this page: the radius search from [Find places within a radius](#find-places-within-a-radius) and the box search from [Find places inside a map box](#find-places-inside-a-map-box). Drag the circle or the box, or focus it and press the arrow keys to move it and `+` or `-` to resize it. Each move runs the search again on this page's store with the shape's position as its [parameters](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#parameter), and the places it returns light up with their names. The statement and its parameters show under the plane as they ran, with `PROFILE` in front so the plan reports what the scan read.

The point index button runs the statement from [Add a point index](#add-a-point-index), or drops the index, and searches again. With eight places the times are too small to show the index at work; the scan's database hits show it: the scan reads every place without the index and only the places the index returns with it. The two Seattle places lie beyond the plane; without the index the scan still reads them.

The `radius` cell's recorded result: 4 places within 2000 m of latitude 45.5231, longitude -122.6765.

| name             | kind    | meters |
| ---------------- | ------- | ------ |
| Riverside Office | office  | 0.0    |
| Bean There       | cafe    | 393.0  |
| Harbor Library   | library | 532.0  |
| Ferry Cafe       | cafe    | 1844.0 |

Not drawn, beyond the plane: to the north-east, North Library and Pier Cafe.

Live: the circle drags across the plane (arrow keys move it, plus and minus resize it), and each move runs the radius search again on the page's database in your browser with the circle as its parameters, lighting up the places it returns and showing the parse, plan and execute times and the scan's database hits; where the page has a box search, a box drags and searches the same way, and where it names its point index, a button creates or drops the index and searches again.

![The places, and the 2000 m radius search as recorded](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/geospatial/element-geo-explorer-1-light.svg)

properties.heading: Verify
properties.text:
`SHOW INDEXES` lists the point index and its state:

```cypher run name=verify
SHOW INDEXES YIELD name, type, labelsOrTypes, properties, state
WHERE type = 'POINT'
RETURN name, type, labelsOrTypes, properties, state
```

```table
| name        | type    | labelsOrTypes | properties | state    |
|-------------|---------|---------------|------------|----------|
| "place_loc" | "POINT" | ["Place"]     | ["loc"]    | "ONLINE" |
1 row
```

An `ONLINE` index and four places within 2 km of the office mean the index is in place and the radius search finds what the map shows.

properties.heading: Import a CSV
properties.text:
This guide shows you how to load rows from CSV files into a relate [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store) with `LOAD CSV`: preview the rows, create nodes and relationships with typed properties, and check the result. Local file reads are denied by default; `--load-csv-dir <dir>` allows the files under one directory, and nothing outside it.

The steps run in a terminal. `LOAD CSV` reads files from the machine's disk, which the in-browser cells on other pages cannot reach.

properties.heading: Allow the directory relate may read
properties.text:
`LOAD CSV` reads only regular files under the directory you allow. The flag wins over the environment variable, and with neither set every local read fails.

| Setting                | Default                 | Meaning                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--load-csv-dir <dir>` | denied                  | Allows files under `<dir>`; the directory must exist when the store opens                                |
| `RELATE_LOAD_CSV_DIR`  | unset                   | The directory when the flag is absent; the Python and Node.js clients read it too when they open a store |
| Size limit per file    | 8,388,608 bytes (8 MiB) | Fixed for the CLI; a larger file fails                                                                   |

| Path in `FROM`                                          | Result                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `'people.csv'`, `'sub/people.csv'`                      | Read, relative to the directory                     |
| `'file:///people.csv'`                                  | Read, relative to the directory                     |
| `'file:///<absolute path>'`                             | Read when the absolute path is inside the directory |
| `'/<absolute path>'`, without `file://`                 | Refused                                             |
| A path with `..`, or a symbolic link that leads outside | Refused                                             |
| `'https://…'` or any other scheme                       | Refused: `LOAD CSV` does not fetch URLs             |

A refused path fails with the same message as a missing file, `LOAD CSV file unavailable`, and the message never names the path.

properties.heading: Create the nodes
properties.text:
Load the people into a new single-file store, `team.rl`. This step writes. `MERGE` matches a person who already exists, so running it twice creates nothing new, and `RETURN count(*)` reports the rows read.

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --load-csv-dir ./import --mode table "LOAD CSV WITH HEADERS FROM 'file:///people.csv' AS row MERGE (p:Person {name: row.name}) SET p.role = row.role RETURN count(*) AS people"
```

```text
+--------+
| people |
+--------+
| 3      |
+--------+
```

properties.heading: Create the relationships with types
properties.text:
The second file connects people to projects. Convert each value as you store it: `toInteger(row.since)` stores a number, so a later `ORDER BY since` or `since >= 2023` compares numbers, not strings. This step writes too.

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --load-csv-dir ./import --mode table "LOAD CSV WITH HEADERS FROM 'file:///works_on.csv' AS row MATCH (p:Person {name: row.person}) MERGE (proj:Project {name: row.project}) SET proj.language = row.language MERGE (p)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(proj) SET w.since = toInteger(row.since) RETURN count(w) AS relationships"
```

```text
+---------------+
| relationships |
+---------------+
| 3             |
+---------------+
```

The conversion functions are `toInteger`, `toFloat` and `toBoolean`, plus `date()` and `datetime()` for ISO 8601 strings. An empty field reads as `''`, and `toInteger('')` is `null`, so an empty cell stores no property. A row with fewer fields than the header maps the missing keys to `null`.

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
Each of these exits with a nonzero [exit code](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#exit-code) and prints the message on stderr:

| Message                                                                                    | Exit code | Cause                                                                                                                                             | Remedy                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `LOAD CSV file unavailable`                                                                | 1         | No `--load-csv-dir` or `RELATE_LOAD_CSV_DIR`, or the file is missing, outside the directory, a symbolic link out of it, a special file, or a URL. | Pass `--load-csv-dir <dir>` and keep the file under it, named by a relative path or a `file:///` path. |
| `Failed to open Relate: semantic error: LOAD CSV invalid configuration`                    | 1         | The directory given to `--load-csv-dir` does not exist.                                                                                           | Create the directory first, or correct the path.                                                       |
| `LOAD CSV file exceeds byte limit`                                                         | 1         | The file is larger than 8,388,608 bytes.                                                                                                          | Split the file and load the parts one statement each.                                                  |
| `type error: LOAD CSV FIELDTERMINATOR must be exactly one character`                       | 6         | `FIELDTERMINATOR` has more or fewer than one character.                                                                                           | Use one character, such as `';'` or `'\t'`.                                                            |
| `syntax error: WriteBeforeCallInTransactions: a write cannot precede CALL IN TRANSACTIONS` | 6         | `LOAD CSV` and `CALL { … } IN TRANSACTIONS` in one statement; `LOAD CSV` counts as a write here.                                                  | Load without `IN TRANSACTIONS`, or split the file and run one statement per part.                      |

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- relate on your `PATH` ([install](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).
- CSV files with a header row, in one directory. The steps write two small ones, so you can follow along in an empty directory.

properties.heading: Preview the rows
properties.text:
Read a file without writing anything: with no `--database`, relate opens an in-memory store that is gone when the command exits. `WITH HEADERS` makes each row a map keyed by the header names.

```bash verify
relate --load-csv-dir ./import --mode table "LOAD CSV WITH HEADERS FROM 'file:///works_on.csv' AS row RETURN row.person AS person, row.since AS since, valueType(row.since) AS type"
```

```text
+---------+--------+-------------------+
| person  | since  | type              |
+---------+--------+-------------------+
| "Ada"   | "2024" | "STRING NOT NULL" |
| "Grace" | "2023" | "STRING NOT NULL" |
| "Grace" | "2022" | "STRING NOT NULL" |
+---------+--------+-------------------+
```

Every value `LOAD CSV` reads is a string, `since` included. The path `file:///works_on.csv` resolves inside the directory `--load-csv-dir` names; `'works_on.csv'` reads the same file.

properties.heading: Put the files in one directory
properties.text:
Create a directory for the files relate may read, and two files in it: the people from the shared example graph, and who works on which project since when.

```bash verify
mkdir import
cat > import/people.csv <<'CSV'
name,role
Ada,engineer
Grace,engineer
Noor,maintainer
CSV
cat > import/works_on.csv <<'CSV'
person,project,language,since
Ada,relate,Rust,2024
Grace,relate,Rust,2023
Grace,opencypher-tck,Gherkin,2022
CSV
```

properties.heading: Read files without a header row
properties.text:
Without `WITH HEADERS`, each row is a list of strings and the header, if the file has one, is the first row:

```bash verify
relate --load-csv-dir ./import --mode table "LOAD CSV FROM 'file:///people.csv' AS row RETURN row[0] AS first, row[1] AS second"
```

```text
+---------+--------------+
| first   | second       |
+---------+--------------+
| "name"  | "role"       |
| "Ada"   | "engineer"   |
| "Grace" | "engineer"   |
| "Noor"  | "maintainer" |
+---------+--------------+
```

For a separator other than a comma, add `FIELDTERMINATOR` with one character, such as `FIELDTERMINATOR ';'`. Fields follow the quoting rules of RFC 4180, the Request for Comments (RFC) that defines CSV: a field in double quotes may hold the separator, a line break, or `""` for one quote.

properties.heading: Related
properties.text:

properties.heading: Verify
properties.text:
Open the store read-only and read the graph back:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode table "MATCH (p:Person)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(proj:Project) RETURN p.name AS person, proj.name AS project, w.since AS since ORDER BY since"
```

```text
+---------+------------------+-------+
| person  | project          | since |
+---------+------------------+-------+
| "Grace" | "opencypher-tck" | 2022  |
| "Grace" | "relate"         | 2023  |
| "Ada"   | "relate"         | 2024  |
+---------+------------------+-------+
```

Three relationships, sorted by number. Noor has no row: `works_on.csv` has no line for Noor.

properties.heading: Indexes and constraints
properties.text: This guide shows you how to add [indexes](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#index) that make lookups fast and [constraints](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#constraint) that keep the data clean, list both, check with `EXPLAIN` that the planner uses an index, and drop them. An index changes how fast a statement runs and never what it returns; a constraint changes which writes succeed. The cells run in page order on one in-memory store; the plan steps also run in a terminal.

properties.heading: Add constraints
properties.text:
A constraint is checked on every write, and on the existing data when you create it. A write that breaks one fails as a whole and changes nothing.

| Kind             | Statement                                                                                                       | Refuses                                                                            |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Uniqueness       | `CREATE CONSTRAINT <name> FOR (n:<Label>) REQUIRE n.<prop> IS UNIQUE`; on relationships, `FOR ()-[r:<TYPE>]-()` | A second node or relationship with the same value. One without the property passes |
| Existence        | `… REQUIRE n.<prop> IS NOT NULL`                                                                                | A node or relationship without the property, or a `REMOVE` of it                   |
| Property type    | `… REQUIRE n.<prop> IS :: <TYPE>`, such as `INTEGER` or `STRING`                                                | A value of another type                                                            |
| Node key         | `… REQUIRE (n.<a>, n.<b>) IS NODE KEY`                                                                          | A node missing any of the properties, or repeating their combination               |
| Relationship key | `FOR ()-[r:<TYPE>]-() REQUIRE r.<prop> IS RELATIONSHIP KEY`                                                     | The same, for relationships                                                        |

A uniqueness constraint and a key constraint each create a range index of the same name, which serves lookups like any range index. This cell adds three constraints: unique project names, a required role, and an integer `since`:

```cypher run name=create-constraints
CREATE CONSTRAINT project_name IF NOT EXISTS FOR (p:Project) REQUIRE p.name IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT person_role_required IF NOT EXISTS FOR (p:Person) REQUIRE p.role IS NOT NULL;
CREATE CONSTRAINT works_on_since IF NOT EXISTS FOR ()-[w:WORKS_ON]-() REQUIRE w.since IS :: INTEGER
```

```table
(no rows) · constraints added: 3
```

A second `relate` project now fails, and the statement writes nothing:

```cypher run name=violation expect=error
CREATE (:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Go'})
```

```table
error: semantic error: ConstraintValidationFailed: `project_name` uniqueness
```

`MERGE` on the constrained key finds the existing node instead of creating a duplicate, so it is the write to use for "create unless it exists":

```cypher run name=merge
MERGE (p:Project {name: 'relate'})
ON CREATE SET p.language = 'Go'
RETURN p.name AS name, p.language AS language
```

```table
| name     | language |
|----------|----------|
| "relate" | "Rust"   |
1 row
```

A constraint that the existing data already breaks is refused when you create it. No project has a `tag`, so this one fails:

```cypher run name=existing-data expect=error
CREATE CONSTRAINT project_tag FOR (p:Project) REQUIRE p.tag IS NOT NULL
```

```table
error: semantic error: ConstraintValidationFailed: `project_tag` requires properties
```

A [graph type](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/schema-clauses/) declares the same rules for a whole graph at once, and an [ontology](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#ontology) can be applied as one ([use an ontology](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/ontology/)).

properties.heading: Check that the planner uses an index
properties.text:
`EXPLAIN` plans a statement without running it, and returns the plan and the planner's notifications. In this page's cells, the uniqueness constraint's index serves a lookup by project name, but nothing serves a lookup by language: the text index on `language` serves `CONTAINS`, not equality, so the planner scans every `Project` and names the range index that would help:

```cypher run name=explain-language
EXPLAIN MATCH (p:Project {language: 'Rust'}) RETURN p.name AS name
```

```table
(no rows)
```

In a browser, the plan viewer draws the plan as a tree. **Compare with the index** creates the range index the notification names on this page's database, plans the statement without it and with it, and shows the two side by side; pressed again, it drops the index.

The plan recorded for cell `explain-language`, as `relate --mode table` prints it:

```text
Query: MATCH (p:Project {language: 'Rust'}) RETURN p.name AS name
Plan:
+---------------------+----+-------------+----------------+
| Operator            | Id | Details     | Estimated Rows |
+---------------------+----+-------------+----------------+
| + ProduceResults    | 0  | 1 item(s)   | -              |
+---------------------+----+-------------+----------------+
| | + NodeByLabelScan | 1  | (p:Project) | 2              |
+---------------------+----+-------------+----------------+
Notifications:
Id 1: INFORMATION 03C91 Relate.Notification.Statement.MissingIndex: the equality predicate on language filters :Project without a range index on (:Project {language}) Remedy: CREATE INDEX relate_Project__language FOR (n:Project) ON (n.language)
```

Notifications, each with its remedy:

- [`03C91` Missing index](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/#notif-03c91) on operator 1: the equality predicate on language filters :Project without a range index on (:Project {language}). Remedy: `CREATE INDEX relate_Project__language FOR (n:Project) ON (n.language)`

In a browser, the viewer's comparison runs `CREATE INDEX relate_Project__language FOR (n:Project) ON (n.language)` on the page's in-memory database only.

Live: the plan is drawn as a tree, and PROFILE runs the statement on the page's database in your browser and adds each operator's rows, time and database hits as bars; the index button creates the index on the page's database, plans the statement with and without it side by side with the changes, and drops it again; a PROFILE downloads as a speedscope file.

In a terminal, `--mode table` prints the plan and the notifications. This step writes the example graph to a new store, `team.rl`:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl "CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace)"
```

Without an index, a lookup by name scans every `Project`, and the planner says which index would help:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode table "EXPLAIN MATCH (p:Project {name: 'relate'}) RETURN p.language AS language"
```

```text
Query: MATCH (p:Project {name: 'relate'}) RETURN p.language AS language
Plan:
+---------------------+----+-------------+----------------+
| Operator            | Id | Details     | Estimated Rows |
+---------------------+----+-------------+----------------+
| + ProduceResults    | 0  | 1 item(s)   | -              |
+---------------------+----+-------------+----------------+
| | + NodeByLabelScan | 1  | (p:Project) | 2              |
+---------------------+----+-------------+----------------+
Notifications:
Id 1: INFORMATION 03C91 Relate.Notification.Statement.MissingIndex: the equality predicate on name filters :Project without a range index on (:Project {name}) Remedy: CREATE INDEX relate_Project__name FOR (n:Project) ON (n.name)
```

The uniqueness constraint's index serves the same lookup. This command writes the constraint to `team.rl`:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl "CREATE CONSTRAINT project_name IF NOT EXISTS FOR (p:Project) REQUIRE p.name IS UNIQUE"
```

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode table "EXPLAIN MATCH (p:Project {name: 'relate'}) RETURN p.language AS language"
```

```text
Query: MATCH (p:Project {name: 'relate'}) RETURN p.language AS language
Plan:
+-------------------+----+---------------------------------------------------+----------------+
| Operator          | Id | Details                                           | Estimated Rows |
+-------------------+----+---------------------------------------------------+----------------+
| + ProduceResults  | 0  | 1 item(s)                                         | -              |
+-------------------+----+---------------------------------------------------+----------------+
| | + NodeIndexSeek | 1  | RANGE INDEX p:Project(name) WHERE name = 'relate' | 1              |
+-------------------+----+---------------------------------------------------+----------------+
```

`NodeIndexSeek` starts from the one node the index finds, and the notification is gone. A plan names an index only when it starts from it: `NodeIndexSeek` for an equality and `NodeIndexSeekByRange` for a range comparison. A point index, a text index, and a range index serving `IN` or `STARTS WITH` work inside the scan's `WHERE` filter instead, so the plan still shows `NodeByLabelScan`; `PROFILE` shows the difference as fewer database hits ([geospatial queries](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/geospatial/#add-a-point-index) has a worked example, and [tune a query](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/tune-a-query/) reads a profile).

properties.heading: Choose an index
properties.text:
Every index has a name, one [label](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#label) or [relationship type](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#relationship-type), and the properties it covers. `IF NOT EXISTS` after the name makes a create a no-op when an index of that name exists.

| Kind                    | Statement                                                                                                                        | Serves                                                                                                                                         |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Range, the default      | `CREATE INDEX <name> FOR (n:<Label>) ON (n.<prop>)`; `CREATE RANGE INDEX` is the same; `ON (n.<a>, n.<b>)` covers two properties | Equality and range comparisons on the property, `IN` a list, and `STARTS WITH`                                                                 |
| Range, on relationships | `CREATE INDEX <name> FOR ()-[r:<TYPE>]-() ON (r.<prop>)`                                                                         | Created and listed; on the verified version, `PROFILE` shows a relationship-property filter still reading every relationship of the type       |
| Text                    | `CREATE TEXT INDEX <name> FOR (n:<Label>) ON (n.<prop>)`                                                                         | `CONTAINS` on a string property                                                                                                                |
| Point                   | `CREATE POINT INDEX <name> FOR (n:<Label>) ON (n.<prop>)`                                                                        | `point.distance(<prop>, <center>) < <bound>` and `point.withinBBox` ([geospatial queries](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/geospatial/)) |
| Full-text               | `CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX <name> FOR (n:<Label>) ON EACH [n.<prop>, …]`                                                             | `SEARCH … FULLTEXT INDEX` ([full-text and hybrid search](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/full-text-and-hybrid-search/))                 |
| Vector                  | `CREATE VECTOR INDEX <name> FOR (n:<Label>) ON (n.<prop>) OPTIONS {…}`                                                           | `SEARCH … VECTOR INDEX` ([vector search](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/vector-search/))                                               |
| Lookup                  | `CREATE LOOKUP INDEX <name> FOR (n) ON EACH labels(n)`                                                                           | Created and listed by `SHOW INDEXES`                                                                                                           |

This cell creates a range index on a person's role, a text index on a project's language, and a two-property index:

```cypher run name=create-indexes
CREATE INDEX person_role IF NOT EXISTS FOR (p:Person) ON (p.role);
CREATE TEXT INDEX project_language IF NOT EXISTS FOR (p:Project) ON (p.language);
CREATE INDEX person_name_role IF NOT EXISTS FOR (p:Person) ON (p.name, p.role)
```

```table
(no rows) · indexes added: 3
```

The search indexes take options and have their own rules; the [search reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/search/) lists them.

properties.heading: Drop an index or a constraint
properties.text:
`DROP INDEX <name>` and `DROP CONSTRAINT <name>` remove one; `IF EXISTS` makes a missing name a no-op. Dropping a constraint also drops the index it owns:

```cypher run name=drop
DROP INDEX person_name_role IF EXISTS;
DROP CONSTRAINT person_role_required IF EXISTS
```

```table
(no rows) · indexes removed: 1, constraints removed: 1
```

An index that belongs to a constraint cannot be dropped on its own:

```cypher run name=drop-owned expect=error
DROP INDEX project_name
```

```table
error: Unable to drop 'project_name': the index belongs to a constraint.
```

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
| Message                                                                                                                                           | Cause                                                                                                                | Remedy                                                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| ``semantic error: ConstraintValidationFailed: `project_name` uniqueness`` (exit code 6)                                                           | A write repeats a unique value or key.                                                                               | Use `MERGE` on the key, or change the value.                         |
| ``semantic error: ConstraintValidationFailed: `<name>` requires properties``                                                                      | A write leaves out a required or key property, or the existing data lacks it when the constraint is created.         | Set the property, or fill it in on the existing data first.          |
| ``semantic error: ConstraintValidationFailed: `<name>` property type``                                                                            | A value of another type than the constraint names.                                                                   | Convert the value, such as `toInteger(row.since)`.                   |
| `semantic error: IndexAlreadyExists` or `semantic error: ConstraintAlreadyExists`                                                                 | The name is taken.                                                                                                   | Add `IF NOT EXISTS`, or check `SHOW INDEXES` and `SHOW CONSTRAINTS`. |
| `semantic error: EquivalentSchemaRuleAlreadyExists`                                                                                               | An index or constraint on the same label and properties exists under another name, such as a constraint's own index. | Keep the existing one.                                               |
| `semantic error: AlreadyExists: there already exists an index (:Person {role}). A constraint cannot be created until the index has been dropped.` | A uniqueness constraint over properties that a range index already covers.                                           | Drop the index, then create the constraint, which brings its own.    |
| `Unable to drop 'project_name': the index belongs to a constraint.` (exit code 1)                                                                 | `DROP INDEX` on a constraint's index.                                                                                | Drop the constraint.                                                 |
| ``semantic error: NoSuchIndex: `<name>` `` or `semantic error: ConstraintNotFound`                                                                | The name does not exist.                                                                                             | Add `IF EXISTS`, or check the name with `SHOW`.                      |

properties.heading: List indexes and constraints
properties.text:
`SHOW INDEXES` and `SHOW CONSTRAINTS` return one row per entry. `YIELD` picks the columns:

```cypher run name=show-constraints
SHOW CONSTRAINTS YIELD name, type, entityType, labelsOrTypes, properties, propertyType
RETURN name, type, entityType, labelsOrTypes, properties, propertyType
ORDER BY name
```

```table
| name                   | type                         | entityType     | labelsOrTypes | properties | propertyType |
|------------------------|------------------------------|----------------|---------------|------------|--------------|
| "person_role_required" | "NODE_PROPERTY_EXISTENCE"    | "NODE"         | ["Person"]    | ["role"]   | null         |
| "project_name"         | "NODE_PROPERTY_UNIQUENESS"   | "NODE"         | ["Project"]   | ["name"]   | null         |
| "works_on_since"       | "RELATIONSHIP_PROPERTY_TYPE" | "RELATIONSHIP" | ["WORKS_ON"]  | ["since"]  | "INTEGER"    |
3 rows
```

```cypher run name=show-indexes
SHOW INDEXES YIELD name, type, labelsOrTypes, properties, owningConstraint, state
RETURN name, type, labelsOrTypes, properties, owningConstraint, state
ORDER BY name
```

```table
| name               | type     | labelsOrTypes | properties       | owningConstraint | state    |
|--------------------|----------|---------------|------------------|------------------|----------|
| "index_1b9dcc97"   | "LOOKUP" | null          | null             | null             | "ONLINE" |
| "index_460996c0"   | "LOOKUP" | null          | null             | null             | "ONLINE" |
| "person_name_role" | "RANGE"  | ["Person"]    | ["name", "role"] | null             | "ONLINE" |
| "person_role"      | "RANGE"  | ["Person"]    | ["role"]         | null             | "ONLINE" |
| "project_language" | "TEXT"   | ["Project"]   | ["language"]     | null             | "ONLINE" |
| "project_name"     | "RANGE"  | ["Project"]   | ["name"]         | "project_name"   | "ONLINE" |
6 rows
```

`owningConstraint` names the constraint an index belongs to, and `state` is `ONLINE` once the index serves reads. The two `LOOKUP` rows, `index_1b9dcc97` and `index_460996c0`, are on every store before any `CREATE INDEX`; they are listed only and can't be dropped. `SHOW RANGE INDEXES`, `SHOW UNIQUE CONSTRAINTS` and the other kinds narrow the list to one kind.

properties.heading: Load the example graph
properties.text:
This cell writes the shared graph: Ada, Grace and Noor, the `relate` and `opencypher-tck` projects, and who works on what.

```cypher run name=seed
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace)
```

```table
(no rows) · nodes created: 5, relationships created: 5, properties set: 13, labels added: 5
```

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- A first look at Cypher, such as [your first graph](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/first-graph/).
- For the terminal steps, relate on your `PATH` ([install](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).

properties.text:
