- [Answer codebase questions text search can't](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/codebase-context-graph/): a worked recipe over a repository's records and dependencies.
- [Codebase context graph](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/problems-relate-solves/#codebase-context-graph): the problem this graph serves.
- [Install and run an extension](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/extensions/install-and-run/): trust tiers, `list`, `remove`.
- [`SEARCH` reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/search/): full-text search options and scoring.

properties.heading: The graph it builds
properties.text:
```mermaid flowchart LR accTitle: Data model: people author commits, commits touch files, files change together accDescr { A Person AUTHORED each Commit they wrote, and a Commit TOUCHED every File it changed. Two files that changed in the same commits are joined by CO_CHANGED, whose count is the number of those commits. } Person(("Person
email · name")) -- "AUTHORED" --> Commit(("Commit
sha · subject
authored_at · files_changed")) Commit -- "TOUCHED" --> File(("File
path · name")) File -- "CO_CHANGED
count" --> File class Person l1 class Commit l2 class File l3 ``` A Person AUTHORED each Commit they wrote, and a Commit TOUCHED every File it changed. Two files that changed in the same commits are joined by CO_CHANGED, whose count is the number of those commits. Each [label](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#label) and [relationship type](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#relationship-type) carries these properties: | Element | Properties | | ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `:Person` | `email` (lowercased; the key), `name` (from that person's newest imported commit) | | `:Commit` | `sha` (the key), `subject`, `authored_at` (a datetime, the author date), `files_changed` | | `:File` | `path` (the key), `name` | | `AUTHORED` | None; from a person to each commit they wrote | | `TOUCHED` | None; from a commit to each file it changed | | `CO_CHANGED` | `count`: the imported commits that changed both files; from the alphabetically smaller `path` to the larger | The extension creates four indexes. Range indexes `file_path`, `commit_sha`, and `person_email` are created before the first write, and the [full-text index](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#full-text-index) `commit_subject` on `Commit.subject` after the last. These rules shape the graph: - Merge commits are left out, and only `HEAD`'s history is read: branches, tags, and the commit graph itself are not imported. - A `:File` is every path a commit touched, including files deleted since. `path` is `DIR` joined with the path git prints, so `planner` gives `planner/src/main.rs`, the same key `fs-to-graph` writes for the same `DIR`. - Each batch of rows commits on its own. A failed run can leave its earlier batches committed; running the same command again completes the import, because every write is a `MERGE` and `count` is overwritten, never added to. - A narrower run, with `--since` or `--max-commits`, overwrites only the pairs it recounts. Import into a new store when the window changes. - An import refuses before it writes anything when `git log` prints more than 134217728 bytes (128 MiB), or when it would write more than 5000000 `CO_CHANGED` pairs.

properties.heading: Verify
properties.text:
Right after the `git-to-graph` run, count the relationships by type, opening the store read-only:

```bash
relate --database ./code.rl --read-only --mode table "MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN type(r) AS type, count(*) AS relationships ORDER BY type"
```

```text
+--------------+---------------+
| type         | relationships |
+--------------+---------------+
| "AUTHORED"   | 5             |
| "CO_CHANGED" | 3             |
| "TOUCHED"    | 9             |
+--------------+---------------+
```

The counts match the run's summary: one `AUTHORED` per commit, 9 `TOUCHED`, and 3 `CO_CHANGED`.

properties.heading: Install and run an extension
properties.text: This guide shows you how to install an [extension](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#extension), run it into a [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store), and remove it. An extension is a package that adds an action to `relate run <name>`; `relate extension install` puts it on the machine, and where it comes from is the trust decision. relate never fetches anything on `relate run`: an action that is not installed fails.

properties.heading: Check a package
properties.text:
`relate extension check <dir>` runs a package folder through the stages a run needs: the manifest, the executable, starting it, and the MCP handshake. It opens no store and installs nothing, and relate fetches nothing. It does start the package's executable, so the package's own code runs with your permissions: check only a package whose source you have read or whose source you trust.

Checking the `greet` package prints one line per stage:

```bash verify
relate extension check ./greet
```

```text
manifest: ok (greet 0.1.0, protocol 2025-06-18)
executable: ok (greet.py)
spawn: ok
initialize: ok (MCP 2025-06-18, server relate 1.0.1)
notifications/initialized: ok
tools/list: ok (the shared tool table: 5 tools; the extension calls 'write_cypher')
pin: not from a GitHub source (unmarked)
```

The last line reports the package's GitHub pin and never changes the [exit code](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#exit-code): 0 when the package would mount, 2 for a problem in the manifest or the files, 1 for a problem when it runs.

properties.heading: Choose a trust tier
properties.text:
Each install source is a trust tier, and the flag you pass picks it. Every tier runs the same manifest, protocol, and name checks, and a failed install leaves nothing behind.

| Tier          | Install with                                            | What relate checks                                                                                                                                                     | What you trust               |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `first-party` | `relate extension install <name>`                       | The channel's index, `extensions.json`, against the release signing key that `relate upgrade` uses, then the package's SHA-256 against the signed index                | relate's release channel     |
| `github-pin`  | `--github <owner>/<repo>@<tag>` or `@<full-commit-sha>` | The tag's commit and the release asset's SHA-256, recorded on the first install; a later install whose tag moved or whose asset changed is refused before any download | One commit of one repository |
| `third-party` | `--url <url>`                                           | That the URL is `https`, or `http` to a loopback address; there is no signature to check                                                                               | Whoever serves the URL       |
| `local`       | `--from <dir>`                                          | That the executable resolves inside the folder; no network, no signature                                                                                               | Whoever controls the folder  |

`relate extension list` names each installed package's tier, and a folder placed in the extensions directory by hand lists as `unmarked`. The first-party channel carries `fs-to-graph` and `git-to-graph`.

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
**`Error: extension install: extension 'greet' is installed local (source: ./greet); refusing a third-party install over it — remove it first: relate extension remove greet`** (exit code 1). An install never replaces a package from another tier. Run `relate extension remove greet`, then install again. A reinstall from the same tier replaces the package.

**`Error: extension install: refusing to touch <home>/.config/relate/extensions/greet: no .relate-provenance.json marker present (the directory was not installed by relate); pass --force to override`** (exit code 1). A folder with that name was placed by hand. Pass `--force` to replace it, or move it aside.

**`Error: extension install: the package's manifest names '<manifest-name>' but the install was for '<name>'`** (exit code 1). Install under the manifest's `name`.

**`Error: extension remove: refusing to remove <home>/.config/relate/extensions/<name>: no .relate-provenance.json marker present (the directory was not installed by relate; remove it manually)`** (exit code 1). relate did not install that folder, so it does not delete it.

**`Error: no installed action 'git-to-graph' — first-party extension available: relate extension install git-to-graph`** (exit code 2). The action is not installed under the extensions directory relate reads; `relate run` fetches nothing. Check `relate extension list`, and check that `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is the same as when you installed it.

properties.heading: Install a package
properties.text:
From the first-party channel, by name. `--version <v>` picks a channel version; the default is the newest listed:

```bash
relate extension install git-to-graph
```

From a folder. This is the offline path, for CI, air-gapped machines, and your own packages:

```bash verify
relate extension install greet --from ./greet
```

```text
installed local extension greet 0.1.0 from ./greet
```

Each install prints one line naming the tier, the package's name and version, and the source. The name you install under must match the manifest's `name`. `install` copies two files, the manifest and the executable, and nothing else from the folder.

From a URL. The URL serves a gzip-compressed tar archive whose only members are `extension.json` and the executable, at the archive's root, with no directory entries:

```bash
tar --format ustar -czf greet-0.1.0.tar.gz -C greet extension.json greet.py
relate extension install greet --url https://<host>/greet-0.1.0.tar.gz
```

The installed line names the tier and the URL. This output came from a test server on the loopback address:

```text
installed third-party extension greet 0.1.0 from http://127.0.0.1:8897/greet-0.1.0.tar.gz
```

Any other URL, such as plain `http` to a host that is not loopback, is refused before anything is fetched (exit code 2):

```bash verify
relate extension install word-count --url http://example.com/word-count-0.1.0.tar.gz
```

```text
Error: extension install: --url accepts only https URLs (or plain http to the loopback interface); 'http://example.com/word-count-0.1.0.tar.gz' is neither
```

From a GitHub release, pinned. The release must carry an asset named `<name>-<version>-<os>-<arch>.tar.gz` for this machine:

```bash
relate extension install <name> --github <owner>/<repo>@<tag>
```

The first install records the pin in `extensions-trust.json` in the relate config directory. `relate extension list --trust` prints the recorded pins. When a tag later resolves to another commit, the install is refused until you pass `--re-approve` (accept what the tag resolves to now) or `--approve <full-commit-sha>` (accept only that commit). A repository without `@<tag>` is refused:

```bash verify
relate extension install greet --github relatedb/greet
```

```text
Error: extension install: --github 'relatedb/greet' needs a pin: owner/repo@tag or owner/repo@<full-commit-sha> (an untagged repository is a moving target)
Usage: relate extension init <name> [--lang sh|py|ts|rust]
       relate extension install <name> [--github REPO@TAG|@SHA] [--url URL] [--from DIR] [--version V] [--force] [--re-approve | --approve SHA]
       relate extension list [--available | --trust]
       relate extension remove <name> [--forget-pin]
       relate extension check <dir>
Run 'relate extension --help' for more information.
```

There is no upgrade action. To move to a newer version, install again with a newer `--version` or pin, which runs the tier's checks again.

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- relate on your `PATH`: `relate --version` prints its version ([Install relate](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).
- The runtime the extension's executable needs, such as `python3` for a Python package. The first-party `fs-to-graph` and `git-to-graph` packages are self-contained binaries; `git-to-graph` also runs `git`.
- Network access for the channel, `--github`, and `--url` installs. `--from` and every other action on this page work offline.

The examples install a package scaffolded with `relate extension init greet`, which writes a `greet/` folder holding a Python package:

```bash verify
relate extension init greet
```

properties.heading: Related
properties.text:
- [Write an extension](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/extensions/write-an-extension/): scaffold, check, and run your own package.
- [`relate extension`](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/extension/): every action and flag.
- [`relate run`](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/run/): the run command and its exit codes.
- [Keep an agent safe](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/agent-safety/): the permission matrix, including the extension tiers.
- [Security reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/security/): what each install source verifies.
- [Import git history with git-to-graph](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/extensions/git-to-graph/): a first-party package to install from the channel.

properties.heading: Remove a package
properties.text:
```bash verify
relate extension remove greet
```

```text
removed extension greet (<home>/.config/relate/extensions/greet)
```

`remove` deletes only a folder that carries the provenance marker; a folder placed by hand is refused, and there is no `--force`. It keeps a recorded GitHub pin, so a reinstall is still compared with it; `--forget-pin` clears the pin too.

properties.heading: Run an extension
properties.text:
The manifest defines each action's flags, and `relate run <name> --help` prints them:

```bash verify
relate run greet --help
```

```text
Usage: relate run greet [--name VALUE]

Run the installed extension 'greet' (v0.1.0) as a batched import into a store the host owns.
The child walks its source and drives the import as an MCP client; the
host alone owns the store, the caps and the exit codes.

  -d, --database PATH   Database to import into (default :memory:).
                         An explicit --database exits after the import; without
                         it, a TTY opens the shell on the in-memory graph.
  --name VALUE          A string flag (default 'there')
```

A run writes to the store named by `-d`, which relate opens and owns; the extension never sees its path. This run writes one node to a new `team.rl`:

```bash verify
relate run greet --name Ada -d ./team.rl
```

```text
greet: Hello Ada world! — wrote 1 sample node(s), the store holds 1
  MATCH (n:Scaffold) RETURN n
```

The first line is the extension's summary, and the indented lines are starter queries. With `-d`, the run exits after the summary. Without `-d`, it imports into an in-memory store and, on a terminal, opens the interactive shell on it and offers the starters there.

The store is an ordinary store afterwards:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode table "MATCH (n:Scaffold) RETURN n.id AS id, n.note AS note"
```

```text
+-----------+-------+
| id        | note  |
+-----------+-------+
| "example" | "Ada" |
+-----------+-------+
```

A run exits 0 on success, 2 for a usage problem found before the extension starts (a flag the manifest does not declare, a value of the wrong kind, a name that is not installed), and 1 when the extension fails.

properties.heading: See what is installed
properties.text:
`relate extension list` reads the installed set offline:

```bash verify
relate extension list
```

```text
greet 0.1.0 local ./greet
```

Each line holds the name, version, tier, and source. `relate extension list --available` prints the first-party channel's catalog instead; it needs the network and fails, naming the index URL, when offline.

properties.heading: Verify
properties.text:
Install the package again and check the installed copy. The last line now names the `local` tier from its provenance marker:

```bash verify
relate extension install greet --from ./greet
relate extension check "$HOME/.config/relate/extensions/greet"
```

```text
installed local extension greet 0.1.0 from ./greet
manifest: ok (greet 0.1.0, protocol 2025-06-18)
executable: ok (greet.py)
spawn: ok
initialize: ok (MCP 2025-06-18, server relate 1.0.1)
notifications/initialized: ok
tools/list: ok (the shared tool table: 5 tools; the extension calls 'write_cypher')
pin: not from a GitHub source (local)
```

`relate run --help` lists every installed action with its version.

properties.heading: Where packages live
properties.text:
Each package is one folder under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/relate/extensions/<name>/`. When `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is unset, empty, or a relative path, the folder is `~/.config/relate/extensions/<name>/`:

```bash verify
ls -A "$HOME/.config/relate/extensions/greet"
```

```text
.relate-provenance.json
extension.json
greet.py
```

`.relate-provenance.json` is the marker `install` writes, recording the tier and the source:

```bash verify
cat "$HOME/.config/relate/extensions/greet/.relate-provenance.json"
```

```text
{"tier":"local","source":"./greet"}
```

That folder is the only place relate looks for extensions. It never reads one from the working directory, so cloning a repository cannot add an action to `relate run`.

properties.heading: Write an extension
properties.text:
This guide shows you how to write an [extension](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#extension): a package that `relate run <name>` starts, which reads some source and writes what it finds into a store that relate owns. You scaffold a Python package, change its manifest and its `walk()` function so it counts the words in a folder of notes, check it, install it, run it, and query the result. It takes about 15 minutes.

An extension is a client of the Model Context Protocol ([MCP](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#mcp)). relate starts it as a child process, writes its flag values to its stdin as one JSON line, and then answers its tool calls. The extension never sees the store path: the host opens the store, frames the writes, and owns the exit code.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  accTitle: One extension run
  accDescr {
    relate opens the store, starts the extension, and writes its flag values to its stdin as one JSON line.
    The extension sends initialize and notifications/initialized, then tool calls such as write_cypher, which relate runs against the store and answers.
    The extension's last call is report_output, which relate prints as the run's summary before it exits.
  }
  Open["relate run opens the store and starts the extension"] --> Flags["relate writes the flag values to the extension's stdin, one JSON line"]
  Flags --> Hello["The extension sends initialize, then notifications/initialized"]
  Hello --> Calls["The extension sends tools/call requests; relate runs each one against the store and answers"]
  Calls --> Report["The extension calls report_output; relate prints the summary and exits"]
```

relate opens the store, starts the extension, and writes its flag values to its stdin as one JSON line. The extension sends initialize and notifications/initialized, then tool calls such as write_cypher, which relate runs against the store and answers. The extension's last call is report_output, which relate prints as the run's summary before it exits.

properties.heading: Check the package
properties.text:
`relate extension check` runs the package through the stages a run needs. It opens no store and relate fetches nothing, but it does start the package's executable:

```bash verify
relate extension check ./word-count
```

```text
manifest: ok (word-count 0.1.0, protocol 2025-06-18)
executable: ok (word-count.py)
spawn: ok
initialize: ok (MCP 2025-06-18, server relate 1.0.1)
notifications/initialized: ok
tools/list: ok (the shared tool table: 5 tools; the extension calls 'write_cypher')
pin: not from a GitHub source (unmarked)
```

It stops at the first stage that fails. It exits 2 for a problem in the manifest or the files, 1 for a problem when the extension runs, and 0 when the package would mount. The walk itself does not run.

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
**`executable: failed: the extension executable ./word-count/word-count.py is not executable`** (exit code 2). The file lost its execute bit, which a copy or an archive can do. Run `chmod +x word-count/word-count.py` and check again.

**`manifest: failed: extension 'word-count' declares protocol '<revision>'; this host speaks '2025-06-18'`** (exit code 2). Set `protocol` to `2025-06-18`.

**`Error: the extension child exited with 1: <message>`** (exit code 1). The extension failed, and `<message>` is what it wrote to stderr; the generated glue writes its own failures there too. Under `whole-import`, nothing from the run is committed.

**`Error: invalid --min-length: 'five' is not an integer`** or **`Error: unexpected argument to run word-count: --min-lenght`** (exit code 2). The command line does not match the manifest's flag table. relate prints the action's usage line and, for a misspelled flag, a `Did you mean` line. `relate run word-count --help` lists the flags.

**`Error: the extension wrote no MCP request within 10s`** (exit code 1). The executable started but never sent `initialize`. After that first request, relate waits as long as the walk takes.

**A run still behaves like the old code.** `relate run` starts the installed copy, not your working directory. Run `relate extension install word-count --from ./word-count` again.

properties.heading: Install and run it
properties.text:
Make a folder of notes to count:

```bash verify
mkdir notes
printf 'Ada fixed the planner bug.\nGrace reviewed the planner change and the parser change.\n' > notes/standup.md
printf 'The parser tests pass.\nNoor wants planner examples before the release.\n' > notes/retro.md
```

Install the package from its directory. `install` copies the manifest and the executable, so run it again after every edit:

```bash verify
relate extension install word-count --from ./word-count
```

```text
installed local extension word-count 0.1.0 from ./word-count
```

Run it into a new [single-file store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#single-file-store). The run writes to the store named by `-d`; with no `-d` it imports into an in-memory store:

```bash verify
relate run word-count notes -d ./words.rl
```

```text
word-count: 2 files, 13 distinct words
  MATCH (:File)-[m:MENTIONS]->(w:Word) RETURN w.text AS word, sum(m.count) AS uses ORDER BY uses DESC, word LIMIT 5
```

`notes` is the `DIR` positional, and `--min-length` takes its default of 4. With `-d`, the run exits after the summary.

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- relate on your `PATH`: `relate --version` prints its version ([Install relate](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).
- `python3` on your `PATH`. The Python template uses only the standard library, so there is nothing to install.

`relate extension init` writes the same package in four languages. Each needs its own runtime:

| `--lang`       | Executable                                        | Runtime                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `py` (default) | `<name>.py`                                       | `python3`                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `sh`           | `<name>.sh`                                       | `bash`                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `ts`           | `<name>.ts`                                       | Node.js 22.18 or later, which runs TypeScript by stripping the types                                                                                                                                              |
| `rust`         | `Cargo.toml` and `src/main.rs`, built to `<name>` | A Rust toolchain. The generated `Cargo.toml` takes `relate-wire`, `serde` and `serde_json` from the relate workspace, so outside an upstream checkout, point each one at a path or a version before `cargo build` |

properties.heading: Related
properties.text:
- [Install and run an extension](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/extensions/install-and-run/): the trust tiers, `list`, `remove`, and where packages live.
- [`relate extension`](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/extension/): every action and flag.
- [`relate run`](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/run/): the run command and its exit codes.
- [Import a directory tree with fs-to-graph](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/extensions/fs-to-graph/): a first-party extension that walks a directory tree.
- [Security and trust](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/security-and-trust/): why relate runs only installed packages and never fetches on `run`.

properties.heading: Scaffold the package
properties.text:
```bash verify
relate extension init word-count
```

```text
created py extension 'word-count' in <dir>/word-count
  extension.json  the manifest (mount name, MCP revision, flag table)
  word-count.py   the executable: generated glue plus your walk()
  README.md       the quickstart for this package

next:
  relate extension install word-count --from <dir>/word-count
  relate run word-count -d ./store
```

The path in the output is your working directory. `init` always creates a new directory and refuses one that exists, so it never overwrites your files.

```bash verify
ls word-count
```

```text
README.md
extension.json
word-count.py
```

The package that relate installs is two files: `extension.json` and the executable. `README.md` stays behind.

properties.heading: Verify
properties.text:
Open the store read-only and ask for the most used words:

```bash verify
relate --database ./words.rl --read-only --mode table "MATCH (:File)-[m:MENTIONS]->(w:Word) RETURN w.text AS word, sum(m.count) AS uses ORDER BY uses DESC, word LIMIT 3"
```

```text
+-----------+------+
| word      | uses |
+-----------+------+
| "planner" | 3    |
| "change"  | 2    |
| "parser"  | 2    |
+-----------+------+
```

A flag from the manifest works like any other flag. `--min-length 7` keeps only the longer words:

```bash verify
relate run word-count notes --min-length 7 -d ./long.rl
```

```text
word-count: 2 files, 4 distinct words
  MATCH (:File)-[m:MENTIONS]->(w:Word) RETURN w.text AS word, sum(m.count) AS uses ORDER BY uses DESC, word LIMIT 5
```

Running the same import again leaves the counts as they are, because every write is a `MERGE`.

properties.heading: Write the manifest
properties.text:
The scaffold's manifest declares one sample flag, `--name`:

```bash verify
cat word-count/extension.json
```

```text
{
  "kind": "command",
  "name": "word-count",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "protocol": "2025-06-18",
  "flags": [
    {"kind": "string", "name": "name", "default": "there"}
  ],
  "commit": "per-batch",
  "executable": "word-count.py"
}
```

Replace it with a manifest that takes a folder and a minimum word length. `relate run` parses its command line against this table, so the extension gets every flag already resolved to its value or its default.

```bash verify
cat > word-count/extension.json <<'EOF'
{
  "kind": "command",
  "name": "word-count",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "protocol": "2025-06-18",
  "flags": [
    {"kind": "integer", "name": "min-length", "default": 4}
  ],
  "positional": {"name": "DIR"},
  "commit": "whole-import",
  "executable": "word-count.py"
}
EOF
```

| Field                  | Required          | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------------- | ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `kind`                 | yes               | `command`, the only kind                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `name`                 | yes               | The name in `relate run <name>`; it must match the name you install it under, and it cannot be a relate command word such as `query`                                                         |
| `version`              | yes               | The package's own version, shown by `relate extension list`                                                                                                                                  |
| `protocol`             | yes               | The MCP revision; it must be `2025-06-18`, the one this relate serves                                                                                                                        |
| `flags`                | yes, may be empty | One entry per flag: `string`, `integer`, `boolean` (bare, sets `true`) or `repeatable`, each with a `default` of its kind; `database` and `db` are reserved for the host                     |
| `positional`           | no                | At most one positional argument, such as `{"name": "DIR"}`; it reaches the extension under that exact key                                                                                    |
| `commit`               | yes               | `whole-import`: one [transaction](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#transaction) for the whole run, rolled back on any failure. `per-batch`: each writing call commits on its own |
| `requires-fresh-store` | no                | `true` refuses a store that already holds nodes, before the extension starts; default `false`                                                                                                |
| `hidden`               | no                | `true` keeps it out of listings; default `false`                                                                                                                                             |
| `executable`           | yes               | The file relate starts, relative to the package directory; a path that leaves the directory is refused                                                                                       |

The manifest is decoded strictly: an unknown field or a default of the wrong kind fails the load and names the value.

properties.heading: Write the walk
properties.text:
Everything in `word-count.py` before `walk()` is generated glue: it reads the flag values, runs the MCP handshake, and sends `tools/call` requests. Replace the sample constants and `walk()` with this code, which writes one `:File` node per Markdown file, one `:Word` node per word, and a `MENTIONS` relationship with the count:

```bash verify
cat > walk.py <<'EOF'
WRITE = """UNWIND $rows AS row
MERGE (f:File {path: row.file})
MERGE (w:Word {text: row.word})
MERGE (f)-[m:MENTIONS]->(w)
SET m.count = row.count"""

READ = """MATCH (f:File)-[m:MENTIONS]->(w:Word)
RETURN count(DISTINCT f) AS files, count(DISTINCT w) AS words"""


def walk(client: Client, envelope: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    """Count the words in every Markdown file under DIR."""
    import re
    from collections import Counter
    from pathlib import Path

    root = Path(envelope.get("DIR", "."))
    min_length = envelope["min-length"]
    rows = []
    for path in sorted(root.rglob("*.md")):
        words = re.findall(r"[a-z]+", path.read_text().lower())
        counts = Counter(w for w in words if len(w) >= min_length)
        for word, count in sorted(counts.items()):
            rows.append({"file": path.relative_to(root).as_posix(), "word": word, "count": count})
    chunk = client.caps.get("maxRowsPerStatement", 1000)
    for start in range(0, len(rows), chunk):
        batch = rows[start:start + chunk]
        client.call("write_cypher", {"statement": WRITE, "parameters": {"rows": batch}})
    found = client.call("read_cypher", {"statement": READ})["rows"][0]
    client.call(
        "report_output",
        {
            "text": f"{NAME}: {found['files']} files, {found['words']} distinct words",
            "starters": [
                "MATCH (:File)-[m:MENTIONS]->(w:Word) "
                "RETURN w.text AS word, sum(m.count) AS uses ORDER BY uses DESC, word LIMIT 5"
            ],
        },
    )
EOF
python3 - <<'EOF'
from pathlib import Path
exe = Path("word-count/word-count.py")
src = exe.read_text()
start, end = src.index('WRITE = """'), src.index("def main(")
exe.write_text(src[:start] + Path("walk.py").read_text() + "\n\n" + src[end:])
EOF
```

The `python3` step splices `walk.py` into the executable in place of the sample, from `WRITE = """` up to `def main(`; pasting the code into the file by hand does the same.

Three things in the walk matter for every extension:

- The rows travel as the `$rows` [statement](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#statement) parameter, never spliced into the Cypher text.
- `write_cypher` takes at most 1000 rows per call. The handshake publishes the cap as `maxRowsPerStatement`, so the walk sizes its chunks from it.
- The last call is `report_output`. Its `text` is the summary line relate prints, and each `starters` entry prints indented under it.

The extension can call five tools: `write_cypher`, `read_cypher` (reads only), `update_schema` (index and constraint statements only), `batch_cypher` (several statements in one transaction), and `report_output`.

properties.heading: Use relate with the Claude Agent SDK
properties.text:
This guide shows you how to give an agent built with the Claude Agent SDK read access to a relate graph. relate serves a [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store) over [MCP](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#mcp) on stdio with `--read-only`. The SDK starts that server as a child process, and the agent queries the graph through relate's `read_cypher` tool. Every step before the model call runs without a Claude credential, so you can check what the agent gets before it makes one.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: The SDK starts relate as a read-only MCP server
  accDescr {
    Your program calls the Claude Agent SDK, which starts relate serve as a child process and talks MCP to it over stdin and stdout.
    relate serve opens the team store read-only and answers read_cypher and get_schema calls.
    A separate writer, such as your app, can keep writing the directory store; the server reads it as of its start, or follows it with --read-only=live.
  }
  P("Your program") --> S["Claude Agent SDK"]
  S -- "MCP over stdio" --> R["relate serve --read-only"]
  R -- "reads" --> T[("./team store")]
  A("Your app") -. "writes" .-> T
```

Your program calls the Claude Agent SDK, which starts relate serve as a child process and talks MCP to it over stdin and stdout. relate serve opens the team store read-only and answers read_cypher and get_schema calls. A separate writer, such as your app, can keep writing the directory store; the server reads it as of its start, or follows it with --read-only=live.

properties.heading: Call the query tool
properties.text:
An agent's query is a `tools/call` request for `read_cypher`, with a statement and its parameters. The response also carries timings that change on every run, so this check keeps only the rows:

```bash verify
printf '%s\n' \
  '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"read_cypher","arguments":{"statement":"MATCH (p:Person)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(:Project {name: $project}) RETURN p.name AS name, w.since AS since ORDER BY since","parameters":{"project":"relate"}}}}' \
  | relate serve --mcp stdio --database ./team --read-only 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -o '\\"rows\\":\[[^]]*\]'
```

```text
\"rows\":[{\"name\":\"Grace\",\"since\":2023},{\"name\":\"Ada\",\"since\":2024}]
```

Two people work on `relate`: Grace since 2023 and Ada since 2024. The whole response also carries the columns, column types, statistics, notifications, the plan, and timings.

A write sent to the same tool comes back as a tool error, with `isError: true`, and the store is unchanged:

```bash verify
printf '%s\n' \
  '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"read_cypher","arguments":{"statement":"MATCH (p:Person {name: $name}) DETACH DELETE p","parameters":{"name":"Ada"}}}}' \
  | relate serve --mcp stdio --database ./team --read-only 2>/dev/null
```

```text
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"result":{"content":[{"text":"Only MATCH queries are allowed for read-query","type":"text"}],"isError":true}}
```

properties.heading: Check the tools the agent sees
properties.text:
`relate serve --mcp stdio` speaks MCP's JSON-RPC on stdin and stdout, one message per line, until stdin closes. It is the command the SDK starts. Send it the opening messages an MCP host sends:

```bash verify
printf '%s\n' \
  '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"check","version":"0"}}}' \
  '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list","params":{}}' \
  | relate serve --mcp stdio --database ./team --read-only 2>/dev/null
```

```text
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"capabilities":{"tools":{}},"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","serverInfo":{"name":"relate-mcp","version":"1.0.1"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"tools":[{"annotations":{"destructiveHint":false,"idempotentHint":true,"openWorldHint":false,"readOnlyHint":true,"title":"Read Cypher"},"description":"Execute one read-only Cypher statement. Returns the result's rows. Write and schema (DDL) statements are rejected.","inputSchema":{"properties":{"parameters":{"default":{},"description":"The statement's parameters; a `rows` array feeds `$rows`.","type":"object"},"statement":{"description":"The Cypher statement.","type":"string"}},"required":["statement"],"type":"object"},"name":"read_cypher"},{"annotations":{"destructiveHint":false,"idempotentHint":true,"openWorldHint":false,"readOnlyHint":true,"title":"Get Schema"},"description":"Get the schema of the graph store: node labels with their property keys and inferred types, and the relationship types between them. `sample_size` bounds how many nodes and relationships are examined per label (larger is slower but more accurate; -1 examines all).","inputSchema":{"properties":{"sample_size":{"description":"The sample size used to infer the graph schema. Larger samples are slower, but more accurate. Smaller samples are faster, but might miss information. -1 samples the whole graph.","type":"integer"}},"type":"object"},"name":"get_schema"}]}}
```

Opened with `--read-only`, the server lists two tools, `read_cypher` and `get_schema`, both annotated `readOnlyHint: true`. `write_cypher` is not listed at all. The startup banner goes to stderr, which `2>/dev/null` drops, so stdout carries nothing but JSON-RPC.

properties.heading: Create the store
properties.text:
The agent reads `./team`, a [directory store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#directory-store) holding the small team graph the Get started pages use. A directory store lets your app keep writing while a [read-only](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#read-only) server reads it; a single-file `.rl` store that a writer holds refuses the read-only open. Plain `--read-only` serves the store as it was when the server started, so the agent sees later writes only after the server restarts. `--read-only=live` follows the writer's commits on a directory store; it refuses a `.rl` store and `:memory:`.

Write the seed script:

```bash verify
cat > team.cypher <<'EOF'
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace);
EOF
```

Run it into the store. This step writes, so it opens `./team` without `--read-only`:

```bash verify
relate query --database ./team --mode envelope < team.cypher
```

```text
{"columnTypes":[],"columns":[],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":1.769083,"execute_ms":1.4763330000000001,"lex_parse_ms":0.015375000000000002,"lower_ms":0.018000000000000002,"parse_ms":0.277375,"plan_ms":0.009708,"result_generation_ms":0.00020800000000000001,"rewrite_ms":0.00045900000000000004},"truncated":false}
```

The `CREATE` returns no rows; the store now holds three people and two projects.

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
| Message                                                                                                                                   | Cause                                                                               | Remedy                                                                                                                                                  |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Only MATCH queries are allowed for read-query` (a tool error)                                                                            | The agent sent a write or a schema statement to `read_cypher`                       | Expected on a read-only server. To let the agent write, serve the store without `--read-only` and add `mcp__relate__write_cypher` to the allowed tools. |
| `Error: semantic error: ParameterMissing: Expected parameter(s): name` (a tool error)                                                     | The statement uses `$name`, and the call's `parameters` has no `name`               | Pass every `$parameter` in the call's `parameters` object.                                                                                              |
| `Error: Failed to open Relate: storage error: read-only open requires an existing database at <path>` on the server's stderr, exit code 1 | `--database` names a store that doesn't exist; a read-only open never creates one   | Create the store first, or fix the path. A relative path resolves against the directory the server starts in, so an absolute path avoids surprises.     |
| `Error: Failed to open Relate: storage locked: <path>` on the server's stderr, exit code 1                                                | `--database` names a single-file `.rl` store that another process holds for writing | Serve a directory store, which allows a read-only open beside a writer, or stop the writer first.                                                       |
| The agent's answers miss recent writes (no error)                                                                                         | Plain `--read-only` serves the store as it was when the server started              | Serve a directory store with `--read-only=live`, or restart the server.                                                                                 |

The [errors reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/) lists every MCP refusal, with its JSON-RPC code where it has one.

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- relate on your `PATH` ([Install relate](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).
- The Claude Agent SDK: `pip install claude-agent-sdk` (Python 3.10 or later) or `npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` (Node.js 18.14 or later). The SDK programs in [Register the server with the SDK](#register-the-server-with-the-sdk) were checked against `claude-agent-sdk` 0.2.179 and `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` 0.3.319, as of 2026-11-07. The SDK changes faster than relate, so its own documentation wins if a name differs.
- A Claude credential for the model call, such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in the environment. Only the agent program in [Register the server with the SDK](#register-the-server-with-the-sdk) needs it.

properties.heading: Register the server with the SDK
properties.text:
The SDK starts each stdio entry of its MCP server map as a child process. It names that server's tools `mcp__<server>__<tool>`, so relate's tools arrive as `mcp__relate__read_cypher` and `mcp__relate__get_schema`.

Build the options first. Constructing them makes no model call and needs no credential. The Python SDK raises `TypeError` on an option name it doesn't know, so this program checks every name before the agent runs:

```python run name=options title="options.py"
from claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeAgentOptions

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    mcp_servers={
        "relate": {
            "type": "stdio",
            "command": "relate",
            "args": ["serve", "--mcp", "stdio", "--database", "./team", "--read-only"],
        }
    },
    tools=[],
    allowed_tools=["mcp__relate__get_schema", "mcp__relate__read_cypher"],
    permission_mode="dontAsk",
    strict_mcp_config=True,
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(" ".join([options.mcp_servers["relate"]["command"], *options.mcp_servers["relate"]["args"]]))
    print(options.allowed_tools)
    print(options.tools, options.permission_mode, options.strict_mcp_config)
```

```text
relate serve --mcp stdio --database ./team --read-only
['mcp__relate__get_schema', 'mcp__relate__read_cypher']
[] dontAsk True
```

The agent program uses the same options and makes the model call, so it needs the credential from the prerequisites. The Python version imports them from `options.py`:

### Python

```python title="agent.py"
import asyncio

from claude_agent_sdk import ResultMessage, query

from options import options


async def main() -> None:
    async for message in query(prompt="Who works on the relate project, and since when?", options=options):
        if isinstance(message, ResultMessage):
            print(message.result)


asyncio.run(main())
```

### Node.js

```js title="agent.mjs"
import { query } from "@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk";

const options = {
  mcpServers: {
    relate: {
      type: "stdio",
      command: "relate",
      args: ["serve", "--mcp", "stdio", "--database", "./team", "--read-only"],
    },
  },
  tools: [],
  allowedTools: ["mcp__relate__get_schema", "mcp__relate__read_cypher"],
  permissionMode: "dontAsk",
  strictMcpConfig: true,
};

for await (const message of query({ prompt: "Who works on the relate project, and since when?", options })) {
  if (message.type === "result" && message.subtype === "success") console.log(message.result);
}
```

To allow writes, remove `--read-only`; the server then also lists `write_cypher`, which the SDK names `mcp__relate__write_cypher`.

The other options keep the agent to relate's two tools:

| Python option               | Node.js option              | Effect                                                                                                |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `tools=[]`                  | `tools: []`                 | Turns off the SDK's built-in tools (shell, file reads and edits), so relate's tools are the only ones |
| `allowed_tools`             | `allowedTools`              | Pre-approves the listed tools, so they run without a permission prompt                                |
| `permission_mode="dontAsk"` | `permissionMode: "dontAsk"` | Denies a call to any tool that is not pre-approved, instead of prompting                              |
| `strict_mcp_config=True`    | `strictMcpConfig: true`     | Ignores MCP servers configured elsewhere, such as a project `.mcp.json`                               |

Each query the agent makes is the `tools/call` request from [Call the query tool](#call-the-query-tool), so the rows it reads are the rows that check printed.

> **Bound the agent's reads**
>
> `--safe` on the same `relate serve` command refuses a read with no `LIMIT` and no aggregate, so an exploratory `MATCH (n) RETURN n` can't pull the whole graph into the model's context. The refusal comes back as a tool error that says to add `LIMIT <n>`.

properties.heading: Replay the agent's calls
properties.text:
An agent run with these options touches the graph only through `tools/call` requests: the model picks one of the two tools and its arguments, the SDK sends the request to the server, and the reply goes back to the model as the tool's result. The trace below replays the calls this page's question needs, one at a time, in the order this page checks them: the schema, the query from [Call the query tool](#call-the-query-tool), the delete that tool refuses, and the count from [Verify](#verify). It is a replay of those calls, not a transcript of a model run. No model chose them, and a model given the same prompt may make fewer calls, or other ones.

The trace runs in your browser, on an in-memory store holding the same graph as `./team`. This cell builds it with the statement from `team.cypher`:

```cypher run name=team
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace)
```

```table
(no rows) · nodes created: 5, relationships created: 5, properties set: 13, labels added: 5
```

Each step shows the request the SDK sends for `mcp__relate__<tool>` and what relate's tool returns for it, built from the engine's result:

```json data=agent-calls
{"steps": [
  {"tool": "get_schema",
   "note": "`mcp__relate__get_schema` with no arguments: the labels, their property keys and types, and the relationship types between them, which is what the agent can read about the graph before it writes a statement.",
   "arguments": {}},
  {"tool": "read_cypher",
   "note": "`mcp__relate__read_cypher` with the statement and `$project` of the request in Call the query tool: who works on `relate`, and since when.",
   "arguments": {"statement": "MATCH (p:Person)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(:Project {name: $project}) RETURN p.name AS name, w.since AS since ORDER BY since",
    "parameters": {"project": "relate"}}},
  {"tool": "read_cypher",
   "note": "The delete sent to `read_cypher` in Call the query tool. The server's gate reads the statement's plan, finds a write, and answers with a tool error; the statement never runs.",
   "arguments": {"statement": "MATCH (p:Person {name: $name}) DETACH DELETE p",
    "parameters": {"name": "Ada"}},
   "expect": "error"},
  {"tool": "read_cypher",
   "note": "The count from Verify, sent as a tool call: the three people are all still there after the refused delete.",
   "arguments": {"statement": "MATCH (p:Person) RETURN count(p) AS people"}}
]}
```

The trace starts on the database the cells up to `team` build. Each step below ran when the page was recorded, one after another on that database, through the mapping the MCP tryout uses; each result is what relate serve's tool returns for that call, built from the engine's result. No agent and no server took part in the recording.

**Step 1 of 4: `get_schema`.** `mcp__relate__get_schema` with no arguments: the labels, their property keys and types, and the relationship types between them, which is what the agent can read about the graph before it writes a statement.

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_schema","arguments":{}}}
```

| Label   | Nodes | Properties                       | Relationships out                                          |
| ------- | ----- | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Person  | 3     | name (String), role (String)     | WORKS_ON to Project; KNOWS to Person; MAINTAINS to Project |
| Project | 2     | language (String), name (String) | -                                                          |

**Step 2 of 4: `read_cypher`.** `mcp__relate__read_cypher` with the statement and `$project` of the request in Call the query tool: who works on `relate`, and since when.

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"read_cypher","arguments":{"statement":"MATCH (p:Person)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(:Project {name: $project}) RETURN p.name AS name, w.since AS since ORDER BY since","parameters":{"project":"relate"}}}}
```

| name  | since |
| ----- | ----- |
| Grace | 2023  |
| Ada   | 2024  |

**Step 3 of 4: `read_cypher`.** The delete sent to `read_cypher` in Call the query tool. The server's gate reads the statement's plan, finds a write, and answers with a tool error; the statement never runs.

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"read_cypher","arguments":{"statement":"MATCH (p:Person {name: $name}) DETACH DELETE p","parameters":{"name":"Ada"}}}}
```

Tool error: `Only MATCH queries are allowed for read-query`.

**Step 4 of 4: `read_cypher`.** The count from Verify, sent as a tool call: the three people are all still there after the refused delete.

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"read_cypher","arguments":{"statement":"MATCH (p:Person) RETURN count(p) AS people"}}}
```

| people |
| ------ |
| 3      |

Live: Step sends the next call and Play all sends the rest, each to the page's database in your browser on the store the cells build up to the trace's starting cell, and each step shows the result `relate serve`'s tool returns for that call, built from the engine's live result; a trace that would write twice starts on an emptied database, and the database is emptied again when the trace ends, so the page's cells run on what they write.

The second step's rows are the ones [Call the query tool](#call-the-query-tool) printed from the server, and the third step's error is the same text. A server opened with `--read-only` lists no `write_cypher`, so the trace has no write that succeeds.

properties.heading: Use relate with CrewAI
properties.text: This guide shows you how to give a CrewAI agent a custom tool that reads a relate graph while your app keeps writing it. The tool is a `BaseTool` subclass whose `_run` opens the [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store) [read-only](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#read-only), runs one fixed [statement](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#statement) with the project name as a parameter, and closes the connection. Because each call opens anew, it sees every commit the app made before it. The tool runs without a model, so the whole program is checked offline; only the crew run needs a credential.

properties.heading: Give the tool to a crew
properties.text:
Replace the check block at the end of `team_tool.py` with an agent, a task, and a crew. This part needs the model's credential:

```python
from crewai import Agent, Crew, Task

analyst = Agent(
    role="Team analyst",
    goal="Answer questions about who works on which project",
    backstory="You answer only from the team graph.",
    tools=[team_graph],
    llm="anthropic/claude-opus-5-5",
)
question = Task(
    description="Who works on relate, and since when?",
    expected_output="One line per person, with their role and the year they started.",
    agent=analyst,
)
print(Crew(agents=[analyst], tasks=[question]).kickoff())
owner.close()
```

`llm` names the provider and the model as `<provider>/<model>`. The agent can call `team_graph` with a project name and write its answer from the lines it gets back.

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
| Message                                                                                                                                                                                       | Cause                                                                                                  | Remedy                                                                                   |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `error 42000: storage locked: <path>` (the tool's answer)                                                                                                                                     | The store is a single-file `.rl` store that the app holds for writing, and a read-only open refuses it | Keep the data in a directory store, as `./team` is, so the tool reads beside the writer. |
| `error 42000: storage error: read-only open requires an existing database at <path>` (the tool's answer)                                                                                      | `store` names a directory that holds no store; a read-only open never creates one                      | Create the store with a writable open first, as the setup block does, or fix the path.   |
| `Anthropic native provider not available, to install: uv add "crewai[anthropic]"` (`ImportError`, when the `Agent` is created)                                                                | `llm` names an Anthropic model and the provider's extra isn't installed                                | Install `crewai[anthropic]`, or the extra for the provider you name.                     |
| `error 42N18: semantic error: WriteOnReadOnlyAccessDatabase: No write operations are allowed on this database. The database is in read-only mode on this Neo4j instance.` (the tool's answer) | A write reached a read-only connection                                                                 | Expected: the guard held. Writes belong on the app's own writable connection.            |

The [errors reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/) lists the Python exception class for each engine error.

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- Python 3.10 to 3.13 (`crewai` 1.15.37 requires a version below 3.14), with the relate [client](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#client) and CrewAI in their own virtual environment: `pip install relate-db crewai`. CrewAI pins some of the libraries the other framework guides use to older releases, such as `openai` and `pydantic`, so a separate environment keeps them apart. The package is `relate-db`; the import is `import relate`. The CrewAI code on this page was checked against `crewai` 1.15.37, as of 2026-11-08.
- For [Give the tool to a crew](#give-the-tool-to-a-crew) only: a model's provider package and credential, such as `pip install "crewai[anthropic]"` with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in the environment.
- relate on your `PATH` for [Verify](#verify) ([Install relate](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).

CrewAI 1.15.37 sends usage telemetry to CrewAI's own collector unless `CREWAI_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true` or `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true` is set. The relate client sends no usage metrics ([Privacy and telemetry](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/privacy-and-telemetry/)).

properties.text:
The tool's second call already shows the app's commit. The same check from the CLI, read-only, in the directory the program ran in:

```bash
relate --database ./team --read-only --mode table "MATCH (p:Person)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck'}) RETURN p.name AS name, w.since AS since ORDER BY since"
```

```text
+---------+-------+
| name    | since |
+---------+-------+
| "Grace" | 2022  |
| "Lin"   | 2026  |
+---------+-------+
```

Grace from the team graph and Lin from the app's later commit: the rows the tool's second call returned. Running the program again leaves the same two rows.

properties.heading: Write the tool
properties.text:
The program opens `./team`, a [directory store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#directory-store), for writing in a setup block that stands in for the app, writes the small team graph the Get started pages use, and keeps that connection open. `TeamGraphTool` reads the store on its own read-only connections. The last block calls the tool the way a crew's agent does, then commits a new person on the app's connection and calls the tool again:

```python run env=crewai name=team-tool title="team_tool.py"
import relate
from crewai.tools import BaseTool
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

TEAM = """
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace)
"""

PEOPLE_ON = """
MATCH (p:Person)-[r:WORKS_ON|MAINTAINS]->(:Project {name: $project})
RETURN p.name AS name, p.role AS role, type(r) AS how, r.since AS since
ORDER BY name
"""


class ProjectInput(BaseModel):
    project: str = Field(description='The project\'s exact name, such as "relate".')


class TeamGraphTool(BaseTool):
    name: str = "team_graph"
    description: str = "List the people who work on or maintain a project, with their role and since when."
    args_schema: type[BaseModel] = ProjectInput
    store: str = "./team"

    def _run(self, project: str) -> str:
        try:
            # Read-only: the engine refuses every write on this connection.
            with relate.connect(self.store, read_only=True) as conn:
                rows = conn.execute(PEOPLE_ON, {"project": project}).fetchall()
        except relate.Error as e:
            return f"error {e.gql_status}: {e}"
        if not rows:
            return f"No one works on or maintains a project named {project!r}."
        return "\n".join(
            f"{r['name']} ({r['role']}) {r['how']} {project}" + (f" since {r['since']}" if r["since"] is not None else "")
            for r in rows
        )


# Setup: the app that owns ./team writes the team graph, and keeps its writable connection open.
owner = relate.connect("./team")
if owner.execute("MATCH (p:Person) RETURN count(p) AS n").single()["n"] == 0:
    owner.execute(TEAM)

team_graph = TeamGraphTool()

# Check: call the tool the way a crew's agent does, without a model.
print(team_graph.run(project="relate"))

# The app commits a new person while its connection stays open; the tool's next call sees her.
owner.execute(
    "MATCH (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck'}) "
    "MERGE (lin:Person {name: 'Lin', role: 'engineer'}) "
    "MERGE (lin)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2026}]->(tck)"
)
print(team_graph.run(project="opencypher-tck"))
print(team_graph.run(project="relate-engine"))
owner.close()
```

```text
Ada (engineer) WORKS_ON relate since 2024
Grace (engineer) WORKS_ON relate since 2023
Noor (maintainer) MAINTAINS relate
Grace (engineer) WORKS_ON opencypher-tck since 2022
Lin (engineer) WORKS_ON opencypher-tck since 2026
No one works on or maintains a project named 'relate-engine'.
```

The first call lists who works on and maintains `relate`. The second shows Lin, whom the app committed while its own connection stayed open: a directory store takes one writer and several read-only opens beside it. The third call names a project that doesn't exist and gets a sentence back instead of an error. The parts that matter:

- **`args_schema`** is the input the crew's agent fills in. The `Field` description tells the model what `project` holds, and CrewAI validates the call against it before `_run` runs.
- **A connection per call.** A relate connection belongs to the thread that opened it, and a long-lived read-only connection sees the graph as it was when it opened. Opening inside `_run` keeps the open and the statement on the thread that runs the tool, and makes each call current.
- **Answers are text.** `_run` returns a string, the form a CrewAI agent reads, including for an engine error, which comes back as `error <gql_status>: <message>` instead of raising.
- **`MERGE` keeps the app's write idempotent**, so a second run of the program leaves one Lin, not two.

Each layer of the guard refuses something different:

| Layer                                  | Refuses                                                                                 | Enforced by |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| `relate.connect(path, read_only=True)` | Every write and checkpoint on that connection; a path with no store                     | The engine  |
| The fixed statement `PEOPLE_ON`        | Any Cypher the model writes: the model passes only `project`, which binds as `$project` | The tool    |

properties.heading: Use relate with LangChain
properties.text: This guide shows you how to give a LangChain agent a tool that recalls what an agent's memory holds, from a relate [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store), without letting the agent change it. Your app writes the memory; the agent gets one `recall` tool that opens the store [read-only](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#read-only) on every call and follows the graph from a name to the episodes that mention it and the people who work on it. The tool runs without a model, so you can check what the agent gets before it makes a call.

properties.heading: Give the tool to an agent
properties.text:
`create_agent` takes a model name and the tools. Replace the check lines at the end of `recall_tool.py` with this; it needs the model's credential:

```python
from langchain.agents import create_agent

agent = create_agent(
    "anthropic:claude-opus-5-5",
    tools=[recall],
    system_prompt="Answer from memory. Call recall with the exact name of a person or project.",
)
result = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What happened on relate this week?"}]})
print(result["messages"][-1].content)
```

The model name is `<provider>:<model>`, and the provider's package must be installed. The model can call `recall`, read the lines it returns, and answer from them.

properties.heading: How this differs from the LangGraph guide
properties.text:
[Use relate with LangGraph](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/integrations/langgraph/) builds a `StateGraph` by hand, whose steps write and recall memory. This page hands a read-only tool to LangChain's `create_agent`, which builds the agent loop itself:

|                       | This page                                | The LangGraph guide                             |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Who writes memory     | Your app, on its own writable connection | The graph's `remember` tool                     |
| What the agent can do | Read, through `recall`                   | Write and read, through `remember` and `recall` |
| The connection        | A new read-only one per call             | One writable connection on a dedicated thread   |
| The agent loop        | `create_agent`                           | A `StateGraph` with two nodes                   |

Both store memory the same way: each turn is an `Episode` [node](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#node) `IN_CONVERSATION` a `Conversation`, and an episode `MENTIONS` the `Person` and `Project` nodes of the team graph the Get started pages use. [Model agent memory](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/agents/model-agent-memory/) explains the model this one reduces.

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
| Message                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Cause                                                                                                                       | Remedy                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Relate connection used from a thread other than the one that opened it: connections are thread-affine (DB-API threadsafety = 1). Create the connection on the thread that uses it.` (`relate.ProgrammingError`) | The tool used a connection opened outside it, such as one at module level, from the worker thread `create_agent` runs it on | Open the connection inside the tool, as `recall` does.                                 |
| `storage error: read-only open requires an existing database at <path>` (`relate.OperationalError`)                                                                                                              | `STORE` names a directory that holds no store; a read-only open never creates one                                           | Create the store with a writable open first, as the setup block does, or fix the path. |
| `storage locked: <path>` (`relate.OperationalError`)                                                                                                                                                             | The store is a single-file `.rl` store that the app holds for writing, and a read-only open refuses it                      | Keep memory in a directory store, as `./memory` is, so the tool reads beside the app.  |
| `` Initializing ChatAnthropic requires the langchain-anthropic package. Please install it with `pip install langchain-anthropic` `` (`ImportError`)                                                              | `create_agent` got an `anthropic:` model name without the provider's package                                                | Install `langchain[anthropic]`, or the package for the provider you name.              |

The [errors reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/) lists the Python exception class for each engine error.

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- Python 3.10 or later, with the relate [client](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#client) and LangChain: `pip install relate-db langchain`. The package is `relate-db`; the import is `import relate`. The LangChain code on this page was checked against `langchain` 1.4.9 and `langchain-core` 1.7.6, as of 2026-11-08.
- For [Give the tool to an agent](#give-the-tool-to-an-agent) only: a chat model's integration package and credential, such as `pip install "langchain[anthropic]"` with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in the environment.
- relate on your `PATH` for [Verify](#verify) ([Install relate](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).

properties.text:
