properties.heading: Rewrite the queries
properties.text:
A join along a foreign key becomes a step along a relationship, and a join table becomes one hop. Who works on a project with Ada, in SQL, joins `works_on` to itself and to both tables around it:

```bash verify
sqlite3 -header -list team.db "SELECT other.name AS teammate, pr.name AS project
FROM people AS ada
JOIN works_on AS mine ON mine.person_id = ada.id
JOIN works_on AS theirs ON theirs.project_id = mine.project_id AND theirs.person_id <> ada.id
JOIN people AS other ON other.id = theirs.person_id
JOIN projects AS pr ON pr.id = mine.project_id
WHERE ada.name = 'Ada'
ORDER BY teammate"
```

```text
teammate|project
Grace|relate
```

In Cypher, the same question is one pattern. The store opens read-only:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode table "MATCH (:Person {name: 'Ada'})-[:WORKS_ON]->(proj:Project)<-[:WORKS_ON]-(other:Person)
RETURN other.name AS teammate, proj.name AS project
ORDER BY teammate"
```

```text
+----------+----------+
| teammate | project  |
+----------+----------+
| "Grace"  | "relate" |
+----------+----------+
```

A `LEFT JOIN`, which keeps a row when the joined row is missing, becomes `OPTIONAL MATCH`. Every issue with its project, and its assignee when it has one:

```bash verify
sqlite3 -header -list team.db "SELECT i.title, pr.name AS project, p.name AS assignee
FROM issues AS i
JOIN projects AS pr ON pr.id = i.project_id
LEFT JOIN people AS p ON p.id = i.assignee_id
ORDER BY i.opened"
```

```text
title|project|assignee
Scenario for OPTIONAL MATCH ordering|opencypher-tck|Grace
Plan cache misses on quoted labels|relate|Ada
Add a SQLite migration guide|relate|
```

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode table "MATCH (i:Issue)-[:FILED_IN]->(proj:Project)
OPTIONAL MATCH (i)-[:ASSIGNED_TO]->(p:Person)
RETURN i.title AS title, proj.name AS project, p.name AS assignee
ORDER BY i.opened"
```

```text
+----------------------------------------+------------------+----------+
| title                                  | project          | assignee |
+----------------------------------------+------------------+----------+
| "Scenario for OPTIONAL MATCH ordering" | "opencypher-tck" | "Grace"  |
| "Plan cache misses on quoted labels"   | "relate"         | "Ada"    |
| "Add a SQLite migration guide"         | "relate"         | <null>   |
+----------------------------------------+------------------+----------+
```

The rest of a SQL query carries over clause by clause:

| SQL                                 | Cypher                                                              |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `JOIN` on a foreign key             | A relationship step, `(a)-[:TYPE]->(b)`                             |
| A join table between two tables     | One relationship hop, with its columns as relationship properties   |
| `LEFT JOIN`                         | `OPTIONAL MATCH`                                                    |
| `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT …)`           | `WHERE EXISTS { <pattern> }`                                        |
| `GROUP BY`                          | The non-aggregated expressions in `RETURN` or `WITH` group the rows |
| A recursive common table expression | A variable-length pattern, `-[:TYPE*1..5]->`, or `SHORTEST`         |

properties.heading: Run the load
properties.text:
This command writes to `./team.rl`. `relate query` reads the script from stdin, and each `--fetch-params <name>=<file>` binds one export file as a parameter:

```bash verify
relate query --database ./team.rl \
  --fetch-params people=export/people.json \
  --fetch-params projects=export/projects.json \
  --fetch-params issues=export/issues.json \
  --fetch-params works_on=export/works_on.json \
  --fetch-params knows=export/knows.json \
  < load.cypher
```

The load prints nothing: no statement returns rows, and the exit code is 0. A second run with the same files matches every key instead of creating anything, and says so on stderr for each statement that wrote nothing:

```bash verify
relate query --database ./team.rl \
  --fetch-params people=export/people.json \
  --fetch-params projects=export/projects.json \
  --fetch-params issues=export/issues.json \
  --fetch-params works_on=export/works_on.json \
  --fetch-params knows=export/knows.json \
  < load.cypher
```

```text
note: write statement 4 of 8 changed nothing; the graph is unchanged
note: write statement 5 of 8 changed nothing; the graph is unchanged
note: write statement 6 of 8 changed nothing; the graph is unchanged
note: write statement 8 of 8 changed nothing; the graph is unchanged
```

Statements 1, 2, 3 and 7 have no note because their `SET` writes the same values again. When the database changes, export again and run the same load: it updates those properties in place and adds the new rows and references. It does not delete what the database deleted.

properties.heading: Verify
properties.text:
Count the rows in the SQLite database and the nodes and relationships in the store, then compare. The first command writes the counts SQLite reports to `./expected.json`; a nullable foreign key counts only its non-`NULL` values, the rows that become relationships. The second opens the store read-only:

```bash verify
sqlite3 -json team.db "SELECT
  (SELECT count(*) FROM people) AS Person,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM projects) AS Project,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM issues) AS Issue,
  (SELECT count(maintainer_id) FROM projects) AS MAINTAINS,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM issues) AS FILED_IN,
  (SELECT count(assignee_id) FROM issues) AS ASSIGNED_TO,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM works_on) AS WORKS_ON,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM knows) AS KNOWS" > expected.json
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode table --fetch-params expected=expected.json 'WITH $expected[0] AS counts
UNWIND keys(counts) AS name
RETURN name, counts[name] AS in_sqlite,
       COUNT { MATCH (n) WHERE name IN labels(n) } + COUNT { MATCH ()-[r]->() WHERE type(r) = name } AS in_relate
ORDER BY name'
```

```text
+---------------+-----------+-----------+
| name          | in_sqlite | in_relate |
+---------------+-----------+-----------+
| "ASSIGNED_TO" | 2         | 2         |
| "FILED_IN"    | 3         | 3         |
| "Issue"       | 3         | 3         |
| "KNOWS"       | 1         | 1         |
| "MAINTAINS"   | 1         | 1         |
| "Person"      | 3         | 3         |
| "Project"     | 2         | 2         |
| "WORKS_ON"    | 3         | 3         |
+---------------+-----------+-----------+
```

Equal columns mean every row arrived, and every foreign key found the row it names. A relationship count lower than its row count is a foreign key whose `MATCH` found no node, which drops the row without an error.

properties.heading: Write the load script
properties.text:
The script writes the nodes first, then one statement per foreign key and per join table, so every `MATCH` on an id finds a node that already exists. Each file arrives whole as a list, and `UNWIND` turns it into one row per record:

```bash verify
cat > load.cypher <<'CYPHER'
UNWIND $people AS row
MERGE (p:Person {id: row.id})
SET p.name = row.name, p.role = row.role;

UNWIND $projects AS row
MERGE (p:Project {id: row.id})
SET p.name = row.name, p.language = row.language;

UNWIND $issues AS row
MERGE (i:Issue {id: row.id})
SET i.title = row.title, i.opened = date(row.opened);

UNWIND $projects AS row
MATCH (proj:Project {id: row.id}), (p:Person {id: row.maintainer_id})
MERGE (p)-[:MAINTAINS]->(proj);

UNWIND $issues AS row
MATCH (i:Issue {id: row.id}), (proj:Project {id: row.project_id})
MERGE (i)-[:FILED_IN]->(proj);

UNWIND $issues AS row
MATCH (i:Issue {id: row.id}), (p:Person {id: row.assignee_id})
MERGE (i)-[:ASSIGNED_TO]->(p);

UNWIND $works_on AS row
MATCH (p:Person {id: row.person_id}), (proj:Project {id: row.project_id})
MERGE (p)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(proj)
SET w.since = row.since;

UNWIND $knows AS row
MATCH (a:Person {id: row.person_id}), (b:Person {id: row.other_id})
MERGE (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b);
CYPHER
```

Three choices make the script safe to rerun and true to the source:

- `MERGE` on the key alone, then `SET` for the other columns. A `MERGE` on every column would create a second node when one value changes.
- A `NULL` foreign key matches nothing. The `opencypher-tck` project has no maintainer, so its `MATCH` returns no row and the statement writes no `MAINTAINS` for it.
- `date(row.opened)` turns the ISO 8601 text into a `DATE`, so `ORDER BY` and range comparisons work on dates.

properties.heading: Pull a subgraph from Neo4j
properties.text: This guide shows you how to copy part of a Neo4j or Aura database into a local relate store with [relate pull](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#pull). It runs Cypher statements against the source over Neo4j's HTTP Query API and writes what they return, with the source's constraints and indexes, into a new store. A pull needs a running Neo4j or Aura database, which the docs checks don't have, so only the refusals relate makes before it connects are replayed on this page; the rest follows the `relate pull` specification.

properties.heading: Expect the dialect differences
properties.text: The copy runs Neo4j's Cypher with the exceptions [Differences from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/differences-from-neo4j/) lists, each with the error relate returns and the form to write instead; there are no procedure libraries such as APOC. Run the application's statements against the copy before relying on it. `relate serve --database ./mirror --read-only --bolt <port>` puts the copy behind Bolt for Neo4j drivers and tools.

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
- **`Error: HTTP request to <url> failed: io: Connection refused (os error <n>)`** (exit code 1). Nothing listens at the Query API address. Check `NEO4J_URI`, and that the server has the Query API enabled. Against a port where nothing listens, with the operating system's error number removed:

  ```bash verify
  NEO4J_URI=http://127.0.0.1:9 NEO4J_USERNAME=neo4j NEO4J_PASSWORD='<password>' relate pull --query "MATCH (n) RETURN n" --database ./mirror 2>&1 | sed -E 's/ \(os error [0-9]+\)$//'
  ```

  ```text
  Error: HTTP request to http://127.0.0.1:9/db/neo4j/query/v2 failed: io: Connection refused
  ```

- **`Error: NEO4J_URI bolt port <port> has no Query API mapping (7687 → 7474); use an explicit http(s) NEO4J_URI`** (exit code 1). A Bolt URI on a port other than 7687. Give the Query API's own address.

- **`Error: NEO4J_<VAR> missing from environment`** (URI, USERNAME or PASSWORD) or **`Error: NEO4J_<VAR> missing from env file`** (exit code 1). The variable is not set, or the `--from` file lacks it. Add it to the file, or export it.

- **`Error: destination database is not empty; …`** or **`Error: shape query RETURN must be graph elements …`** (exit code 1). Pull into a new path; return nodes, relationships, or paths ([Select the subgraph](#select-the-subgraph)).

- **`Error: typed wire decode failed: property "<key>" on element <element id>: unsupported typed value "Base64"`** (exit code 1). A property holds a byte array, which a store can't keep. Remove or convert that property on the source, or leave those nodes out of the statements.

- **`Error: pull cannot target :memory: (--database must persist)`** (exit code 2). Name a directory or a `.rl` path.

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- relate on your `PATH` ([Install relate](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).
- A Neo4j or Aura database that answers the HTTP Query API (`POST /db/<database>/query/v2`), and a user that can read the part you want.
- A destination path for the new store: a directory, or a path ending in `.rl` for a single file. `:memory:` is refused, because the copy has to outlive the command.

properties.heading: Rehearse a change on a copy
properties.text:
To try a migration before running it on the source, clone the pulled store and run the migration on the clone, so the pull stays as it came:

```bash
relate clone ./mirror ./mirror-rehearsal
relate query --database ./mirror-rehearsal < migration.cypher
```

The [migration rehearsal recipe](https://relatedb.ai/cookbook/migration-rehearsal/) checks what a migration changed. [Push a subgraph to Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/neo4j/push-to-neo4j/) copies a result back.

properties.heading: Related
properties.text:
- [`relate pull`](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/pull/): every flag and exit code.
- [Push a subgraph to Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/neo4j/push-to-neo4j/): the same connection, the other direction.
- [Differences from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/differences-from-neo4j/): what to expect when the copy runs Neo4j statements.
- [Clone and convert a store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/clone-and-convert/): copies of the pulled store in any layout.
- [Neo4j subgraph mirror](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/problems-relate-solves/#neo4j-subgraph-mirror) in the capability catalog.

properties.heading: Run the pull
properties.text:
On success, `relate pull` prints one line and exits 0; the counts depend on the source:

```text
pulled <nodes> new / <reused> reused nodes, <rels> new / <reused> reused rels (+ <c> constraints, <i> indexes; <s> schema skipped) to ./mirror
```

The destination must be empty: a pull never merges into existing data, so refresh a copy by pulling into a new path. A store that holds anything is refused before relate connects:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team --mode envelope "CREATE (:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'})"
relate pull --from neo4j.env --query "MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p" --database ./team
```

```text
{"columnTypes":[],"columns":[],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":1.376958,"execute_ms":1.215708,"lex_parse_ms":0.003334,"lower_ms":0.003584,"parse_ms":0.153834,"plan_ms":0.002,"result_generation_ms":0.00033299999999999996,"rewrite_ms":0.00025},"truncated":false}
Error: destination database is not empty; pull writes into an empty database only
```

A failed pull leaves an empty store at the destination path, which the next pull may use.

properties.heading: Select the subgraph
properties.text:
`--query` takes the statements that pick the subgraph: inline Cypher, a `;`-separated list, a file path, or `-` for stdin. Every statement must `RETURN` graph elements, nodes, relationships or paths; relate checks this before it connects:

```bash verify
relate pull --from neo4j.env --query "MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p.name" --database ./names
```

```text
Error: shape query RETURN must be graph elements (nodes/rels/paths), not projections/scalars/aggregates; rejected item: p.name
```

Return each relationship with its two endpoints, as in `RETURN p, r, x`, or return a path. `--param <name>=<value>` binds a parameter of the source statement. These statements pick who works on which project, and who maintains `relate`:

```bash
relate pull --from neo4j.env \
  --query "MATCH (p:Person)-[r:WORKS_ON]->(x:Project) RETURN p, r, x; MATCH path = (:Person)-[:MAINTAINS]->(:Project {name: \$project}) RETURN path" \
  --param project=relate \
  --database ./mirror
```

The statements share one load: a node two statements return is written once, and the store is checkpointed once, at the end.

properties.heading: Verify
properties.text:
Count what arrived, by label, and compare with the same count on the source. The copy opens read-only:

```bash
relate --database ./mirror --read-only --mode envelope "MATCH (n) RETURN labels(n) AS labels, count(*) AS nodes ORDER BY nodes DESC"
```

`relate info --database ./mirror` prints the node, relationship, index and constraint counts without opening the store.

properties.heading: What lands in the store
properties.text:
The copy holds each returned node with its [labels](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#label) and properties, and each relationship with its [type](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#relationship-type), endpoints and properties, as the source stores them. The source's [element ids](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#element-id) are not copied: the local nodes and relationships get new ids. Everything lands in the `neo4j` namespace.

Values keep their Cypher type, because relate asks the Query API for its typed JSON form:

| Source type                                                        | Stored as                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Scalars, temporal values, `POINT`, `UUID`, `VECTOR`, lists of them | The same type; a `TIME` or `DATETIME` keeps its offset, a `ZONED DATETIME` its named zone, a point its SRID, a vector its coordinate type |
| `BYTE ARRAY`                                                       | Not stored: the pull fails and names the element and property                                                                             |

After the data, the pull copies the source's schema as `CREATE … IF NOT EXISTS` statements:

| Source schema                                                                                                                              | In the copy                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Uniqueness, existence, node key, relationship key and property type [constraints](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#constraint) | The same constraint                                                                                                                     |
| `RANGE`, `TEXT` and `POINT` indexes                                                                                                        | The same index                                                                                                                          |
| Indexes that back a constraint, `LOOKUP` indexes, indexes that are not `ONLINE`                                                            | Left out; the copy creates its own                                                                                                      |
| `FULLTEXT` and `VECTOR` indexes                                                                                                            | Skipped with a warning on stderr, such as `warning: pull skipped index "<name>" (unsupported kind)`, and counted under `schema skipped` |

A skipped entry never fails the pull; create those indexes in the copy with `CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX` or `CREATE VECTOR INDEX` ([Search](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/search/)).

properties.heading: Write the connection file
properties.text:
`relate pull` reads `NEO4J_URI`, `NEO4J_USERNAME`, `NEO4J_PASSWORD` and `NEO4J_DATABASE` (default `neo4j`) from the env file `--from` names, in the `KEY=VALUE` format of Aura's credentials file, or from the environment without `--from`. Replace the placeholders, and make the file readable only by you:

```bash verify
cat > neo4j.env <<'EOF'
NEO4J_URI=neo4j+s://<instance-id>.databases.neo4j.io
NEO4J_USERNAME=neo4j
NEO4J_PASSWORD=<password>
NEO4J_DATABASE=neo4j
EOF
chmod 600 neo4j.env
```

A file others can read still loads, with a warning. relate turns the URI forms Neo4j tools print into a Query API address:

| `NEO4J_URI`                                         | The Query API relate calls                                       |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `https://<host>:<port>` or `http://<host>:<port>`   | That address, as given                                           |
| `neo4j+s://<instance-id>.databases.neo4j.io` (Aura) | `https://<instance-id>.databases.neo4j.io`                       |
| `neo4j://<host>:7687` or `bolt://<host>:7687`       | `http://<host>:7474`                                             |
| `neo4j://` or `bolt://` on any other port           | Refused: pass the `http(s)` address of the Query API             |
| A URI with a user or password in it                 | Refused: credentials go in `NEO4J_USERNAME` and `NEO4J_PASSWORD` |

Requests go to `<address>/db/<NEO4J_DATABASE>/query/v2` with HTTP Basic authentication, and relate refuses to send the password over plain `http://` to any host but the loopback interface. A Bolt URI for another machine maps to such an address:

```bash verify
NEO4J_URI=neo4j://neo4j.invalid:7687 NEO4J_USERNAME=neo4j NEO4J_PASSWORD='<password>' relate pull --query "MATCH (n) RETURN n" --database ./plaintext-check
```

```text
Error: refusing to send Basic auth credentials in the clear: Query API URL http://neo4j.invalid:7474/db/neo4j/query/v2 is http:// to a non-loopback host; pass --allow-plaintext to accept the risk, or use an https:// NEO4J_URI
```

Use the `https://` address, or pass `--allow-plaintext` on a network you trust.

properties.heading: Push a subgraph to Neo4j
properties.text: This guide shows you how to copy part of a relate store into a Neo4j or Aura database with [relate push](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#push), the mirror of `relate pull` over the same connection. Push reads the [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store), groups its nodes by [label](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#label) and its relationships by [type](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#relationship-type), and sends them as batched `MERGE` statements on merge keys, so running the same push twice leaves the remote as one push did. It never deletes anything on the remote. A push needs a running Neo4j or Aura database, which the docs checks don't have: the plans on this page come from `--dry-run`, which touches no remote, and a real push's report follows the `relate push` specification.

properties.heading: Choose what happens to rows that exist
properties.text:
`--nodes-update` and `--rels-update` take a policy, for every label or type or per name (`Person=replace,Project=skip`):

| Policy          | A row the remote already has                 | Remote-only properties |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `add` (default) | Updated with `SET +=`                        | Kept                   |
| `replace`       | Updated with `SET =`                         | Removed                |
| `skip`          | Left as it is; only missing rows are created | Kept                   |

`--updated-at <property>[,<property>]` names timestamp properties: a row strictly newer on the remote is skipped and counted `remoteNewer`. The same push run twice lands the same remote state under `add` and `skip`, with relationships merged structurally (the fallback when a type has no key), and with `--updated-at` where it applies.

properties.heading: Give each label a merge key
properties.text:
Push takes each label's merge key from the store's uniqueness and key [constraints](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#constraint), composite keys included. Create a uniqueness constraint on the property that identifies a node, `name` here, and plan again:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team --mode envelope "CREATE CONSTRAINT person_name IF NOT EXISTS FOR (p:Person) REQUIRE p.name IS UNIQUE"
relate --database ./team --mode envelope "CREATE CONSTRAINT project_name IF NOT EXISTS FOR (p:Project) REQUIRE p.name IS UNIQUE"
relate push --to neo4j.env --database ./team --dry-run
```

```text
{"columnTypes":[],"columns":[],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":1.0729170000000001,"execute_ms":0.9659580000000001,"lex_parse_ms":0.003167,"lower_ms":0.000917,"parse_ms":0.1025,"plan_ms":0.000958,"result_generation_ms":0.000125,"rewrite_ms":0.000125},"truncated":false}
{"columnTypes":[],"columns":[],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":0.9187909999999999,"execute_ms":0.814792,"lex_parse_ms":0.003583,"lower_ms":0.000958,"parse_ms":0.09929099999999999,"plan_ms":0.000875,"result_generation_ms":0.00025,"rewrite_ms":0.000125},"truncated":false}
entity                            total  created  updated  skipped  warn  merge key  policy  batches
Person                                3        3        0        0     0  name       add           1
Project                               2        2        0        0     0  name       add           1
(Person)-[:KNOWS]->(Person)           1        1        0        0     0             add           1
(Person)-[:MAINTAINS]->(Project)      1        1        0        0     0             add           1
(Person)-[:WORKS_ON]->(Project)       3        3        0        0     0             add           1
Person: UNWIND $rows AS row MERGE (n:`Person` {`name`: row.key.`name`}) SET n += row.props
Project: UNWIND $rows AS row MERGE (n:`Project` {`name`: row.key.`name`}) SET n += row.props
(Person)-[:KNOWS]->(Person): UNWIND $rows AS row MATCH (a:`Person` {`name`: row.start.`name`}) MATCH (b:`Person` {`name`: row.end.`name`}) MERGE (a)-[r:`KNOWS`]->(b) SET r += row.props
(Person)-[:MAINTAINS]->(Project): UNWIND $rows AS row MATCH (a:`Person` {`name`: row.start.`name`}) MATCH (b:`Project` {`name`: row.end.`name`}) MERGE (a)-[r:`MAINTAINS`]->(b) SET r += row.props
(Person)-[:WORKS_ON]->(Project): UNWIND $rows AS row MATCH (a:`Person` {`name`: row.start.`name`}) MATCH (b:`Project` {`name`: row.end.`name`}) MERGE (a)-[r:`WORKS_ON`]->(b) SET r += row.props
dry run: 5 entities, 10 rows planned; nothing was sent
```

A dry run does not read the remote, so it counts every row as `created`. Every value travels as a typed parameter, so a date, a point or a vector keeps its Cypher type on the remote. `--merge-key <Label>:<property>[,<property>]`, once per label, keys a label without a constraint or overrides its key.

Relationships merge on their type's key: a `--rel-key <TYPE>:<property>` override, else the type's relationship uniqueness or key constraint. With neither, as here, push merges one relationship of a type between two nodes, `MERGE (a)-[r:T]->(b)`, and two parallel relationships of one type between the same nodes collapse into one on the remote. `--rel-mode create` sends `CREATE` instead, which a second push repeats.

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
- **Every label shows `(unkeyed)` and nothing is sent.** The store has no uniqueness or key constraint for those labels. Create one, or pass `--merge-key <Label>:<property>`.
- **Relationships counted `dangling`.** The scope leaves out one of their endpoints. Widen `--labels`, or push with `--types`, which brings both endpoints.
- **`Error: storage locked: <path>`** (exit code 1). Another process holds the store open for writing. Push when it exits, or push from a copy made with `relate clone`.
- **`Error: push failed: pre-read of <Label> failed: refusing to send Basic auth credentials in the clear: …`** (exit code 1). `NEO4J_URI` resolves to `http://` on another machine. Use the `https://` address.
- **`Error: NEO4J_URI missing from env file`** (exit code 1). The `--to` file lacks the variable; with a URI as `--to`, the username and password must be in the environment.
- **`Error: unknown update policy "<value>" (expected add, replace or skip)`** (exit code 2). Fix the policy name.

properties.heading: Plan the push
properties.text:
`--dry-run` prints the plan, per label and relationship type, and the statements it would send, reading only the local store. With no merge keys defined, it skips everything:

```bash verify
relate push --to neo4j.env --database ./team --dry-run
```

```text
entity                                      total  created  updated  skipped  warn  merge key  policy  batches
Person (unkeyed)                                3        0        0        3     0             add           0
Project (unkeyed)                               2        0        0        2     0             add           0
(Person)-[:KNOWS]->(Person) (unkeyed)           1        0        0        1     0             add           0
(Person)-[:MAINTAINS]->(Project) (unkeyed)      1        0        0        1     0             add           0
(Person)-[:WORKS_ON]->(Project) (unkeyed)       3        0        0        3     0             add           0
dry run: 5 entities, 10 rows planned; nothing was sent
```

A label with no merge key is skipped, never guessed: without a key, a second push could not find the nodes the first one wrote. Relationships between such nodes are skipped too.

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- relate on your `PATH` ([Install relate](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).
- A Neo4j or Aura database that answers the HTTP Query API, and a user that can write.
- The connection file from [Pull a subgraph from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/neo4j/pull-from-neo4j/#write-the-connection-file); `--to` reads the same four variables. This guide writes one with placeholders, and a store holding the shared example graph:

```bash verify
cat > team.cypher <<'EOF'
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace);
EOF
relate query --database ./team < team.cypher
cat > neo4j.env <<'EOF'
NEO4J_URI=neo4j+s://<instance-id>.databases.neo4j.io
NEO4J_USERNAME=neo4j
NEO4J_PASSWORD=<password>
NEO4J_DATABASE=neo4j
EOF
chmod 600 neo4j.env
```

`--to` also takes a Query API URI directly, with the username and password from `NEO4J_USERNAME` and `NEO4J_PASSWORD` in the environment.

properties.heading: Related
properties.text:
- [`relate push`](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/push/): every flag, default, and exit code.
- [Pull a subgraph from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/neo4j/pull-from-neo4j/): the connection file and the other direction.
- [Indexes and constraints](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/cypher/indexes-and-constraints/): the constraints push takes its merge keys from.
- [Differences from Neo4j](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cypher/differences-from-neo4j/): where the two dialects differ.
- [Neo4j subgraph mirror](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/problems-relate-solves/#neo4j-subgraph-mirror) in the capability catalog.

properties.heading: Run the push
properties.text:
Drop `--dry-run` to send the batches, 5000 rows per statement by default (`--batch-size`):

```bash
relate push --to neo4j.env --database ./team
```

Before each write, push reads the remote's current rows by their merge keys, so its report, the plan's table with real counts, says what it created, updated, and skipped and why. The last line holds the totals and a time that varies:

```text
pushed <rows> rows in <statements> statements (<bytes> bytes) in <time> ms
```

`--json` prints the report as one JSON object, with `created`, `updated` and `skipped` (by reason) per entity and the totals.

Push takes the store's writer lock while it runs, a dry run included, as a writable open does, so run it while no other process writes the store. A dry run leaves the store's contents unchanged.

properties.heading: Scope the push
properties.text:
Without a scope, push sends the whole store. One of three flags narrows it:

| Flag                   | Pushes                                                                                         |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--labels <L1>,<L2>`   | Nodes with these labels, and the relationships whose two endpoints are both in scope           |
| `--types <T1>,<T2>`    | Relationships of these types, with both their endpoints                                        |
| `--query <statements>` | What the statements return: nodes, relationships or paths, as `relate pull --query` takes them |

A relationship whose other end is out of scope is counted as `dangling` and not sent. Push only the people:

```bash verify
relate push --to neo4j.env --database ./team --labels Person --dry-run
```

```text
entity                       total  created  updated  skipped  warn  merge key  policy  batches
Person                           3        3        0        0     0  name       add           1
(Person)-[:KNOWS]->(Person)      1        1        0        0     0             add           1
(dangling)                       4        0        0        4     0             skip          0
Person: UNWIND $rows AS row MERGE (n:`Person` {`name`: row.key.`name`}) SET n += row.props
(Person)-[:KNOWS]->(Person): UNWIND $rows AS row MATCH (a:`Person` {`name`: row.start.`name`}) MATCH (b:`Person` {`name`: row.end.`name`}) MERGE (a)-[r:`KNOWS`]->(b) SET r += row.props
dry run: 3 entities, 8 rows planned; nothing was sent
```

The four `WORKS_ON` and `MAINTAINS` relationships point at projects, which are out of scope.

properties.heading: Verify
properties.text:
Push again with `--json`. Once the first push landed, the remote's pre-read finds every row, so every entity reports `"created":0` and its rows under `updated`:

```bash
relate push --to neo4j.env --database ./team --json
```

Then run a count such as `MATCH (p:Person) RETURN count(p) AS people` on both sides and compare.

properties.heading: What push refuses
properties.text:
Usage errors stop a push before it touches the remote:

```bash verify
relate push --to neo4j.env --database ./team --labels Person --types WORKS_ON
```

```text
Error: push takes one of --query, --labels, or --types (none pushes the whole store)
Usage: relate push --to CREDS --database PATH [--query Q | --labels L1,L2 | --types T1,T2] [--batch-size N] [--nodes-update POLICY] [--rels-update POLICY] [--updated-at NAME[,NAME]] [--rel-mode MODE] [--merge-key LABEL:PROP[,PROP]] [--rel-key TYPE:PROP[,PROP]] [--unkeyed-labels ACTION] [--dry-run] [--json] [--allow-plaintext]
Run 'relate push --help' for more information.
```

| Refused                                                       | Why                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--database :memory:` (exit code 2)                           | Push reads a store on disk                                                                                                                |
| Two or more of `--query`, `--labels`, `--types` (exit code 2) | One scope per push                                                                                                                        |
| `--namespace` (exit code 2)                                   | Push always reads the `neo4j` namespace                                                                                                   |
| A label with no merge key                                     | Skipped and counted `unkeyed`, unless `--merge-key` gives one or `--unkeyed-labels create` sends `CREATE` rows that a second push repeats |
| A byte-array property                                         | Fails the push: a byte array can't be stored as a property, and there is no string fallback                                               |
| `http://` to a host other than the loopback interface         | Refused before any request, as in `relate pull`, unless `--allow-plaintext` is given                                                      |
| Deleting remote data                                          | Never done: a node deleted locally stays on the remote                                                                                    |

A batch that fails stops the push. The error names the label or type, the batch and its row range, and the report still prints, listing the batches that landed. Exit code 1.

properties.heading: Recover from a crash
properties.text: This guide shows you how to bring a store back after the process that had it open crashed, was killed, or lost power. Usually there is nothing to repair. The next open loads the store's last [snapshot](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#snapshot) and replays the [WAL](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#wal) on top of it, so under the default `full` [durability mode](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#durability-mode) every write that was acknowledged comes back.

properties.heading: Check the store without opening it
properties.text:
`relate info` reads a store's metadata cold: no open, no lock, no replay. It can run beside a writer and changes nothing.

```bash verify
relate info --database ./team.rl
```

```text
layout: .rl bundle
superblock version: 1
codec: parquet
format version: 5
checkpoint LSN: 1
commit timestamp: 1
total bytes: 36864
wal segments past checkpoint: 1
nodes (at checkpoint LSN 1): 5
relationships (at checkpoint LSN 1): 5
indexes: 0
constraints: 0
```

The counts are the snapshot's, taken at the last checkpoint: 5 relationships, without the new one. The log sequence number (LSN) numbers each commit. `wal segments past checkpoint` counts the WAL files that may hold commits newer than the snapshot; replay applies them.

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
- **`Failed to open Relate: storage error: WAL checksum mismatch`, exit code 1.** A WAL record before the end of the log is damaged. A crash leaves damage only at the end, which replay drops, so this comes from damage to the file itself. Replay stops at the record instead of skipping it, and a retry, a `--read-only` open and `relate clone` all fail the same way. Keep the damaged store for a report, and restore your latest backup ([Back up and restore a store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/backup-and-restore/), [storage errors](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/#cli-fatal-error-storage)).
- **A storage error whose message contains `may have been written by a newer Relate`.** A WAL record parses as valid but this binary can't decode it, so a newer relate wrote it. Open the store with that newer release ([Upgrade a store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/upgrade-a-store/)).
- **`Failed to open Relate: storage locked: <path>`, exit code 5.** A process still holds the store: the crashed process didn't exit, or something restarted it. Find it and stop it ([Share one store between two processes](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/two-processes-one-store/)).
- **Recent writes are missing after recovery.** The store ran under `everysecond` or `snapshot` durability, which acknowledge writes before they are safe on disk. The `full` mode keeps every acknowledged write ([Choose a durability mode](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/durability-modes/)).

properties.heading: Look at what recovery restores
properties.text:
A [read-only](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#read-only) open loads the snapshot and replays the WAL in memory, then writes nothing: no trim, no checkpoint. Use it to see what the store holds before anything changes on disk:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode envelope "MATCH (p:Person)-[:MAINTAINS]->(project:Project) RETURN p.name AS person, project.name AS project ORDER BY project"
```

```text
{"columnTypes":["STRING","STRING"],"columns":["person","project"],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[{"person":"Noor","project":"opencypher-tck"},{"person":"Noor","project":"relate"}],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":0.408,"execute_ms":0.22716699999999998,"lex_parse_ms":0.033,"lower_ms":0.043084000000000004,"parse_ms":0.112125,"plan_ms":0.060000000000000005,"result_generation_ms":0.00025,"rewrite_ms":0.007917},"truncated":false}
```

The relationship the crashed session committed is there. Replay restored it.

properties.heading: Open the store once for writing
properties.text:
A writable open replays the WAL the same way, trims a torn tail if there is one, and writes a checkpoint when it exits. This step opens `team.rl` for writing on purpose, to finish the recovery; the statement itself only reads:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --mode envelope "MATCH ()-[m:MAINTAINS]->() RETURN count(m) AS maintains"
```

```text
{"columnTypes":["INTEGER"],"columns":["maintains"],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[{"maintains":2}],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":0.352291,"execute_ms":0.18625,"lex_parse_ms":0.03025,"lower_ms":0.041916999999999996,"parse_ms":0.104875,"plan_ms":0.052666,"result_generation_ms":0.000209,"rewrite_ms":0.008167},"truncated":false}
```

A checkpoint writes the committed graph to a fresh snapshot, so the next open replays less WAL; a read-only open never checkpoints. It is not a backup: it overwrites the store's own snapshot, and a copy you can restore from comes from `relate clone`. The other points at which a checkpoint runs are in [WAL and checkpoints](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/storage/wal-and-checkpoints/#when-a-checkpoint-runs).

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- `relate` on your `PATH` ([Install relate](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).
- The crashed process is gone. A process that exits, however it exits, releases its lock on the store.
- A backup made with `relate clone`, for the one case replay can't fix ([Back up and restore a store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/backup-and-restore/)).

properties.heading: Rehearse a crash
properties.text:
These steps crash a session on a scratch copy of the shared example graph, then recover it. On a store that crashed for real, start at [Check the store without opening it](#check-the-store-without-opening-it).

Create the example graph as `team.rl`:

```bash verify
cat > team.cypher <<'EOF'
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace);
EOF
relate query --database ./team.rl < team.cypher
```

Now run a script whose first statement commits one new relationship, Noor maintaining `opencypher-tck`, and whose second statement takes minutes. One second in, `kill -9` ends the process before it can checkpoint:

```bash verify
cat > work.cypher <<'EOF'
MATCH (noor:Person {name: 'Noor'}), (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck'}) CREATE (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(tck);
UNWIND range(1, 100000) AS a RETURN sum(reduce(s = 0, x IN range(1, 10000) | s + x)) AS total;
EOF
relate query --database ./team.rl < work.cypher > /dev/null &
sleep 1
kill -9 $!
wait $! 2>/dev/null
echo "exit=$?"
```

```text
exit=137
```

Exit code 137 is the shell's report of a process ended by signal 9. The new relationship is committed in the WAL, but no [checkpoint](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#checkpoint) has written it to the snapshot.

properties.heading: Related
properties.text:
- [Choose a durability mode](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/durability-modes/): what each mode can lose in a crash.
- [Back up and restore a store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/storage/backup-and-restore/): the copy to restore when replay can't help.
- [Errors: storage errors](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/#cli-fatal-error-storage): the storage error entry with its recorded forms.
- [Storage and durability](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/storage-and-durability/): the write path, the WAL, and checkpoints.

properties.heading: Verify
properties.text:
The snapshot now holds the recovered relationship:

```bash verify
relate info --database ./team.rl
```

```text
layout: .rl bundle
superblock version: 1
codec: parquet
format version: 5
checkpoint LSN: 2
commit timestamp: 2
total bytes: 45056
wal segments past checkpoint: 1
nodes (at checkpoint LSN 2): 5
relationships (at checkpoint LSN 2): 6
indexes: 0
constraints: 0
```

The checkpoint moved from LSN 1 to LSN 2, and the snapshot counts 6 relationships.

properties.heading: What an open does after a crash
properties.text:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: What an open does after a crash
  accDescr {
    Opening a store loads its last snapshot, then replays every WAL record committed after that snapshot's checkpoint.
    A damaged record before the end of the WAL stops the open with a storage error.
    A record the crash cut short at the very end is dropped.
    A writable open then trims that record from the file and checkpoints when it exits; a read-only open leaves the files as they are.
  }
  O("Open the store") --> L["Load the last snapshot"]
  L --> R["Replay WAL records after its checkpoint"]
  R --> D{"Damaged record before the end?"}
  D -- "yes" --> F["Open fails: storage error, exit code 1"]
  D -- "no" --> T["Drop a record cut short at the end"]
  T --> M{"Writable open?"}
  M -- "yes" --> W["Trim the WAL, run statements, checkpoint on exit"]
  M -- "no" --> K["Run reads, change nothing on disk"]
```

Opening a store loads its last snapshot, then replays every WAL record committed after that snapshot's checkpoint. A damaged record before the end of the WAL stops the open with a storage error. A record the crash cut short at the very end is dropped. A writable open then trims that record from the file and checkpoints when it exits; a read-only open leaves the files as they are.

A crash in the middle of writing a WAL record leaves a torn tail: the last record is cut short. That record's commit was never acknowledged under `full` durability, because a commit returns only after its record is synced. relate drops the torn record and prints nothing about it. A writable open also removes it from the file; a read-only open leaves it in place and ignores it.

properties.heading: Choose a durability mode
properties.text: This guide shows you how to choose and set a [durability mode](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#durability-mode): the rule for when a commit counts as safe on disk. The default, `full`, syncs the [WAL](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#wal) to disk before a commit returns, so a crash loses no acknowledged write. `everysecond` and `snapshot` return before that sync, and a crash can lose writes they already acknowledged.

properties.heading: Bound the snapshot window
properties.text:
Under `snapshot`, the time between checkpoints is the loss window. A one-shot run or `relate query` takes `--checkpoint-interval-secs N`; `relate serve` doesn't accept that flag and takes only `RELATE_CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL_SECS`. The default is 300 seconds. `0` turns off only the timer: checkpoints still run when a WAL segment fills, on a clean exit, and on `.checkpoint`.

```bash
RELATE_CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL_SECS=30 relate serve --database ./team.rl --http 7474 --durability-mode snapshot
```

properties.heading: Choose one
properties.text:
- If every acknowledged write must survive a crash, keep `full`. It is the only mode with no loss window.
- If losing about the last second of writes is acceptable, such as a cache you can rebuild, choose `everysecond`. Commits stop waiting for each sync.
- If the writes can be redone from their source, such as a bulk load you can rerun, choose `snapshot`. Pair it with a checkpoint interval that bounds what a rerun has to redo.

properties.heading: Compare the modes
properties.text:
To sync is to force written data out of the operating system's cache onto the disk (`fsync`). Each mode decides when the WAL is synced relative to the moment a commit returns:

| Mode             | A commit returns               | The WAL is synced                                                                                                  | A crash can lose                                                                                     |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `full` (default) | After its WAL record is synced | Before each commit, or group of commits, is acknowledged                                                           | No acknowledged write                                                                                |
| `everysecond`    | After it applies in memory     | About once a second, in the background                                                                             | About the last second of acknowledged writes; slow storage or a delayed sync makes the window longer |
| `snapshot`       | After it applies in memory     | Never on commit; only a completed [checkpoint](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#checkpoint) is durable | Every write since the last completed checkpoint, up to 300 seconds of writes under the default timer |

A killed process can lose the window too, not only a power cut. In a test on this release, a write to a `.rl` store was acknowledged and the process was killed with `kill -9` half a second later, three times per mode. Under `full` the write was there on the next open every time; under `everysecond` and `snapshot` it was gone every time. In one more `snapshot` run, it was still gone with 3 seconds between the write and the kill.

The mode is a setting of the process that opens the store, not of the store. The next open picks its own, and an open that sets nothing gets `full`.

Each mode's loss window for one crash, a few seconds after a completed checkpoint.

**What a crash can lose.** The durability mode decides when a commit is acknowledged relative to the WAL sync. It is a setting of the process that opens the store (`--durability-mode` or `RELATE_DURABILITY_MODE`, default `full`), not of the store.

The picture's timeline: 8 writes are acknowledged in the 4.6 s after a completed checkpoint, then the process crashes. A killed process can lose the window as well as a power cut.

| Mode          | The WAL is synced                                        | Acknowledged writes the crash at 4.6 s can lose |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `full`        | Before each commit, or group of commits, is acknowledged | None: all 8 come back                           |
| `everysecond` | About once a second, in the background                   | The 2 writes after the last sync, at 4 s        |
| `snapshot`    | Never on commit; only a completed checkpoint is durable  | All 8, every write since the checkpoint         |

Under `everysecond`, slow storage or a delayed sync makes the window longer than about a second. Under `snapshot`, the window runs until the next completed checkpoint: up to 300 seconds of writes under the default timer, fewer when a WAL segment fills first.

Live: Commit, Checkpoint and Crash step through what relate does with the WAL, the in-memory graph and the snapshot (inside one `.rl` file in the file view), and a mode switch with a crash slider shades what `full`, `everysecond` and `snapshot` can lose; under reduced motion each step waits for Next. It is a diagram of documented behaviour: no engine runs.

![What each durability mode can lose in a crash, as relate documents it](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/durability-modes/element-loss-windows-light.svg)

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
- **`Error: invalid --durability-mode: semantic error: invalid durability mode "<value>"; expected full, everysecond, or snapshot`, exit code 2.** The flag's value is misspelled. Use one of the three names.
- **`Error: invalid RELATE_DURABILITY_MODE: semantic error: invalid durability mode "<value>"; expected full, everysecond, or snapshot`, exit code 2.** The variable holds something else. Fix it or unset it ([the variable's error](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/#cli-invalid-env-durability-mode)). The clients refuse to open too: Python's `relate.connect()` raises `OperationalError` and Node.js throws, each with a message that names `RELATE_DURABILITY_MODE`.
- **Writes acknowledged just before a crash are missing.** The process ran under `everysecond` or `snapshot`, and the crash fell inside the loss window. Switch to `full` if those writes matter ([Recover from a crash](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/crash-and-recovery/)).

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- `relate` on your `PATH` ([Install relate](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).
- A [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store) on disk, a directory or a `.rl` file. An in-memory store forgets everything at exit in every mode.

properties.heading: Related
properties.text:
- [`--durability-mode`](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/flags/#durability-mode) in the flags reference.
- [Recover from a crash](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/crash-and-recovery/): what an open restores after a crash.
- [Storage and durability](https://relatedb.ai/docs/concepts/storage-and-durability/): the WAL, snapshots, and checkpoints, and why there are three modes.

properties.heading: Set it for a server
properties.text:
`relate serve` takes the same flag, with the same order: the flag, then `RELATE_DURABILITY_MODE`, then `full`. This server is writable on purpose, since the mode only matters for writes:

```bash
relate serve --database ./team.rl --http 7474 --durability-mode everysecond
```

properties.heading: Set it for an environment
properties.text:
`RELATE_DURABILITY_MODE` sets the mode for every open that doesn't set one itself. The flag wins over the variable. The Python and Node.js clients read the same variable when they open a store, so it is how an app chooses a mode.

This run writes to `team.rl` under `snapshot`, set by the variable: Grace maintains `relate` now.

```bash verify
RELATE_DURABILITY_MODE=snapshot relate --database ./team.rl --mode envelope "MATCH (grace:Person {name: 'Grace'}), (r:Project {name: 'relate'}) CREATE (grace)-[:MAINTAINS]->(r) RETURN grace.name AS person, r.name AS project"
```

```text
{"columnTypes":["STRING","STRING"],"columns":["person","project"],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[{"person":"Grace","project":"relate"}],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":0.6042909999999999,"execute_ms":0.364666,"lex_parse_ms":0.008749999999999999,"lower_ms":0.011375,"parse_ms":0.224375,"plan_ms":0.009792,"result_generation_ms":0.00041600000000000003,"rewrite_ms":0.000458},"truncated":false}
```

properties.heading: Set it for one run
properties.text:
`--durability-mode` applies to the run it's on. To follow along, create the shared example graph as `team.rl` first:

```bash verify
cat > team.cypher <<'EOF'
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace);
EOF
relate query --database ./team.rl < team.cypher
```

This run writes to `team.rl` under `everysecond`: it records that Noor maintains `opencypher-tck` too.

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --durability-mode everysecond --mode envelope "MATCH (noor:Person {name: 'Noor'}), (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck'}) CREATE (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(tck) RETURN noor.name AS person, tck.name AS project"
```

```text
{"columnTypes":["STRING","STRING"],"columns":["person","project"],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[{"person":"Noor","project":"opencypher-tck"}],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":0.657292,"execute_ms":0.431542,"lex_parse_ms":0.006583,"lower_ms":0.011,"parse_ms":0.212583,"plan_ms":0.008417,"result_generation_ms":0.00020800000000000001,"rewrite_ms":0.000375},"truncated":false}
```

A one-shot run checkpoints when it exits cleanly, so this write is on disk by the time the command returns. The window matters for processes that stay open, such as `relate serve`, an app that uses a client, or a long script.

properties.heading: Verify
properties.text:
Read the store back read-only. Both writes are there, next to the example's original `MAINTAINS` relationship:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --mode envelope "MATCH (p:Person)-[:MAINTAINS]->(project:Project) RETURN p.name AS person, project.name AS project ORDER BY person, project"
```

```text
{"columnTypes":["STRING","STRING"],"columns":["person","project"],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[{"person":"Grace","project":"relate"},{"person":"Noor","project":"opencypher-tck"},{"person":"Noor","project":"relate"}],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":0.40049999999999997,"execute_ms":0.22204200000000002,"lex_parse_ms":0.033457999999999995,"lower_ms":0.040958,"parse_ms":0.109625,"plan_ms":0.059834,"result_generation_ms":0.000209,"rewrite_ms":0.008208},"truncated":false}
```

properties.heading: Size a store and its memory
properties.text: This guide shows you how to estimate the memory a store needs, measure the size of a real one, and cap its growth. relate holds the whole graph in memory: opening a [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store) loads its last [snapshot](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#snapshot) and replays the [WAL](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#wal) into RAM, and there is no buffer pool or spill to disk. The graph you query has to fit in the process's memory, with room for the statements that run on it.

properties.heading: Allow for process memory
properties.text:
The process needs more memory than the logical size, and the most while a store opens. Two measurements of this release:

| Measurement                                                                                                                               | Process memory for the graph                              |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Once loaded: a served process after writes filled four graph shapes of about 33 MB logical each (Linux x86_64 in a 2 GB, 2-CPU container) | 1.22 to 1.54 times the logical size                       |
| Peak while opening a `.rl` store and decoding its snapshot: stores of 10,000 to 1,000,000 nodes on macOS arm64, median of 3 runs          | 2.5 to 3.9 times the logical size; 2.5 at 1,000,000 nodes |

For the worked example (2,586,000,000 logical bytes), that is about 3.2 to 4.0 GB once loaded, and about 6.5 GB while the store opens, at the 2.5 ratio of the largest measured store (rounded to 0.1 GB). The open is the peak, so size the machine from it. Statements need working memory on top: one value a statement builds, such as a list, may reach 256 MiB under the default `--expression-memory-limit`.

The size on disk is not a guide to memory: a 1,000,000-node `.rl` store of 187,416,576 bytes, measured with this release, holds 1,390,890,109 logical bytes.

properties.heading: Cap the graph's size
properties.text:
`--logical-graph-size-limit SIZE` caps the logical size. It takes bytes, or a number with `mb` or `gb` (powers of 1000) or `mib` or `gib` (powers of 1024). The default is unlimited, and `0` means unlimited too. `RELATE_LOGICAL_GRAPH_SIZE_LIMIT` sets it for every run in an environment, and `relate serve` takes the same flag.

Set the cap below the memory you can give the process, divided by the open-peak ratio from [Allow for process memory](#allow-for-process-memory). A write that would grow the graph past the cap then fails with an error you can read, instead of the operating system ending the process.

This statement tries to add a node to `team.rl` under a cap of 6,500 bytes, which the 6,403-byte graph leaves no room for:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --logical-graph-size-limit 6500 --mode envelope "CREATE (:Person {name: 'Ines', role: 'engineer'})"
echo "exit=$?"
```

```text
capacity exceeded: used=6555 limit=6500
{"error":{"code":"fatal_error","exit_code":1,"kind":"capacity","message":"capacity exceeded: used=6555 limit=6500","retryable":false}}
exit=1
```

What the cap does when a write reaches it:

| Situation                                                      | Result                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A write whose counted change would take the graph past the cap | Fails before it reaches the WAL, with exit code 1, kind `capacity` and `retryable: false`; nothing is written. A `SET` counts as a change even when the new value is the same size, so it needs room under the cap                                                |
| `used` and `limit` in the message                              | The logical size the write was checked at, and the cap in bytes. For a `CREATE`, `used` is the live size, which [Measure a real store](#measure-a-real-store) relies on; for a `SET` it is higher than the live size (101 bytes higher in the runs for this page) |
| A read                                                         | Runs; reads are never checked                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `DELETE`                                                       | Runs, and frees logical bytes at once                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Opening a store already over the cap                           | Loads the whole graph. Until deletes free enough room, every write except a `DELETE` fails, even a `SET` or `REMOVE` that doesn't grow the graph                                                                                                                  |

properties.heading: Estimate from counts
properties.text:
relate counts the size of a graph in logical bytes. The [logical graph size](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#logical-graph-size) is its own tally of the live nodes, relationships, properties, and index entries. That tally is what `--logical-graph-size-limit` compares against. It leaves out the WAL buffers, statement working memory and allocator overhead, which the next section adds back.

These figures were measured with the relate version this page is verified against: 10,000 elements of one shape written into a fresh `.rl` store, the store's logical size read with the method in [Measure a real store](#measure-a-real-store), and the difference divided by 10,000.

| Element                                          | Logical bytes each                                              | Shape measured                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| A node with one label                            | 212                                                             | `(:Item)`                                              |
| Each further label on a node                     | 45                                                              | `(:Item:Thing)`                                        |
| Integer or float properties on one node          | 64 for 1, 128 for 2, 244 for 3, 256 for 4, 476 for 5, 512 for 8 | `{a: i, b: i, …}`, all integers; one float measured 64 |
| A string property, instead of an integer         | 8 more, plus the string's length in UTF-8 bytes                 | 8 and 1,000 ASCII characters; 8 two-byte characters    |
| A boolean property                               | 57                                                              | `{b: true}`                                            |
| A list of 384 floats, such as an embedding       | 3,147 (an average over 100 nodes)                               | `{v: [x IN range(1, 384) \| toFloat(x)]}`              |
| A relationship with no properties                | 444 at 1 relationship per node, 344 at 5, 320 at 20             | one type, `(a)-[:LINKS]->(b)`                          |
| A relationship property (integer)                | 60                                                              | `{w: j}`                                               |
| An entry in a range index on an integer property | 61 to 64                                                        | `CREATE INDEX … ON (n.i)`                              |

Property costs grow in steps, not one property at a time, so a node with 5 properties costs nearly as much as one with 8.

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
- **`capacity exceeded: used=… limit=…`, exit code 1.** A write reached `--logical-graph-size-limit`. Raise the cap if the machine has the memory, delete data you no longer need, or split the graph across stores. The [errors reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/#engine-graph-size-cap) has the entry.
- **`This statement tried to commit a single WAL record of at least <used>.`** One commit's WAL record would be over the 64 MiB per-record cap, which is separate from the size limit. Commit the data in smaller transactions, such as batches of a bulk load ([WAL payload cap](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/#engine-wal-payload-cap)).
- **`Error: invalid --logical-graph-size-limit: semantic error: invalid memory limit unit 'kb'; use bytes, mb, mib, gb, or gib`, exit code 2.** The size has a unit relate doesn't accept. Write it in bytes or with one of the four units.
- **The process ends with no relate error while the graph grows.** The operating system stopped it for memory. Under the default `full` durability mode, every write it acknowledged is in the WAL and comes back on the next open ([Recover from a crash](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/crash-and-recovery/)). Size the machine from the open peak, and set a cap below it.

properties.heading: Measure a real store
properties.text:
`relate info` reads a store's metadata without opening it, including the node and relationship counts at its last [checkpoint](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#checkpoint). To follow along, create the shared example graph first:

```bash verify
cat > team.cypher <<'EOF'
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace);
EOF
relate query --database ./team.rl < team.cypher
```

Read its counts:

```bash verify
relate info --database ./team.rl
```

```text
layout: .rl bundle
superblock version: 1
codec: parquet
format version: 5
checkpoint LSN: 1
commit timestamp: 1
total bytes: 36864
wal segments past checkpoint: 1
nodes (at checkpoint LSN 1): 5
relationships (at checkpoint LSN 1): 5
indexes: 0
constraints: 0
```

The counts go straight into the estimate. To read the logical size itself, try a write against a size limit of 1 byte: the refusal reports the live size as `used`. `--load` with a new `--database` path does it on a copy, `probe.rl`, so the original store is never opened for writing:

```bash verify
relate --load ./team.rl --database ./probe.rl --logical-graph-size-limit 1 --mode envelope "CREATE (:Probe)"
```

The first two lines are stderr, the last is the error object on stdout:

```text
--load ./team.rl: loaded into ./probe.rl
capacity exceeded: used=6555 limit=1
{"error":{"code":"fatal_error","exit_code":1,"kind":"capacity","message":"capacity exceeded: used=6555 limit=1","retryable":false}}
```

The example graph is 6,403 logical bytes. Remove the copy when you're done:

```bash verify
rm ./probe.rl
```

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- `relate` on your `PATH` ([Install relate](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).
- Either the node, relationship, and property counts you expect, or a store to measure.

properties.heading: Related
properties.text:
- [Limits and sizing](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/storage/limits-and-sizing/): every limit relate enforces, with its default.
- [`--logical-graph-size-limit`](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/flags/#logical-graph-size-limit) in the flags reference.
- [Choose a durability mode](https://relatedb.ai/docs/guides/operate/durability-modes/): what a crash can lose while the graph is in memory.

properties.heading: Verify
properties.text:
Read the store under the same cap, read-only. The read runs, and the refused write left the 3 people as they were:

```bash verify
relate --database ./team.rl --read-only --logical-graph-size-limit 6500 --mode envelope "MATCH (p:Person) RETURN count(p) AS people"
```

```text
{"columnTypes":["INTEGER"],"columns":["people"],"notifications":[],"planCache":"miss","rows":[{"people":3}],"timings":{"elapsed_ms":0.34058299999999997,"execute_ms":0.164833,"lex_parse_ms":0.029375,"lower_ms":0.042624999999999996,"parse_ms":0.112292,"plan_ms":0.05450000000000001,"result_generation_ms":0.000292,"rewrite_ms":0.008417},"truncated":false}
```

properties.heading: Work an example
properties.text:
Take a memory graph for an agent: 1,000,000 `:Memory` nodes with an integer `id`, a 20-character `name` and an 8-character `kind`, 5,000,000 `RELATES_TO` relationships (5 out of each node) with an integer `since`, and a range index on `id`.

| Part                                                                                        | Count     | Bytes each | Logical bytes |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | ---------- | ------------- |
| Nodes: label, 3 properties, 28 bytes of strings (measured; the per-element table gives 500) | 1,000,000 | 502        | 502,000,000   |
| Relationships at 5 per node, 1 integer property                                             | 5,000,000 | 404        | 2,020,000,000 |
| Index entries on `id`                                                                       | 1,000,000 | 64         | 64,000,000    |
| Total                                                                                       |           |            | 2,586,000,000 |

A one-hundredth model of the same graph (10,000 nodes, 50,000 relationships, the same index) measured 25,901,217 logical bytes, which scales to 2,590,121,700: the estimate is within 0.2% of it.

properties.heading: Troubleshooting
properties.text: This guide shows you how to get from an error to its fix. Find the message in the tables, follow the reference link for the error's cause and exit code, and follow the fix link for the steps. Every row points at a page; the [errors reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/) holds the complete entry for each one.

properties.heading: Collect a report
properties.text:
When a row says to report, or no row fits, these four things let someone else reproduce the problem without your data:

| Part                                   | How to get it                                                                                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The relate version                     | `relate --version`; `relate --version --json` adds the operating system and architecture                                                                                         |
| The store's layout, format, and counts | `relate info --database <path> --json`, which reads metadata only: layout, format, counts, and each index and constraint with its label and property keys, never property values |
| The error object and exit code         | The failing command with `--mode envelope`, then `echo "exit=$?"`                                                                                                                |
| The statement and the flags            | The command line as run, with any `RELATE_` environment variables that were set                                                                                                  |

The version check prints two lines:

```bash verify
relate --version
```

```text
Relate v1.0.1
License: Apache 2.0 (binary)
```

properties.heading: If it goes wrong
properties.text:
- **The message is in no table.** Search the [errors reference](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/errors/) for its first words; it lists every error with its cause and remedy.
- **The exit code is 3, 4, or 8.** relate reserves those codes and doesn't produce them. Check which program in the pipeline returned it ([exit codes](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/cli/exit-codes-and-errors/)).
- **`internal error`.** An engine invariant failed, which is not the statement's fault. [Collect a report](#collect-a-report) with the statement that caused it.

properties.heading: Prerequisites
properties.text:
- The error's text from stderr and the command's [exit code](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#exit-code).
- `relate` on your `PATH` ([Install relate](https://relatedb.ai/docs/get-started/install/)).
- To follow along, the shared example graph as `team.rl`:

```bash verify
cat > team.cypher <<'EOF'
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada', role: 'engineer'}),
       (grace:Person {name: 'Grace', role: 'engineer'}),
       (noor:Person {name: 'Noor', role: 'maintainer'}),
       (relate:Project {name: 'relate', language: 'Rust'}),
       (tck:Project {name: 'opencypher-tck', language: 'Gherkin'}),
       (ada)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2024}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2023}]->(relate),
       (grace)-[:WORKS_ON {since: 2022}]->(tck),
       (noor)-[:MAINTAINS]->(relate),
       (ada)-[:KNOWS]->(grace);
EOF
relate query --database ./team.rl < team.cypher
```

properties.heading: Read the error
properties.text:
Run the failing command again with `--mode envelope` and print the exit code. In this example, the [store](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#store)'s name is misspelled, `tema.rl`, so a read-only open finds nothing to open:

```bash verify
relate --database ./tema.rl --read-only --mode envelope "MATCH (p:Person) RETURN count(p) AS people"
echo "exit=$?"
```

The path starts with the working directory, shown as `<dir>`. The first line is stderr, the second the [error object](https://relatedb.ai/docs/reference/glossary/#error-object) on stdout:

```text
Failed to open Relate: storage error: database not found: <dir>/tema.rl
{"error":{"code":"fatal_error","exit_code":1,"kind":"storage","message":"storage error: database not found: <dir>/tema.rl","retryable":false}}
exit=1
```

The error object's `code` is the class and `exit_code` the exit code, `kind` narrows the class, and `retryable` says whether running the same command again can succeed. `retryable` is `true` for a write-write conflict (exit 5) and for a `--concurrent-logical-workspace-limit` refusal while other statements hold the shared pool (exit 1, kind `resource`; reachable when statements run concurrently, as under `relate serve`). A one-shot CLI run meets only the first. A message's start is enough to find its row: `<name>` marks a part that varies, and `…` marks text left out.
